knowledge_statements.statement_title: Total convergence of sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines total convergence through cosmic compactification of Euclidean sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let C^
u\subset\mathbb R^n and let C\subset\mathbb R^n be closed. Then
\[C^
u\xrightarrow{\mathrm t}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{csm}C^
u\xrightarrow{\mathrm c}\operatorname{csm}C,\]
equivalently, \(C^
u\xrightarrow{\mathrm c}\operatorname{csm}C\) when the sets are viewed in \(\operatorname{csm}\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence of Euclidean sets converges totally to a closed set when its cosmic compactifications converge cosmically to the compactification of that set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous approximation of a subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines continuous approximation on X by Hausdorff continuity for every positive parameter and exact recovery from the convexified family limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A family \(Cf(\mathbf{x},\varepsilon)\) is a continuous approximation of \(\partial f\) on \(X\) if
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0,\quad Cf(\cdot,\varepsilon)\text{ is Hausdorff continuous on }X,
\]
and
\[
\forall\mathbf{x}\in X,\quad \partial f(\mathbf{x})=\operatorname{conv}C_Lf(\mathbf{x}).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family continuously approximates the subdifferential on X when it is Hausdorff continuous in x for every positive parameter and its convexified limit equals the subdifferential at every point of X.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall\varepsilon>0,\ Cf(\cdot,\varepsilon)\text{ is Hausdorff continuous on }X\bigr]\land\bigl[\forall\mathbf{x}\in X,\ \partial f(\mathbf{x})=\operatorname{conv}C_Lf(\mathbf{x})\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inner and Outer Limits of a Closed-Valued Multifunction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-based inner and outer limits, their common limit, and domain consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed-valued and define \(\operatorname{dist}(z,\Phi(x))=\inf_{v\in\Phi(x)}\|v-z\|\). Then \(\liminf_{y\to x}\Phi(y)=\{z:\lim_{y\to x}\operatorname{dist}(z,\Phi(y))=0\}\) and \(\limsup_{y\to x}\Phi(y)=\{z:\liminf_{y\to x}\operatorname{dist}(z,\Phi(y))=0\}\). With the source's limit convention, \(\liminf_{y\to x}\Phi(y)\subseteq\Phi(x)\subseteq\limsup_{y\to x}\Phi(y)\). Equality of the inner and outer limits defines \(\lim_{y\to x}\Phi(y)\). A nonempty inner limit implies \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\Phi)\), whereas a nonempty outer limit implies that a sequence of points in \(\operatorname{dom}\Phi\) converges to \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inner limit consists of points whose distance to the multifunction values tends to zero for all nearby arguments; the outer limit uses a lower-limit condition and captures approach along nearby arguments. Equality defines the multifunction limit. A nonempty inner limit forces the base point into the domain interior, while a nonempty outer limit only forces sequential approach by domain points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \liminf_{y\to x}\Phi(y)=\limsup_{y\to x}\Phi(y)\Rightarrow \lim_{y\to x}\Phi(y)\text{ exists};\quad \liminf_{y\to x}\Phi(y)\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\Phi).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any sequence of subsets of Euclidean space, the outer limit contains the points whose every neighborhood intersects infinitely many sets, while the inner limit contains the points whose every neighborhood intersects all sufficiently late sets. These are equivalently characterized by convergent subselections or eventual selections and by epsilon-enlargements. The distance to the empty set is identically infinity; for a nonempty set, the distance function is finite, continuous, and 1-Lipschitz.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood definitions at a point for multifunctions between Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Gamma:\mathbb R^nightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) and \(x^0\in\mathbb R^n\). It is upper semicontinuous at \(x^0\) if, for every open \(V\supseteq\Gamma(x^0)\), there exists an open \(U
i x^0\) such that \(\Gamma(x)\subseteq V\) for all \(x\in U\). It is lower semicontinuous at \(x^0\) if, for every open \(V\) satisfying \(\Gamma(x^0)\cap V
e\varnothing\), there exists an open \(U
i x^0\) such that \(\Gamma(x)\cap V
e\varnothing\) for all \(x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is upper semicontinuous at a point when all nearby images remain inside every open set containing the image at that point. It is lower semicontinuous when every open set meeting the image at that point also meets every sufficiently nearby image.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Gamma\text{ is upper or lower semicontinuous at }x^0\text{ according to the respective neighborhood condition.}

children.title: Cluster-Point Realizations
children.top_down_role: Realization of outer-limit membership through convergent selections.

assumptions_latex: \((C_n)\) is a sequence of subsets of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}C_n\) if and only if \(x\) is realized as a limit of selected points along an increasing subsequence.

notation.meaning: Outer set limit of the sequence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential realization of outer-limit membership in metric spaces.

source_refs.locator: A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in X\),
\[
x\in\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}C_n
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{there exist }n_k\uparrow\infty\text{ and }x_k\in C_{n_k}\text{ such that }x_k\to x.
\]
Thus outer-limit membership permits both the indices and the realizing points to be selected. Empty sets may occur, provided the selected indices correspond to nonempty sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point lies in the outer limit exactly when points from an infinite subsequence of the sets converge to it.

children.title: Escape Beyond Bounded Regions
children.top_down_role: Cluster behavior affected by selections escaping bounded regions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}C_n=\varnothing\) exactly when the sets eventually avoid every bounded region.

notation.meaning: Closed Euclidean ball of radius R

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional escape criterion; bounded compactness is essential.

source_refs.locator: A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The following conditions are equivalent:
\[
\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}C_n=\varnothing,
\]
and
\[
\text{for every }R>0\text{ there exists }N\in\mathbb N\text{ such that }C_n\cap\overline B(0,R)=\varnothing\text{ for all }n\ge N.
\]
Equivalently, every selection \(x_k\in C_{n_k}\) with \(n_k\uparrow\infty\) eventually leaves each bounded subset of \(\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, the outer limit is empty exactly when the sets eventually escape every bounded region.

children.title: Inner Set Limits
children.top_down_role: Lower limiting behavior of varying sets.

assumptions_latex: \((C_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) is a sequence of subsets of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}C_n\) consists exactly of points approached by every sufficiently late set.

notation.meaning: Distance from x to C, with distance to the empty set infinite

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-space definition of the Painlevé–Kuratowski inner limit.

source_refs.locator: A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The inner set limit of \((C_n)\) is
\[
\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}C_n
:=\left\{x\in X:\text{ for every }r>0\text{ there exists }N\in\mathbb N\text{ such that }C_n\cap B(x,r)\ne\varnothing\text{ for all }n\ge N\right\}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
x\in\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}C_n
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d(x,C_n)\to0,
\]
where \(d(x,\varnothing)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inner limit contains precisely the points approached by every sufficiently late set in the sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner Set Limits

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a sequence of open sets converging to an open limit in a specified topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (\Omega_n)_{n\in\mathbb N} be a sequence of open sets converging in a specified topology to an open set \Omega. The sequence has the compactivorous property if, for every compact set K\subset\Omega, there exists N\in\mathbb N such that K\subset\Omega_n for every n\ge N.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall K\subset\Omega\;\bigl(K\text{ compact}\implies\exists N\in\mathbb N\;\forall n\ge N,\ K\subset\Omega_n\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower semicontinuity and closedness of a set-valued map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential definitions for a multifunction between nonempty subsets of Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X and Y be nonempty subsets of Euclidean spaces and T:X\rightrightarrows Y. The map T is lower semicontinuous on X if, for every x\in X, every sequence x_n\to x in X, and every y\in T(x), there exist y_n\to y with y_n\in T(x_n) for all sufficiently large n; equivalently, T(x)\subseteq\operatorname*{Lim\,inf}_{n\to\infty}T(x_n). The map T is closed on X if \operatorname{gph}T is closed in X\times Y: whenever (x_n,y_n)\to(x,y) and y_n\in T(x_n) for every n, one has y\in T(x); equivalently, \operatorname*{Lim\,sup}_{n\to\infty}T(x_n)\subseteq T(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is lower semicontinuous when every point in a limiting value can be approximated by points in the nearby values. It is closed when every limit of graph points remains in its graph. These properties are respectively expressible through the Painlevé–Kuratowski lower and upper limits.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ and }Y\text{ are subsets of Euclidean spaces}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is lower semicontinuous iff }T(x)\subseteq\operatorname*{Lim\,inf}_{n}T(x_n),\quad T\text{ is closed iff }\operatorname*{Lim\,sup}_{n}T(x_n)\subseteq T(x).

notation.meaning: A point selected from the nth set

source_refs.locator: A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in X\),
\[
x\in\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}C_n
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{there exist }N\in\mathbb N\text{ and points }x_n\in C_n\text{ for all }n\ge N\text{ such that }x_n\to x.
\]
The selection uses every sufficiently large index, unlike an outer-limit realization, which may use only a subsequence.

children.title: Persistent Reachability
children.top_down_role: Persistence of nearby set points across the full limiting regime.

assumptions_latex: \((C_n)\) is a sequence of subsets of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A point belongs to the inner limit exactly when every neighborhood remains reachable from all sufficiently late sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood formulation, valid without a metric.

source_refs.locator: A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in X\), persistent reachability is the condition
\[
\forall U\in\mathcal N(x)\;\exists N_U\in\mathbb N\;\forall n\ge N_U:\quad U\cap C_n\ne\varnothing.
\]
The topological inner limit is exactly the set of persistently reachable points:
\[
\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}C_n
=\left\{x\in X:x\text{ satisfies persistent reachability}\right\}.
\]
The threshold \(N_U\) may depend on the neighborhood \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every neighborhood of an inner-limit point intersects all sufficiently late sets, with the threshold allowed to depend on the neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Reachability

source_witnesses.locator: A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The neighborhood formulation is mathematically coherent, but the cited variational-analysis page does not establish support for the asserted arbitrary-topological-space scope. A topology source with a precise definition or theorem locator is required.

children.title: Diagonal Selection
children.top_down_role: Diagonal techniques for coordinating multiple approximation requirements.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A diagonal block selection produces points \(x_n\in C_n\) converging to \(x\).

notation.meaning: Accuracy required on the jth block
First index of the jth block

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive diagonal realization of an inner-limit point.

source_refs.locator: A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose recursively \(1\le N_1<N_2<\cdots\) so that
\[
C_n\cap B(x,\varepsilon_j)\ne\varnothing
\quad\text{whenever }n\ge N_j.
\]
For each block \(N_j\le n<N_{j+1}\), select
\[
x_n\in C_n\cap B(x,\varepsilon_j).
\]
Then \(d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon_j\) on the \(j\)-th block, hence \(x_n\to x\). The output is the full-tail selection \((x_n)_{n\ge N_1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose increasingly late index blocks with shrinking neighborhood tolerances, then select one feasible point per index; the resulting diagonal sequence converges.
knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal Selection

source_witnesses.locator: A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Refined Ascoli–Arzelà theorem with countably many exceptional times
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise sequential compactness and continuity of a limit curve in a metric-topological setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $T>0$, let $K\subset\mathcal S$ be sequentially compact with respect to $\sigma$, and let $u_n:[0,T]\to\mathcal S$ satisfy $u_n(t)\in K$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$ and $t\in[0,T]$. Suppose that a symmetric function $\omega:[0,T]^2\to[0,+\infty)$ satisfies $\limsup_{n\to\infty}d(u_n(s),u_n(t))\leq\omega(s,t)$ for all $s,t\in[0,T]$, and $\lim_{(s,t)\to(r,r)}\omega(s,t)=0$ for every $r\in[0,T]\setminus\mathcal C$, where $\mathcal C$ is at most countable. Then there are a subsequence $(u_{n(k)})$ and a curve $u:[0,T]\to\mathcal S$ such that $u_{n(k)}(t)\overset{\sigma}{\rightharpoonup}u(t)$ for every $t\in[0,T]$, and $u$ is $d$-continuous on $[0,T]\setminus\mathcal C$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If metric-space-valued curves take values in a sequentially compact set and their limiting oscillations are controlled by a modulus that vanishes along the diagonal except at at most countably many times, then a subsequence converges pointwise in the sigma topology to a curve that is metric-continuous away from those exceptional times.
assumptions_latex: K\subset\mathcal S\text{ is sequentially compact with respect to }\sigma
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,n(k)\uparrow\infty,\ \exists\,u:[0,T]\to\mathcal S:\quad u_{n(k)}(t)\overset{\sigma}{\rightharpoonup}u(t)\ \forall t\in[0,T],\quad u\text{ is }d\text{-continuous on }[0,T]\setminus\mathcal C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ursescu Interior–Closure Identities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two dual identities for countable families in a complete metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a complete metric space. (i) For every sequence \((C_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) of closed subsets of \(\mathcal X\), \[\overline{\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}\operatorname{int}C_n}=\overline{\operatorname{int}\!\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}C_n\right)}.\] (ii) For every sequence \((C_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) of open subsets of \(\mathcal X\), \[\operatorname{int}\!\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}\overline{C_n}\right)=\operatorname{int}\overline{\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}C_n}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a complete metric space, the closure of the union of the interiors of any countable family of closed sets equals the closure of the interior of their union. Dually, the interior of the intersection of the closures of any countable family of open sets equals the interior of the closure of their intersection.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal X,d)\) is a complete metric space.
For (i), \((C_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) is a sequence of closed subsets of \(\mathcal X\).
For (ii), \((C_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) is a sequence of open subsets of \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \overline{\bigcup_n\operatorname{int}C_n}=\overline{\operatorname{int}(\bigcup_n C_n)}\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{int}(\bigcap_n\overline{C_n})=\operatorname{int}\overline{\bigcap_n C_n},\text{ respectively.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Kuratowski inner and outer limits for sequences and parameterized set families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential and domain-relative definitions, distance-function representations, closedness, inclusion, and convergence by equality of inner and outer limits in Euclidean spaces. The all-index sequence formulations require nonempty set values; equivalently, eventual membership makes the definitions insensitive to finitely many indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty sets A_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n, define
\[\liminf_{i\to\infty}A_i=\{x:\exists x_i\to x,\ x_i\in A_i\ \forall i\},\]
\[\limsup_{i\to\infty}A_i=\{x:\exists i_j\uparrow\infty,\ \exists x_j\to x,\ x_j\in A_{i_j}\ \forall j\}.\]
With \(d_A(x)=\inf_{y\in A}\lVert x-y\rVert\),
\[\liminf_iA_i=\{x:\limsup_i d_{A_i}(x)=0\},\qquad \limsup_iA_i=\{x:\liminf_i d_{A_i}(x)=0\}.\]
Both limit sets are closed, possibly empty, and
\[\liminf_iA_i\subseteq\limsup_iA_i.\]
When they coincide, their common value is the Kuratowski limit \(\lim_iA_i\).

For \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^k\), a nonempty-valued family \(S:D\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\), and a point \(x\) approachable from \(D\), write \(y_i\xrightarrow{D}x\) when \(y_i\in D\) and \(y_i\to x\). Then
\[\liminf_{y\xrightarrow{D}x}S(y)=\{\xi:\forall (y_i\xrightarrow{D}x)\ \exists\xi_i\to\xi,\ \xi_i\in S(y_i)\ \forall i\},\]
\[\limsup_{y\xrightarrow{D}x}S(y)=\{\xi:\exists y_i\xrightarrow{D}x,\ \exists\xi_i\to\xi,\ \xi_i\in S(y_i)\ \forall i\}.\]
Equivalently,
\[\liminf_{y\xrightarrow{D}x}S(y)=\{\xi:\limsup_{\substack{y\to x\\y\in D}}d_{S(y)}(\xi)=0\},\qquad \limsup_{y\xrightarrow{D}x}S(y)=\{\xi:\liminf_{\substack{y\to x\\y\in D}}d_{S(y)}(\xi)=0\}.\]
These sets are closed, possibly empty, and the inner limit is contained in the outer limit. Taking \(D=\{1,1/2,1/3,\ldots\}\), \(x=0\), and \(S(1/i)=A_i\) recovers the sequential definitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Kuratowski inner limit contains points that can be approximated using every set in the sequence, whereas the outer limit permits approximation along a subsequence. Distance functions characterize the two limits through limsup and liminf, respectively. Both limits are closed and possibly empty, the inner limit lies in the outer limit, and equality defines set convergence. For a set-valued family on a parameter domain, the localized inner limit requires approximation along every parameter sequence approaching the base point, while the localized outer limit requires one such sequence. The same distance characterizations and basic properties apply. The all-index formulations presume nonempty set values; eventual membership gives the corresponding tail-insensitive formulation.

x\in\overline D,\qquad y_i\xrightarrow{D}x\iff y_i\to x\text{ and }y_i\in D\ \forall i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \liminf_iA_i\subseteq\limsup_iA_i,\qquad \liminf_{y\xrightarrow{D}x}S(y)\subseteq\limsup_{y\xrightarrow{D}x}S(y),\quad\text{all four sets are closed (possibly empty), and convergence is defined by equality of the corresponding inner and outer limits.}

The convergence \(C_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{PK}}C\) holds if and only if both conditions are satisfied:

1. Whenever \(n_k\uparrow\infty\), \(x_k\in C_{n_k}\), and \(x_k\to x\), one has \(x\in C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With \(d(x,\varnothing):=+\infty\), the metric descriptions are
\[
\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}C_n
=\left\{x\in X:\liminf_{n\to\infty}d(x,C_n)=0\right\},
\]
and
\[
\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}C_n
=\left\{x\in X:\lim_{n\to\infty}d(x,C_n)=0\right\}.
\]
Consequently, if the two set limits coincide with \(C\), then \(d(x,C_n)\to0\) for every \(x\in C\), while every convergent selection from a subsequence has its limit in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In metric spaces, zero lower-limit distance characterizes the outer limit, while distance converging to zero characterizes the inner limit.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because every neighborhood of \(\omega_1\) meets \(A\), one has
\[
\omega_1\in\overline A
=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}C_n
=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}C_n.
\]
However, no sequence \((x_n)\subset A\) converges to \(\omega_1\): the supremum of countably many countable ordinals is a countable ordinal strictly below \(\omega_1\). Hence the topological set limits contain \(\omega_1\), but no point selection from the sets converges to it.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of compactness by closed sets and nets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Four equivalent compactness criteria for a subset of a Hausdorff space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathcal X\), where \(\mathcal X\) is Hausdorff. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topological spaces, continuity, compactness, and product topology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compound foundational statement covering elementary topology, product topology, and product compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A topology on a set X is a family \mathcal F\subseteq 2^X containing \varnothing and X, closed under finite intersections and arbitrary unions. A neighborhood of x is an open set containing x; C\subseteq X is closed iff X\setminus C is open. A map \phi:X\to Y is continuous iff \phi^{-1}(U) is open for every open U\subseteq Y, equivalently iff for every x\in X and every neighborhood U of \phi(x), some neighborhood W of x satisfies \phi(W)\subseteq U. A topology \mathcal F_2 is stronger than \mathcal F_1 iff \mathcal F_1\subseteq\mathcal F_2. A set C is compact iff every open cover of C has a finite subcover. The product topology on \prod_{i\in I}X_i is the weakest topology making every coordinate projection continuous; its basic open sets restrict only finitely many coordinates. If every X_i is compact, then \prod_{i\in I}X_i is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A topology contains the empty set and whole space and is closed under finite intersections and arbitrary unions. Closed sets have open complements, continuity is characterized by open preimages or neighborhoods, and compactness means every open cover has a finite subcover. The product topology is the weakest topology making all projections continuous, and every product of compact spaces is compact.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ and }Y\text{ are topological spaces when continuity is considered}.
\{X_i:i\in I\}\text{ is an arbitrary family of topological spaces when the product topology is considered}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \prod_{i\in I}X_i\text{ has the weakest topology making all projections continuous, and }(\forall i\in I,\ X_i\text{ compact})\Rightarrow\prod_{i\in I}X_i\text{ compact}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topological spaces, compactness, and convergence of nets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite foundational extract containing definitions, characterizations, and the subnet-inheritance fact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a set. A family \(\mathsf T\subseteq 2^{\mathcal X}\) is a topology if \(\varnothing,\mathcal X\in\mathsf T\) and \(\mathsf T\) is closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections; its members are open and their complements are closed. A neighborhood of \(x\) contains an open set containing \(x\). A subfamily \(\mathsf B\subseteq\mathsf T\) is a base if \((\forall x)(\forall V\in\mathcal V(x))(\exists B\in\mathsf B)\;x\in B\subseteq V\), in which case every open set is a union of members of \(\mathsf B\). For \(C\subseteq\mathcal X\), \(\operatorname{int}C\) is the largest open subset of \(C\), \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\iff(\exists V\in\mathcal V(x))\,V\subseteq C\); \(\overline C\) is the smallest closed superset of \(C\), \(x\in\overline C\iff(\forall V\in\mathcal V(x))\,V\cap C\ne\varnothing\); \(C\) is dense iff \(\overline C=\mathcal X\), and \(\operatorname{bdry}C=\overline C\setminus\operatorname{int}C\). If \(\mathsf B_i\) bases \(\mathcal X_i\), then \(\{B_1\times B_2:B_i\in\mathsf B_i\}\) bases the product topology. The space is Hausdorff iff distinct points have disjoint neighborhoods. In a Hausdorff space, \(C\) is compact iff every open cover of \(C\) has a finite subcover. A net \((x_a)_{a\in A}\) converges to \(x\) iff \((\forall V\in\mathcal V(x))(\exists b\in A)(\forall a\succcurlyeq b)\;x_a\in V\); every subnet of a convergent net converges to the same limit. A point \(x\) is a cluster point iff \((\forall V\in\mathcal V(x))(\forall b\in A)(\exists a\succcurlyeq b)\;x_a\in V\), equivalently iff some subnet converges to \(x\). A limit of a subsequence is a sequential cluster point of the original sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A topology contains the empty set and whole space and is closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. The extract defines open and closed sets, neighborhoods, bases, interiors, closures, dense sets, boundaries, product topology, Hausdorff separation, compactness by finite subcovers, convergence and cluster points of nets, and sequential cluster points. It also states that every subnet of a convergent net in a Hausdorff space has the same limit and that a point is a cluster point exactly when a subnet converges to it.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal X\text{ is a set and }\mathsf T\subseteq 2^{\mathcal X}.
A\text{ and }B\text{ are directed index sets whenever nets or subnets are considered}.
\mathcal X\text{ is Hausdorff for the stated compactness definition, uniqueness of limits, and subnet fact}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The displayed axioms and quantified conditions define the stated topological notions, and }x_a\to x\Rightarrow x_{k(b)}\to x\text{ for every subnet; moreover, cluster points are exactly subnet limits.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topological properties of set-valued mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects the extract's definitions and stated equivalences, preservation results, Hausdorff-limit property, and continuous outer-approximation theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a set-valued mapping $a:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m$, $\operatorname{dom}a=\{x:a(x)\ne\varnothing\}$, with a mapping on $\Omega$ extended by $a(x)=\varnothing$ outside $\Omega$. It is upper semicontinuous at $x$ when $\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists\delta>0\;\forall x'\in\mathcal B_\delta(x)$, $a(x')\subset a(x)+\mathcal B_\varepsilon$ (where $\varnothing+\mathcal B_\varepsilon=\varnothing$), closed at $x$ when $x_k\to x$, $y_k\to y$, and $y_k\in a(x_k)$ imply $y\in a(x)$, and bounded on $\Omega$ when $\bigcup_{x\in\xi}a(x)$ is bounded for every bounded $\xi\subset\Omega$. Local boundedness at $x$ makes closedness and upper semicontinuity at $x$ equivalent. If $a$ is upper semicontinuous and $f$ is continuous, then $q(x)=\max_{y\in a(x)}f(y)$ is upper semicontinuous. If every $a(x)$ is convex and compact, upper semicontinuity at $x$ is equivalent to upper semicontinuity there of every support function $q_\ell(x)=\max_{y\in a(x)}\langle\ell,y\rangle$, $\ell\in\mathbb R^m$. For nonempty compact sets, $\rho_H(\xi_1,\xi_2)=\max\{\max_{u\in\xi_1}\min_{v\in\xi_2}\|u-v\|,\max_{v\in\xi_2}\min_{u\in\xi_1}\|u-v\|\}$; if compact $\xi_{k+1}\subset\xi_k$ and $\xi=\bigcap_k\xi_k$, then $\rho_H(\xi_k,\xi)\to0$. A compact-valued mapping is continuous at $x$ when $\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists\delta>0$ such that $\rho_H(a(x),a(x'))<\varepsilon$ for all $x'\in\mathcal B_\delta(x)$. Finally, if $\Omega$ is compact and $a$ is bounded and upper semicontinuous with nonempty convex compact values, then for every $\delta,\mu>0$ there is a continuous nonempty convex compact-valued $b$ satisfying $a(x)\subset b(x)\subset a(x+\mathcal B_\delta)+\mathcal B_\mu$; when $\mu=\delta$, equivalently $\operatorname{gr}a\subset\operatorname{gr}b\subset\bar V_\delta(\operatorname{gr}a)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extract defines the domain, upper semicontinuity, closedness, boundedness, Hausdorff distance, and Hausdorff continuity of set-valued mappings. It states that local boundedness makes closedness and upper semicontinuity equivalent; upper semicontinuity is inherited by maximization of a continuous function and, for convex compact values, is characterized by all scalar support functions. Decreasing compact sets converge to their intersection in Hausdorff distance. A bounded upper-semicontinuous mapping on a compact domain with nonempty convex compact values admits arbitrarily close continuous convex compact-valued outer approximations.
assumptions_latex: \text{The individual assertions use the local boundedness, compactness, convexity, continuity, and upper-semicontinuity hypotheses stated above.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated definitions, equivalences, semicontinuity results, Hausdorff convergence property, and continuous outer-approximation inclusion hold.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x\) belongs to \(\operatorname{Ls}A_i\) if and only if there exist a subnet \((A_{i_j})_{j\in J}\) and selections \(x_j\in A_{i_j}\) with \(x_j\to x\). A point \(x\) belongs to \(\operatorname{Li}A_i\) if and only if, for every subnet \((A_{i_j})_{j\in J}\), there are a further subnet \((A_{i_{j_k}})_{k\in K}\) and selections \(x_k\in A_{i_{j_k}}\) such that \(x_k\to x\). Thus equality of these two net-defined sets characterizes Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequences suffice in first-countable spaces but not in arbitrary topological spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a first-countable space, membership in closures and topological set limits can be tested using sequences. This reduction fails in general. In the ordinal space \(X=[0,\omega_1]\), every neighborhood of \(\omega_1\) intersects \(C=[0,\omega_1)\), so \(\omega_1\in\overline C\). Every sequence in \(C\), however, has countable supremum strictly below \(\omega_1\), and therefore cannot converge to \(\omega_1\). Consequently a sequence-only outer-limit test can omit a point detected by the topological net-based outer limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First countability makes sequences adequate. The ordinal space up to the first uncountable ordinal shows that arbitrary spaces require nets.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The one-sided excess of \(A\) over \(B\) is \[e(A,B):=\sup_{a\in A}d(a,B),\qquad d(a,B):=\inf_{b\in B}d(a,b).\] Use the extended-real conventions \(e(\varnothing,B)=0\) and \(e(A,\varnothing)=+\infty\) when \(A\ne\varnothing\). The excess need not be symmetric and satisfies \(e(A,B)=0\) exactly when \(A\subset\overline B\). Its symmetrization is the extended Hausdorff distance \(d_H(A,B):=\max\{e(A,B),e(B,A)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be directed. The net \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) converges globally to \(A\) in the Pompeiu–Hausdorff sense when \[d_H(A_i,A)=\max\left\{\sup_{x\in A_i}d(x,A),\sup_{a\in A}d(a,A_i)\right\}\longrightarrow0.\] Equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), eventually both \(A_i\subset A^{\varepsilon}\) and \(A\subset A_i^{\varepsilon}\) hold, where \(C^{\varepsilon}:=\{x\in X:d(x,C)<\varepsilon\}\). The distance may be infinite before convergence, particularly for unbounded sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global Hausdorff convergence means that each set eventually lies within every positive uniform enlargement of the other.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Sobolev Compactness and Uniform Convergence of Distance Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies on a bounded open domain to ordinary and complementary distance-function families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb R^N\) be bounded and open. If \(\{d_{A_n}\}\) converges weakly in \(W^{1,p}(D)\) for some \(1\le p<\infty\), then it converges weakly in \(W^{1,q}(D)\) for every \(1\le q<\infty\). Convergence in \(C(\overline D)\) implies weak convergence in every \(W^{1,q}(D)\), and weak convergence in one finite-exponent \(W^{1,p}(D)\) implies convergence in \(C(\overline D)\). Moreover, \(C_d(D)\) is weakly compact in \(W^{1,p}(D)\) for every \(1\le p<\infty\). The same assertions hold for \(C_d^c(D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For distance functions on a bounded open domain, weak Sobolev convergence for one finite exponent gives weak convergence for every finite exponent and is equivalent to uniform convergence on the closure. The ordinary and complementary distance-function families are weakly compact for every stated finite exponent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{A_n}\rightharpoonup\text{ in some }W^{1,p}(D)\iff d_{A_n}\text{ converges in }C(\overline D)\), with weak convergence in every finite-exponent Sobolev space and weak compactness of \(C_d(D)\) and \(C_d^c(D)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gromov–Hausdorff Distance and Correspondence Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedding, correspondence, metric, and finite-space formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For metric spaces (\mathcal X,d_{\mathcal X}) and (\mathcal Y,d_{\mathcal Y}), \[d_{GH}(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y):=\inf_{\mathcal Z,f,g}\mathcal H_{\mathcal Z}(f(\mathcal X),g(\mathcal Y)),\] where f and g range over isometric embeddings into a common metric space \mathcal Z. Equivalently, \[d_{GH}(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y)=\frac12\inf_{R\in\mathcal R(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y)}\sup_{(x,y),(x',y')\in R}|d_{\mathcal X}(x,x')-d_{\mathcal Y}(y,y')|.\] On compact metric spaces this defines a metric on isometry classes, and d_{GH}(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y)=0 iff \mathcal X and \mathcal Y are isometric. For finite spaces with distance matrices D,D', the correspondence infimum may be taken over R\in\{0,1\}^{n\times m} satisfying R\mathbf1>0 and R^\top\mathbf1>0, with objective \frac12\max_{i,i',j,j'}R_{ij}R_{i'j'}|D_{ii'}-D'_{jj'}|.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gromov–Hausdorff distance minimizes the Hausdorff distance between common isometric embeddings. It is equivalently half the least distortion of a correspondence; for compact spaces it is a metric up to isometry, and finite correspondences admit a binary-matrix formulation.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal X,d_{\mathcal X})\text{ and }(\mathcal Y,d_{\mathcal Y})\text{ are metric spaces}
f:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Z\text{ and }g:\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Z\text{ are isometric embeddings}
\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\text{ are compact for the metric and zero-distance assertions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_{GH}=\inf_{\mathcal Z,f,g}\mathcal H_{\mathcal Z}(f(\mathcal X),g(\mathcal Y))=\frac12\inf_{R\in\mathcal R(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y)}\operatorname{dis}(R),\quad d_{GH}=0\iff\mathcal X\cong\mathcal Y\text{ for compact spaces}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract states the formula for arbitrary subsets of Euclidean space. Without additional nonemptiness and boundedness conditions or explicit extended-value conventions, the expression need not be a finite metric and empty sets require conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For sets \(A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), the Hausdorff distance is defined by
\[
d_H(A,B)=\max\left\{\sup_{a\in A}\inf_{b\in B}\lVert a-b\rVert,\;\sup_{b\in B}\inf_{a\in A}\lVert b-a\rVert\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hausdorff distance is the maximum of the two directed point-to-set excesses. For arbitrary sets it may require extended-value or empty-set conventions and need not be finite.

children.title: Localized Hausdorff Convergence
children.top_down_role: Hausdorff behavior restricted to local regions.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space with base point \(o\).
\((A_i)_{i\in I}\) and \(A\) are nonempty closed subsets of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_i\to_{LH}A\) iff \(\sup_{x\in B(o,R)}|d(x,A_i)-d(x,A)|\to0\) for every \(R>0\).

notation.meaning: Closed metric ball centered at o

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-function formulation of local Hausdorff convergence on bounded regions.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4, Set Convergence, pp. 108–117

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sets \(A_i\) converge to \(A\) in the localized Hausdorff sense when their distance functions converge uniformly on every bounded ball: \[\forall R>0,\qquad \sup_{x\in B(o,R)}\left|d(x,A_i)-d(x,A)\right|\longrightarrow0.\] Changing the base point does not change this convergence because every ball about one base point is contained in a sufficiently large ball about another. Unlike global Hausdorff convergence, this condition permits components of \(A_i\) to escape every bounded region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Localized Hausdorff convergence is uniform convergence of distance-to-set functions on every bounded ball and ignores components escaping to infinity.
knowledge_statements.title: Localized Hausdorff Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4, Set Convergence, pp. 108–117

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Uniform convergence of distance functions on bounded balls is a coherent convergence notion, but its identification as localized Hausdorff convergence and the exact hypotheses are not established by the broad cited range. A specific definition or equivalence result is needed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infimum and Minimizer Stability under Epi-Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimizers along convergent subsequences in a metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X be a metric space and let f_n:X\to\overline{\mathbb R} epi-converge to f. Then \limsup_{n\to\infty}\inf_{x\in X}f_n(x)\le\inf_{x\in X}f(x). Moreover, if n_k\to\infty, x_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f_{n_k}(x), and x_k\to x^*, then x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x) and \lim_{k\to\infty}\inf_{x\in X}f_{n_k}(x)=\inf_{x\in X}f(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epi-convergence bounds the limiting upper value of the infima by the infimum of the limit function. Any limit of exact minimizers along a subsequence is a minimizer of the limit function, and the corresponding infima converge to its infimum.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the second conclusion, }n_k\to\infty,\ x_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f_{n_k}(x),\text{ and }x_k\to x^*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \limsup_{n\to\infty}\inf_X f_n\le\inf_X f;\qquad x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_X f\ \text{ and }\ \lim_{k\to\infty}\inf_X f_{n_k}=\inf_X f

children.title: Bounded-Window Hausdorff Convergence
children.top_down_role: Hausdorff comparisons formed on bounded observation windows.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space with base point \(o\).
\(I\) is a directed set, \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) is a net of closed subsets of \(X\), and \(A\subset X\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At radius \(R>0\), bounded-window Hausdorff convergence means \(d_H(A_i\cap B(o,R),A\cap B(o,R))\to0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Raw truncation by a fixed closed ball, including possible boundary artifacts.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4, Set Convergence, pp. 108–117

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed \(R>0\), bounded-window Hausdorff convergence on \(B(o,R)\) is defined by \[d_H\bigl(A_i\cap B(o,R),A\cap B(o,R)\bigr)\longrightarrow0.\] The extended Hausdorff distance is used when a truncation is empty. Given radii \((R_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) with \(R_n\to\infty\), convergence on that exhaustion means that the displayed condition holds for every \(n\in\mathbb N\). Raw truncation can exhibit boundary artifacts because intersection with a closed ball need not preserve set convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded-window convergence applies Hausdorff distance after truncation by a fixed ball; convergence on an exhaustion requires this at every specified radius, and boundary points may cause discontinuities.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Window Hausdorff Convergence

children.title: Window-Exhaustion Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Consistency of bounded-window limits across expanding regions.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a proper metric space with base point \(o\).
\((A_i)_{i\in I}\) and \(A\) are nonempty closed subsets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All-radius window convergence implies localized distance convergence; the converse holds at radii \(R\) satisfying \(A\cap\partial B(o,R)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility in proper metric spaces, with exceptional truncation radii excluded.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4, Set Convergence, pp. 108–117

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \[d_H\bigl(A_i\cap B(o,R),A\cap B(o,R)\bigr)\longrightarrow0\] for every \(R>0\), then \(d(\cdot,A_i)\to d(\cdot,A)\) uniformly on every bounded ball. Conversely, localized uniform convergence of the distance functions implies the displayed truncated Hausdorff convergence for every radius \(R\) such that \(A\cap\partial B(o,R)=\varnothing\). Hence any increasing sequence of such regular radii tending to infinity provides a compatible window exhaustion; boundary-contact radii may fail compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exhaustive window convergence yields localized convergence; localized convergence recovers truncated Hausdorff convergence at radii where the limit set misses the boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Window-Exhaustion Compatibility

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4, Set Convergence, pp. 108–117

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatibility result needs an exact source and hypothesis check. In particular, regular radii with \(A\cap\partial B(o,R)=\varnothing\) need not admit an exhaustion: a closed set can meet every sufficiently large sphere. The concluding exhaustion assertion is therefore not valid without an additional existence hypothesis.

children.title: Hausdorff-to-Kuratowski Implications
children.top_down_role: Passage from Hausdorff convergence to Kuratowski convergence.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a directed set and \((X,d)\) is a metric space.
\((A_i)_{i\in I}\) is a net of nonempty subsets of \(X\), \(A\subset X\) is nonempty, and \(d_H(A_i,A)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Li}A_i=\operatorname{Ls}A_i=\overline A\); in particular, if \(A\) is closed, then \(A_i\to_{PK}A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Hausdorff convergence implies net-based Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence to the closure of the Hausdorff target.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4, Section B, Painlevé–Kuratowski Convergence, p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be directed, and suppose that \(d_H(A_i,A)\to0\). Then \[\operatorname{Li}A_i=\operatorname{Ls}A_i=\overline A.\] In particular, when \(A\) is closed, \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) converges to \(A\) in the Painlevé–Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global Hausdorff convergence forces the lower and upper Kuratowski limits to equal the closure of the Hausdorff target; a closed target is therefore the Painlevé–Kuratowski limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Hausdorff-to-Kuratowski Implications

children.title: Kuratowski-to-Hausdorff Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery of Hausdorff convergence from Kuratowski convergence.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a directed set and \((X,d)\) is a compact metric space.
\((A_i)_{i\in I}\) is a net of nonempty closed subsets of \(X\), and \(A\subset X\) is nonempty and closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery on the compact hyperspace of nonempty closed subsets.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4, Section B, Painlevé–Kuratowski Convergence, p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be directed. For nonempty closed subsets of a compact metric space, Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence and Hausdorff convergence coincide. In particular, if \[\operatorname{Li}A_i=\operatorname{Ls}A_i=A,\] then \[d_H(A_i,A)\longrightarrow0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a net of nonempty closed sets in a compact metric space, Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence to a nonempty closed set implies Hausdorff convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Kuratowski-to-Hausdorff Recovery

children.title: Compactness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Role of compactness in equivalence between the two convergence modes.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a directed set and \((X,d)\) is a metric space.
\((A_i)_{i\in I}\) is a net of nonempty closed subsets of one compact set \(K\subset X\), and \(A\subset K\) is nonempty and closed.
For the counterexample, \(X=\mathbb R\), \(A_n=\{0,n\}\) for \(n\in\mathbb N\), and \(A=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under common compact containment, \(A_i\to_{PK}A\) implies \(d_H(A_i,A)\to0\); without it, \(A_n\to_{PK}A\) while \(d_H(A_n,A)=n\not\to0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common compact containment prevents points from escaping undetected to infinity.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4, Set Convergence, pp. 108–117

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be directed. If the nonempty closed sets \(A_i\) and \(A\) are all contained in one compact subset of \(X\), then \[A_i\to_{PK}A\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d_H(A_i,A)	o0.\] Common compact containment is essential: in \(\mathbb R\), let \(A_n=\{0,n\}\) and \(A=\{0\}\). Then \[A_n\to_{PK}A,\qquad d_H(A_n,A)=n\not\to0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common compact containment converts Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence into Hausdorff convergence. Without it, points may escape to infinity while remaining invisible to the Painlevé–Kuratowski limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4, Set Convergence, pp. 108–117

children.title: Unbounded-Set Separation
children.top_down_role: Divergence of the convergence modes for unbounded sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_n\to C\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense, whereas \(d_H(C_n,C)=+\infty\) for every \(n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete escape-to-infinity obstruction separating Kuratowski and global Hausdorff convergence.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_n=\{0\}\cup[n,\infty)\) for \(n\in\mathbb N\), and let \(C=\{0\}\). Then \(C_n\to C\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense, but \(d_H(C_n,C)=+\infty\) for every \(n\). Thus an unbounded component escaping to infinity can be invisible to Kuratowski convergence while preventing global Hausdorff convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sets consisting of zero and a receding unbounded ray converge to {0} in the Kuratowski sense, but their Hausdorff distance from {0} is always infinite.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Set Separation

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Distance-Function Representations
children.top_down_role: Set convergence represented through associated distance profiles.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_n\to C\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense if and only if \(d(x,C_n)\to d(x,C)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to a nonempty set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equivalence between set convergence and pointwise convergence of distance profiles.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(n\), define \(d_{C_n}(x)=\inf_{y\in C_n}\|x-y\|\), and define \(d_C\) analogously. Then
\[
C_n\to C\ \text{in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
d_{C_n}(x)\to d_C(x)\ \text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^d.
\]
Thus a sequence of nonempty closed subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space is represented, for purposes of set convergence, by the pointwise convergence of its real-valued distance functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite-dimensional Euclidean space, closed sets converge in the Kuratowski sense exactly when their distance functions converge at every point.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Distance-Function Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unit Lipschitz Continuity of Set Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Euclidean Lipschitz property of the distance function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^k\) and all \(x,z\in\mathbb{R}^k\), \[\lvert d_C(x)-d_C(z)\rvert\leq \lvert x-z\rvert.\] Thus \(d_C\) is Lipschitz continuous with Lipschitz constant \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance function of any set is globally 1-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lvert d_C(x)-d_C(z)\rvert\leq\lvert x-z\rvert

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness of functional representations of a uniformly regular family of subsets of a bounded domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be nonempty, bounded, and open, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $r,\lambda>0$. Let $\mathcal O\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be open with $(0,e_N)\subset\mathcal O$ and $0\notin\mathcal O$, and suppose $L(D,r,\mathcal O,\lambda)\ne\varnothing$. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness of uniformly controlled C0-epigraph families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness for shape families whose boundaries admit uniformly controlled local continuous graph representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D\subset\mathbb R^N$ be nonempty, bounded, and open. Let $\rho>0$, let $U$ be a bounded open neighborhood of $0$ with $U\subset\{\zeta\in\mathbb R^N:P_H(\zeta)\in B_H(0,\rho)\}$, and set $V=B_H(0,\rho)$. Suppose every $\Omega\in L(D,\rho,U)$ has, at every $x\in\partial\Omega$, a rotated local $C^0$-epigraph representation with graph $a_x^\Omega:V\to\mathbb R$, $a_x^\Omega(0)=0$, and interior locally above the graph. For $h\in\mathcal H$, let $L_0$ consist of those shapes whose local graph functions are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous; let $L_1$ consist of those satisfying $a_x^\Omega(\zeta')\le h(|\zeta'|)$; and let $L_2$ consist of those satisfying $|a_x^\Omega(\xi')-a_x^\Omega(\zeta')|\le h(|\xi'-\zeta'|)$ whenever $|\xi'-\zeta'|<\rho$. Each of $L_0,L_1,L_2$ is possibly empty and has compact oriented-distance representations in $C(\overline D)$ and $W^{1,p}(D)$ for every $1\le p<\infty$; the corresponding ordinary-distance and indicator families satisfy all conclusions of Theorem 13.1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shape families with uniform local continuous epigraph descriptions have compact distance and indicator representations when their graph functions are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous, uniformly dominated, or controlled by the stated common modulus. The qualifying families may be empty.

U\text{ is a bounded open neighborhood of }0
\forall\Omega\in L(D,\rho,U)\ \forall x\in\partial\Omega,\ \partial\Omega\text{ and }\operatorname{int}\Omega\text{ have the stated rotated local }C^0\text{-epigraph representation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_0(D,\rho,U),\ L_1(D,\rho,U,h),\text{ and }L_2(D,\rho,U,h)\text{ are possibly empty families whose oriented-distance representations are compact in }C(\overline D)\text{ and }W^{1,p}(D),\text{ and all corresponding conclusions of Theorem 13.1 hold.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Localized Distance-Profile and Mutual-Enlargement Discrepancies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two radius-dependent discrepancies for nonempty subsets of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \rho\ge0 and nonempty C,D\subset\mathbb R^n, define \delta_\rho(C,D):=\max_{\|x\|\le\rho}|d_C(x)-d_D(x)| and \widehat\delta_\rho(C,D):=\inf\{\eta\ge0\mid C\cap\rho\mathbb B\subset D+\eta\mathbb B,\ D\cap\rho\mathbb B\subset C+\eta\mathbb B\}. In particular, \delta_0(C,D)=|d_C(0)-d_D(0)|. The quantity \delta_\rho is called the \rho-distance and is generally only a pseudodistance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radius-truncated distance-profile discrepancy is the maximum difference between the two distance functions on the ball of radius rho. The mutual-enlargement discrepancy is the smallest enlargement making each set's portion inside that ball lie in the enlargement of the other. At radius zero, the first discrepancy is the absolute difference of the distances from the origin.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Estimates for Localized Set Distances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity, comparison, stabilization, growth, and radius-continuity estimates for localized discrepancies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C_1,C_2\subset\mathbb R^n be nonempty and closed. Both \rho\mapsto\delta_\rho(C_1,C_2) and \rho\mapsto\widehat\delta_\rho(C_1,C_2) are nondecreasing, and \delta_\rho(C_1,C_2) is continuous in \rho. Moreover, \widehat\delta_\rho\le\delta_\rho\le\widehat\delta_{\rho'} whenever \rho'\ge2\rho+\max\{d_{C_1}(0),d_{C_2}(0)\}; if C_1\cup C_2\subset\rho_0\mathbb B, then \widehat\delta_\rho=\delta_\rho=\delta_{\rho_0} for all \rho\ge\rho_0; \delta_\rho\le\max\{d_{C_1}(0),d_{C_2}(0)\}+\rho; and |\delta_\rho-\delta_{\rho_0}|\le2|\rho-\rho_0|. For convex C_1,C_2, the term 2\rho in the comparison may be replaced by \rho. If they are convex and both contain 0, then \widehat\delta_\rho=\delta_\rho for every \rho\ge0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two localized discrepancies increase with the radius, and the distance-profile discrepancy varies continuously and is 2-Lipschitz in the radius. They bound each other after enlarging the comparison radius, stabilize once both sets lie in a fixed ball, and satisfy a linear growth bound. Convexity improves the required enlargement, and convex sets containing the origin make the discrepancies equal at each radius.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat\delta_\rho(C_1,C_2)\le\delta_\rho(C_1,C_2)\le\widehat\delta_{\rho'}(C_1,C_2)\quad\text{if }\rho'\ge2\rho+\max\{d_{C_1}(0),d_{C_2}(0)\},\qquad |\delta_\rho-\delta_{\rho_0}|\le2|\rho-\rho_0|

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With \(d_A(x)=\inf_{a\in A}d(x,a)\) and \(d_B(x)=\inf_{b\in B}d(x,b)\), the extended identity
\[
d_H(A,B)=\sup_{x\in X}\lvert d_A(x)-d_B(x)\rvert
\]
holds. Consequently, for nonempty sets \(C_n,C\subset X\),
\[
d_H(C_n,C)\to0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sup_{x\in X}\lvert d(x,C_n)-d(x,C)\rvert\to0.
\]
Hence Pompeiu--Hausdorff convergence is precisely global uniform convergence of the associated distance functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hausdorff distance equals the global sup-norm difference of distance functions; therefore Hausdorff convergence is exactly uniform distance-function convergence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topology of Geometrically Constrained Distance-Function Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preserves the closedness and openness conditions on the target set and the compactness conditions required for intersection or containment classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\ne\varnothing\) be open in \(\mathbb R^N\), and define
\[
H(S)=\{d_A\in C_d(D):S\subset\overline A\},\quad I(S)=\{d_A\in C_d(D):\overline A\subset S\},\quad J(S)=\{d_A\in C_d(D):\overline A\cap S\ne\varnothing\}.
\]
In \(C_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)\), or in \(C(\overline D)\) when \(D\) is bounded: (a) \(H(S)\) is closed for every \(S\); (b) if \(S\) is closed, then \(I(S)\) is closed, and if additionally \(S\cap\overline D\) is compact, then \(J(S)\) is closed; (c) if \(S\) is open, then \(J(S)\) is open, and if additionally \((\mathbb R^N\setminus S)\cap\overline D\) is compact, then \(I(S)\) is open. If \(D\) is bounded, the map \([A]_d\mapsto\#(\overline A)\) on classes having finitely many connected components is lower semicontinuous, and for every \(c>0\), \(\{d_A\in C_d(D):\#(\overline A)\le c\}\) is compact; in particular, the class for which \(\overline A\) is connected is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Containment and intersection constraints define open or closed families under distance-function convergence under the stated closedness, openness, and compactness assumptions. On bounded holdalls, finite component count is lower semicontinuous, and bounded-component-count classes, including connected sets, are compact.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ closed for the closedness conclusions concerning }I(S)\text{ and }J(S)
S\text{ open for the openness conclusions concerning }J(S)\text{ and }I(S)
D\text{ bounded for the component-count conclusions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H(S)\text{ is closed};\quad S\text{ closed}\Rightarrow I(S)\text{ is closed};\quad S\text{ closed and }S\cap\overline D\text{ compact}\Rightarrow J(S)\text{ is closed};\quad S\text{ open}\Rightarrow J(S)\text{ is open};\quad S\text{ open and }S^c\cap\overline D\text{ compact}\Rightarrow I(S)\text{ is open};\quad D\text{ bounded}\Rightarrow \#(\overline A)\text{ is lower semicontinuous and its stated sublevel classes are compact}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementary Hausdorff Metric
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines complement-distance representations of open subsets and the metric induced on a bounded holdall.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\ne\varnothing\) be open in \(\mathbb R^N\). Define \(\mathcal G(D)=\{\Omega\subset D:\Omega\text{ is open and }\Omega\ne\mathbb R^N\}\) and \(C_d^c(D)=\{d_{\mathbb R^N\setminus\Omega}:\Omega\in\mathcal G(D)\}\). If \(D\) is bounded, define
\[
\rho_H^c(\Omega_2,\Omega_1)=\left\|d_{\mathbb R^N\setminus\Omega_2}-d_{\mathbb R^N\setminus\Omega_1}\right\|_{C(D)}.
\]
For \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset D\), the complement-distance functions vanish on \(\mathbb R^N\setminus D\), and equality on \(D\) holds if and only if \(\Omega_1=\Omega_2\). Hence \(\rho_H^c\) separates points of \(\mathcal G(D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open subset of a holdall is represented by the distance function to its complement. On a bounded holdall, the uniform difference between two complement-distance functions defines the complementary Hausdorff metric and distinguishes the open sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_H^c(\Omega_2,\Omega_1)=\left\|d_{\mathbb R^N\setminus\Omega_2}-d_{\mathbb R^N\setminus\Omega_1}\right\|_{C(D)},\qquad \rho_H^c(\Omega_2,\Omega_1)=0\iff\Omega_1=\Omega_2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hausdorff and Locally Uniform Set Metrics via Distance Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes closure-based equivalence classes, the bounded Hausdorff identity, and the compact-exhaustion metric for open unbounded holdalls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty set \(D\subset\mathbb R^N\), define \([A]_d=\{B\subset\overline D:\overline B=\overline A\}\) and \(\mathcal F_d(D)=\{[A]_d:\varnothing\ne A\subset\overline D\}\). The map \([A]_d\mapsto d_A\) is injective. If \(D\) is bounded, then
\[
\rho([A]_d,[B]_d)=\sup_{x\in D}|d_A(x)-d_B(x)|=\max\left\{\sup_{x\in B}d_A(x),\sup_{y\in A}d_B(y)\right\}=\rho_H([A]_d,[B]_d).
\]
If \(D\) is open, set \(K_k=\{x\in D:d_{\mathbb R^N\setminus D}(x)\ge k^{-1},\ \|x\|\le k\}\), \(q_{K_k}(f)=\max_{x\in K_k}|f(x)|\), and
\[
\rho_\delta([A]_d,[B]_d)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{-k}\frac{q_{K_k}(d_A-d_B)}{1+q_{K_k}(d_A-d_B)}.
\]
This metric represents locally uniform convergence of the distance profiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sets with the same closure are represented by the same distance function. On a bounded holdall, the uniform distance between their distance profiles equals Hausdorff distance. On an open unbounded holdall, a weighted compact-exhaustion metric represents locally uniform convergence of the profiles.
assumptions_latex: D\text{ is open for the compact-exhaustion metric}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [A]_d\mapsto d_A\text{ is injective},\qquad D\text{ bounded}\Rightarrow\rho=\rho_H,\qquad D\text{ open}\Rightarrow\rho_\delta=\delta(d_A,d_B).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fundamental Properties of Set Distance Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Properties of the Euclidean distance function for nonempty, not necessarily closed, sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B\subset\mathbb R^N\) be nonempty. Then \(d_A\) is globally \(1\)-Lipschitz. For every \(x\in\mathbb R^N\), some \(p\in\overline A\) satisfies \(d_A(x)=\lVert p-x\rVert\), and \(d_A=d_{\overline A}\). Moreover, \(\overline A=\{x:d_A(x)=0\}\), \(d_A\equiv0\iff\overline A=\mathbb R^N\), \(\overline A\subset\overline B\iff d_A\ge d_B\), and \(d_{A\cup B}=\min\{d_A,d_B\}\). Finally, \(d_A\) is Fréchet differentiable almost everywhere and \(\lVert\nabla d_A\rVert\le1\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty set's distance function is 1-Lipschitz, attains its distance at a point of the closure, depends only on the closure, and vanishes exactly on that closure. Closure inclusion reverses the pointwise order of distance functions, distance to a union is the pointwise minimum, and the distance function is differentiable almost everywhere with gradient norm at most one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |d_A(y)-d_A(x)|\le\lVert y-x\rVert;\quad d_A=d_{\overline A};\quad \overline A=\{d_A=0\};\quad \overline A\subset\overline B\iff d_A\ge d_B;\quad d_{A\cup B}=\min\{d_A,d_B\};\quad \lVert\nabla d_A\rVert\le1\ \text{a.e.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The distance functions of \(C_n\) converge locally uniformly to the distance function of \(C\) when, for every finite \(R>0\),
\[
\sup_{x\in\overline B_R(x_0)}
\lvert d(x,C_n)-d(x,C)\rvert\longrightarrow0.
\]
Equivalently, convergence is uniform on every bounded subset of \(X\). Replacing \(x_0\) by another base point gives the same condition because every ball about either base point is contained in a sufficiently large ball about the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance functions converge locally uniformly when their maximum difference tends to zero on every bounded ball; this does not depend on the chosen base point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pompeiu–Hausdorff characterization of multifunction continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requires local boundedness at the reference point and nonempty closed values throughout a neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) be locally bounded at \(\bar x\), and suppose \(S(x)\) is nonempty and closed for every \(x\) in some neighborhood of \(\bar x\). Then \(S\) is continuous at \(\bar x\) if and only if \(d_\infty(S(x),S(\bar x))\to0\) as \(x\to\bar x\), where \(d_\infty\) is the Pompeiu--Hausdorff distance.

children.title: Globalization Criteria
children.top_down_role: Conditions linking locally uniform behavior to global uniform behavior.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space with base point \(x_0\).
\(d(\cdot,C_n)\to d(\cdot,C)\) uniformly on every bounded ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(\cdot,C_n)\to d(\cdot,C)\) uniformly on \(X\) if and only if \(\lim_{R\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{x\in X\setminus\overline B_R(x_0)}e_n(x)=0\), with the supremum over the empty set defined as \(0\).

notation.meaning: Closed ball of radius R about the base point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: An exact tail criterion for upgrading bounded-ball uniform convergence to global uniform convergence.

source_refs.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(e_n(x)=\lvert d(x,C_n)-d(x,C)\rvert\). Under uniform convergence on every bounded ball, global uniform convergence holds if and only if
\[
\lim_{R\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\sup_{x\in X\setminus\overline B_R(x_0)}e_n(x)=0.
\]
Here the supremum over the empty set is defined as \(0\). In particular, if \(X\) is bounded, local uniform convergence is global uniform convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local uniform convergence becomes global exactly when distance-profile errors are asymptotically negligible outside sufficiently large balls; on bounded spaces globalization is automatic.
knowledge_statements.title: Globalization Criteria

\[
\sup_{x\in K}\lvert d(x,C_n)-d(x,C)\rvert\longrightarrow0.
\]
Consequently, \(C_n\to C\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For distance profiles of nonempty closed Euclidean sets, convergence on a dense test set forces uniform convergence on every compact set and hence Kuratowski convergence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric characterization and completion of total set convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes total convergence of Euclidean closed sets through the cosmic metric and identifies the topology and completion of the resulting hyperspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The restriction of \(d_{\mathrm{csm}}\) to \(\operatorname{cl\text{-}sets}(\mathbb{R}^n)\) is a metric, and for every sequence \(C^\nu\) and every \(C\) in this space,
\[
C^\nu\xrightarrow{\mathrm t}C
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
d_{\mathrm{csm}}(C^\nu,C)\to0.
\]

children.title: Fell Topology
children.top_down_role: Fell-topological convergence of closed sets.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a locally compact Hausdorff space.
\(\mathcal F(X)\) denotes all closed subsets of \(X\), including \(\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Fell topology is generated by open-set hit conditions and compact-set miss conditions.

notation.meaning: The family of closed sets hitting U.
The family of closed sets missing K.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-set hyperspace definition by hit-open and miss-compact subbasic neighborhoods.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every open set \(U\subset X\) and compact set \(K\subset X\), define
\[
U^- =\{F\in\mathcal F(X):F\cap U\neq\varnothing\},
\qquad
K^+ =\{F\in\mathcal F(X):F\cap K=\varnothing\}.
\]
The Fell topology on \(\mathcal F(X)\) is the topology having all sets \(U^-\) and \(K^+\) as a subbasis. Thus its lower component records intersection with open sets, while its upper component records avoidance only of compact sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fell topology on closed sets is generated by requiring a set to hit specified open sets or miss specified compact sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Fell Topology

children.title: Vietoris Topology
children.top_down_role: Vietoris-topological convergence of set families.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F(X)\) denotes all closed subsets of \(X\), including \(\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Vietoris topology is generated by lower hit sets \(U^-\) and upper containment sets \(U^+\) for open \(U\subset X\).

notation.meaning: The family of closed sets hitting U.
The family of closed sets contained in U.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard full Vietoris topology on the hyperspace of closed subsets.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every open set \(U\subset X\), define
\[
U^- =\{F\in\mathcal F(X):F\cap U\neq\varnothing\},
\qquad
U^+ =\{F\in\mathcal F(X):F\subset U\}.
\]
The Vietoris topology on \(\mathcal F(X)\) is generated by all lower sets \(U^-\) and upper sets \(U^+\). Equivalently, a basic neighborhood imposes finitely many open-set hit requirements together with containment in one open set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Vietoris topology is generated by conditions requiring a closed set to hit chosen open sets and to lie inside a chosen open set.

children.title: Fell–Vietoris Comparison
children.top_down_role: Agreement and separation of the two hyperspace topologies.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F(X)\) is the hyperspace of all closed subsets of \(X\), equipped with the Fell topology \(\tau_F\) and the Vietoris topology \(\tau_V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_F\subseteq\tau_V\); if \(X\) is compact, then \(\tau_F=\tau_V\).

notation.meaning: Fell topology on the closed-set hyperspace.
Vietoris topology on the closed-set hyperspace.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison on the full closed-set hyperspace of a Hausdorff space.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be Hausdorff, and let \(\tau_F\) and \(\tau_V\) denote, respectively, the Fell and Vietoris topologies on \(\mathcal F(X)\). Then
\[
\tau_F\subseteq\tau_V.
\]
If \(X\) is compact, then
\[
\tau_F=\tau_V.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Hausdorff space the Fell topology is no finer than the Vietoris topology, and if the ambient space is compact the two topologies coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Fell–Vietoris Comparison

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_n\) converges to \(C\) in the Wijsman sense exactly when \(d(x,C_n)\to d(x,C)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric hyperspace convergence defined by pointwise distance-profile convergence.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sequence \((C_n)\) converges to \(C\) in the Wijsman sense, written \(C_n\to_W C\), when
\[
\forall x\in X,\qquad d(x,C_n)\longrightarrow d(x,C),
\]
where \(d(x,A)=\inf_{a\in A}d(x,a)\). Equivalently, the Wijsman topology on the nonempty closed subsets of \(X\) is the initial topology induced by the evaluation maps \(A\mapsto d(x,A)\) for all \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Wijsman convergence means pointwise convergence, at every ambient point, of the distance functions associated with nonempty closed sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Wijsman Convergence

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space with base point \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Attouch--Wets convergence is uniform convergence of distance profiles on every bounded ball.

notation.meaning: Closed ball of radius R about the base point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-uniform distance-profile definition on nonempty closed subsets of a metric space.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sequence \((C_n)\) converges to \(C\) in the Attouch--Wets sense, written \(C_n\to_{AW}C\), if for every finite \(R>0\),
\[
\sup_{x\in\overline B_R(x_0)}
\lvert d(x,C_n)-d(x,C)\rvert\longrightarrow0.
\]
The resulting convergence notion is independent of the selected base point \(x_0\). It strengthens Wijsman convergence by replacing pointwise convergence of distance profiles with uniform convergence on every bounded part of the ambient metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Attouch–Wets convergence is uniform convergence of set-distance functions on every bounded ball, independently of the chosen base point.

u	o C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{dl}(C^

children.title: Truncated Set Metrics
children.top_down_role: Set metrics formed through bounded truncation.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space with base point \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(R>0\), \(\delta_R\) is a bounded pseudometric, and \(\delta_R(A,B)=0\) for every \(R>0\) implies \(A=B\).

notation.meaning: Closed radius-R ball about the base point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-ball pseudometrics used to quantify local distance-profile agreement.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(R>0\), define
\[
\delta_R(A,B)=\min\left\{1,\sup_{x\in\overline B_R(x_0)}
\lvert d(x,A)-d(x,B)\rvert\right\}.
\]
Each \(\delta_R\) is a bounded pseudometric on the nonempty closed subsets of \(X\). The family \(\{\delta_R:R>0\}\) separates such sets: if \(\delta_R(A,B)=0\) for every \(R>0\), then \(A=B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bounded-ball, truncated sup discrepancy of distance profiles defines a bounded pseudometric for each radius, and the complete family distinguishes nonempty closed sets.

The weighted set metric is \[d_w(C,D)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}w_k\delta_k(C,D).\] It is a finite-valued metric on \(\mathcal F(X)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Estimates for the integrated set distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds relating the integrated metric, its radius-truncated pseudometrics, and the distances of the sets from the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For all nonempty closed \(C_1,C_2\subset\mathbb R^n\) and all \(\rho\geq0\), \[\operatorname{dl}(C_1,C_2)\geq(1-e^{-\rho})\lvert d_{C_1}(0)-d_{C_2}(0)\rvert+e^{-\rho}\operatorname{dl}_\rho(C_1,C_2),\] \[\operatorname{dl}(C_1,C_2)\leq(1-e^{-\rho})\operatorname{dl}_\rho(C_1,C_2)+e^{-\rho}\bigl(\max\{d_{C_1}(0),d_{C_2}(0)\}+\rho+1\bigr),\] and consequently \[\lvert d_{C_1}(0)-d_{C_2}(0)\rvert\leq\operatorname{dl}(C_1,C_2)\leq\max\{d_{C_1}(0),d_{C_2}(0)\}+1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any two nonempty closed sets and any nonnegative truncation radius, the integrated distance has lower and upper estimates in terms of the truncated distance and the two sets' distances from the origin. In particular, it lies between the absolute difference of those origin distances and their maximum plus one.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Completeness of an intersection of nested metric groups
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General countable-intersection result underlying smooth transformation-group constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{Let }(\mathcal F_k,d_k),\ k\ge0,\text{ be complete metric groups with }\mathcal F_{k+1}\subset\mathcal F_k\text{ and }d_k(F,G)\le d_{k+1}(F,G)\text{ for all }F,G\in\mathcal F_\infty:=\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathcal F_k.\text{ Define }d_\infty(F,G)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}2^{-k}\frac{d_k(F,G)}{1+d_k(F,G)}.\text{ Then }(\mathcal F_\infty,d_\infty)\text{ is a complete metric group. If every }(\mathcal F_k,d_k)\text{ is a topological group, then }(\mathcal F_\infty,d_\infty)\text{ is a topological group}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested intersection of complete metric groups is complete for the bounded weighted sum of the level metrics, provided those metrics are monotone on the intersection. If multiplication and inversion are continuous at every level, they remain continuous on the intersection.
assumptions_latex: \forall k\ge0,\ (\mathcal F_k,d_k)\text{ is a complete metric group}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mathcal F_\infty,d_\infty)\text{ is complete; if all }\mathcal F_k\text{ are topological groups, then }\mathcal F_\infty\text{ is a topological group}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Completeness and quotient geometry of Micheletti transformation groups
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers the specified bounded, smooth, compactly supported, and Lipschitz-derivative regularity classes, with topological-group status only for the stated C-classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{Let }\Theta\in\{\mathcal B^k(\mathbb R^N,\mathbb R^N),C^k(\overline{\mathbb R^N},\mathbb R^N),C_0^k(\mathbb R^N,\mathbb R^N),C^{k,1}(\overline{\mathbb R^N},\mathbb R^N):k\ge0\}\cup\{C^\infty(\overline{\mathbb R^N},\mathbb R^N),C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^N,\mathbb R^N)\}.\text{ Then }(\mathcal F(\Theta),d)\text{ is a complete right-invariant metric group. If }\Theta=C^k\text{ or }C_0^k\text{ for }0\le k\le\infty,\text{ it is also a topological group. For every closed subgroup }\mathcal G,\ d_{\mathcal G}(F\mathcal G,H\mathcal G):=\inf_{G\in\mathcal G}d(F,H\circ G)\text{ is a complete right-invariant metric on }\mathcal F(\Theta)/\mathcal G\text{ inducing its quotient topology. Moreover, if }\varnothing\ne\Omega_0\subset\mathbb R^N\text{ is closed or }\Omega_0=\operatorname{int}\overline{\Omega_0},\text{ then }\mathcal G(\Omega_0):=\{F\in\mathcal F(\Theta):F(\Omega_0)=\Omega_0\}\text{ is a closed subgroup}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each specified finite- or infinite-regularity perturbation space, the associated transformation group is complete under its right-invariant metric. The C^k and compactly supported C^k cases are also topological groups. Quotients by closed subgroups carry the complete right-invariant infimum metric with the quotient topology, and the subgroup preserving a nonempty closed or interior-of-closure set is closed.
assumptions_latex: \Theta\text{ is one of the explicitly listed regularity spaces}
\mathcal G\text{ is a closed subgroup of }\mathcal F(\Theta)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F(\Theta)\text{ is complete and right-invariantly metrized; the stated }C^k\text{ cases are topological groups; }\mathcal F(\Theta)/\mathcal G\text{ is complete with the quotient topology; and }\mathcal G(\Omega_0)\text{ is closed}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complete quotient metric induced by a closed subgroup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General quotient construction for a complete group carrying a right-invariant metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{Let }(\mathcal F,d)\text{ be a group with a complete right-invariant metric and let }\mathcal G\le\mathcal F\text{ be closed. Define }d_{\mathcal G}(F\mathcal G,H\mathcal G):=\inf_{G\in\mathcal G}d(F,H\circ G).\text{ Then }d_{\mathcal G}\text{ is a right-invariant metric on }\mathcal F/\mathcal G,\ (\mathcal F/\mathcal G,d_{\mathcal G})\text{ is complete, and its metric topology equals the quotient topology}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed subgroup of a group with a complete right-invariant metric induces, by minimizing distance over subgroup representatives, a complete right-invariant metric on the coset space. This metric generates exactly the quotient topology.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_{\mathcal G}\text{ is a complete right-invariant quotient metric and }\tau(d_{\mathcal G})=\tau_{\mathrm{quot}}.
