knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth transformation groups as intersections of finite-regularity groups
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the smooth function spaces and their associated perturbation-of-identity groups, records their Fréchet boundary, and represents them as nested intersections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \mathcal B(\mathbb R^N,\mathbb R^N)=\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathcal B^k(\mathbb R^N,\mathbb R^N)=\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}C^k(\overline{\mathbb R^N},\mathbb R^N),\qquad C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^N,\mathbb R^N)=\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}C_0^k(\mathbb R^N,\mathbb R^N).\n\mathcal F(\Theta):=\{I+f:f\in\Theta,\ I+f\text{ bijective},\ (I+f)^{-1}-I\in\Theta\}.\n\mathcal F(\mathcal B)=\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathcal F(\mathcal B^k)=\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathcal F(C^k),\qquad \mathcal F(C_0^\infty)=\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathcal F(C_0^k),\qquad d_k(F,G)\le d_{k+1}(F,G).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smooth and compactly supported smooth perturbation spaces are intersections of their finite-regularity counterparts. Their groups of bijective perturbations of the identity, with inverses in the same class, are likewise intersections of the corresponding finite-regularity groups. The finite-level groups are metric topological groups and their metrics increase with regularity. The smooth spaces are Fréchet rather than Banach, so assumptions requiring a Banach space do not apply directly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F(\Theta)=\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathcal F(\Theta_k),\quad d_k\le d_{k+1},\quad \Theta\text{ is Fréchet but not Banach}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness under Uniform Fat-Segment and Perimeter Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness of oriented-distance, ordinary-distance, boundary-distance, and characteristic-function representations of the admissible shapes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subset\mathbb R^N\) be nonempty, bounded, and open, let \(1\le p<\infty\), and let \(r,\lambda,c'>0\). Let \(\mathcal O\subset\mathbb R^N\) be bounded and open, with \((0,e_N)\subset\mathcal O\) and \(0\notin\mathcal O\), and assume \(L(D,r,\mathcal O,\lambda,c')\ne\varnothing\). Then
\[
\{b_\Omega:\Omega\in L(D,r,\mathcal O,\lambda,c')\}
\]
is compact in \(C(\overline D)\) and in \(W^{1,p}(D)\). The same holds for
\[
\{d_\Omega\},\qquad \{d_{\complement\Omega}\},\qquad \{d_{\partial\Omega}\},
\]
where each family is indexed by \(\Omega\in L(D,r,\mathcal O,\lambda,c')\). Moreover,
\[
\{\chi_\Omega:\Omega\in L(D,r,\mathcal O,\lambda,c')\},\qquad
\{\chi_{\complement\Omega}:\Omega\in L(D,r,\mathcal O,\lambda,c')\}
\]
are compact in \(L^p(D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated geometric and perimeter assumptions, the oriented-distance, set-distance, complement-distance, and boundary-distance families are compact in both the continuous and Sobolev topologies. The shape and complement indicator families are compact in Lp.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global bounded-curvature compactness for distance functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness for nonempty subsets of a bounded Lipschitz holdall under a uniform global Hessian-measure bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb R^N\) be nonempty, bounded, open, and Lipschitz, and let \(\varnothing\ne A_n\subset\overline D\). If \(\|D^2d_{A_n}\|_{M^1(D)}\le c\) for every \(n\), then there exist a subsequence \((A_{n_k})\) and a nonempty set \(A\) such that \(\nabla d_A\in BV(D)^N\) and \(d_{A_{n_k}}\to d_A\) strongly in \(W^{1,p}(D)\) for every \(1\le p<\infty\). Moreover, \(\partial_{ij}d_{A_{n_k}}\to\partial_{ij}d_A\) distributionally on \(D\) for all \(1\le i,j\le N\), and \(\|D^2d_A\|_{M^1(D)}\le c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform Hessian-measure bound for distance functions of nonempty subsets of a bounded Lipschitz holdall yields a subsequence converging strongly in every finite-exponent W1,p space. The limit has BV distance gradient, distributional Hessian convergence, and the same curvature bound.
assumptions_latex: \(\varnothing\ne D\subset\mathbb R^N\) is bounded, open, and Lipschitz
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists (n_k),\exists A\ne\varnothing:\ \nabla d_A\in BV(D)^N,\ \forall 1\le p<\infty,\ d_{A_{n_k}}\to d_A\text{ strongly in }W^{1,p}(D),\ \partial_{ij}d_{A_{n_k}}\to\partial_{ij}d_A\text{ in }\mathcal D'(D),\ \|D^2d_A\|_{M^1(D)}\le c\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness and boundary-measure bounds under a uniform cone property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness is asserted for the characteristic functions in every finite Lp space; the Hausdorff boundary-measure bound is uniform over the admissible family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $D\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be bounded and open with uniformly Lipschitzian boundary, and let $r,\omega,\lambda>0$. Define
\[
L(D,r,\omega,\lambda)=\{\Omega\subset D:\Omega\text{ is Lebesgue measurable and satisfies the uniform cone property for }(r,\omega,\lambda)\}
\]
and
\[
X(D,r,\omega,\lambda)=\{\chi_\Omega:\Omega\in L(D,r,\omega,\lambda)\}.
\]
For every $1\le p<\infty$, $X(D,r,\omega,\lambda)$ is compact in $L^p(D)$. Moreover, there exists $C(D,r,\omega,\lambda)>0$ such that
\[
H_{N-1}(\partial\Omega)\le C(D,r,\omega,\lambda)
\quad\text{for every }\Omega\in L(D,r,\omega,\lambda).
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Prokhorov tightness–compactness theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States both directions and preserves the completeness condition required for the converse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\mathcal K\subset\mathcal P(X)$. If $\mathcal K$ is tight, meaning that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K_\varepsilon\subset X$ such that $\mu(X\setminus K_\varepsilon)\le\varepsilon$ for every $\mu\in\mathcal K$, then $\mathcal K$ is relatively compact for narrow convergence. Conversely, if the separable metric space $X$ admits an equivalent complete metric, then every narrowly relatively compact $\mathcal K\subset\mathcal P(X)$ is tight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every tight family of probability measures is relatively compact for narrow convergence. On a Polish space, relative compactness also implies tightness.
assumptions_latex: For the converse, $X$ admits an equivalent complete metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal K\text{ tight}\Rightarrow\mathcal K\text{ narrowly relatively compact},\qquad X\text{ Polish}\Rightarrow\bigl(\mathcal K\text{ narrowly relatively compact}\Rightarrow\mathcal K\text{ tight}\bigr).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topology of incidence and component-count constraints on complementary distance functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For open subsets of a holdall, represented by distance functions to their complements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subset\mathbb R^N\), define \(H^c(S)=\{d_{\complement\Omega}\in C_d^c(D):S\subset\complement\Omega\}\), \(I^c(S)=\{d_{\complement\Omega}\in C_d^c(D):\complement\Omega\subset S\}\), and \(J^c(S)=\{d_{\complement\Omega}\in C_d^c(D):\complement\Omega\cap S\ne\varnothing\}\). If \(D\) is nonempty and open, \(H^c(S)\) is closed in \(C_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)\). If \(S\) is closed, \(I^c(S)\) is closed; if additionally \(S\cap\overline D\) is compact, then \(J^c(S)\) is closed. If \(S\) is open, \(J^c(S)\) is open; if additionally \(\complement S\cap\overline D\) is compact, then \(I^c(S)\) is open. For bounded open \(D\), replace \(C_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)\) by \(C(\overline D)\). In that bounded case, the finite component-count map \(\complement\Omega\mapsto\#(\complement\Omega)\) is lower semicontinuous; hence, for each \(c\ge0\), \(\{d_{\complement\Omega}:\#(\complement\Omega)\le c\}\) is compact in \(C(\overline D)\), and the hole-free subfamily is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Containment and intersection constraints on complements have predictable closed or open behavior under distance-function convergence, depending on whether the reference set is closed or open and on the stated compactness conditions. On a bounded holdall, the finite number of complement components is lower semicontinuous, so bounded-component and hole-free families are compact.
assumptions_latex: \(\varnothing\ne D\subset\mathbb R^N\) is open; the corresponding bounded case uses \(C(\overline D)\)
Closedness of \(J^c(S)\) additionally assumes \(S\cap\overline D\) compact
Openness of \(I^c(S)\) additionally assumes \(\complement S\cap\overline D\) compact
The component-count conclusions assume \(D\) is nonempty, bounded, and open, and \(\#(\complement\Omega)<\infty\) on the map's domain
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H^c(S)\text{ is closed};\quad S\text{ closed}\Rightarrow I^c(S)\text{ closed};\quad S\text{ closed},\ S\cap\overline D\text{ compact}\Rightarrow J^c(S)\text{ closed};\quad S\text{ open}\Rightarrow J^c(S)\text{ open};\quad S\text{ open},\ \complement S\cap\overline D\text{ compact}\Rightarrow I^c(S)\text{ open};\quad \#(\complement\Omega)\text{ is lower semicontinuous and its sublevel families are compact.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness, Local Boundedness, and Semicontinuity of a Multifunction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a set-valued map \(\Phi:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) at a point and on a set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Phi:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\): (a) \(\Phi\) is closed at \(\bar x\) if \(x^k\to\bar x\), \(y^k\in\Phi(x^k)\), and \(y^k\to\bar y\) imply \(\bar y\in\Phi(\bar x)\). (b) It is locally bounded at \(\bar x\) if some open neighborhood \(\mathcal N\) of \(\bar x\) makes \(\bigcup_{x\in\mathcal N\cap\operatorname{dom}\Phi}\Phi(x)\) bounded. (c) It is lower semicontinuous at \(\bar x\) if every open \(\mathcal U\) meeting \(\Phi(\bar x)\) also meets every \(\Phi(x)\) for all \(x\) in some neighborhood of \(\bar x\). (d) It is upper semicontinuous at \(\bar x\) if every open \(\mathcal V\supseteq\Phi(\bar x)\) contains \(\Phi(x)\) for every \(x\) in some neighborhood of \(\bar x\). (e) It is continuous at \(\bar x\) if it is both lower and upper semicontinuous there. It is closed, lower semicontinuous, upper semicontinuous, or continuous on \(S\) when the corresponding property holds at every point of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closedness preserves membership under convergent graph sequences; local boundedness uniformly bounds nearby values; lower semicontinuity preserves intersection with open sets; upper semicontinuity keeps nearby values inside every open set containing the reference value; continuity means both semicontinuities. Each property extends pointwise to a set.
assumptions_latex: S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ for the setwise definitions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated sequential, boundedness, and open-set conditions define closedness, local boundedness, lower semicontinuity, upper semicontinuity, and continuity at }\bar x\text{ and on }S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness and compact-subset persistence under complementary-distance convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For open subsets represented through distance functions to their complements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^N\) be nonempty and open. Then \(C_d^c(D)\) is closed in \(C_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)\). If \(D\) is bounded, then \(C_d^c(D)\) is compact in \(C_0(D)\), and \((\mathcal G(D),\rho_H^c)\) is a compact metric space. Moreover, if \(\Omega_n,\Omega\in\mathcal G(D)\) and \(d_{\complement\Omega_n}\to d_{\complement\Omega}\) in \(C_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)\), then for every compact \(K\subset\Omega\) there exists \(N(K)>0\) such that \(K\subset\Omega_n\) for every \(n\ge N(K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The class of complementary distance functions is locally uniformly closed. On a bounded holdall it is compact, as is the corresponding metric space of open sets. Under locally uniform convergence of complementary distance functions, every compact subset of the limiting open set eventually lies in every approximating open set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inner- and Outer-Limit Characterizations of Multifunction Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For closed-valued finite-dimensional multifunctions, including the local-boundedness condition needed for the converse continuity implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) be closed-valued and let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). Then: (a) \(\Phi\) is lower semicontinuous at \(x\) if and only if \(\liminf_{y\to x}\Phi(y)=\Phi(x)\). (b) \(\Phi\) is closed at \(x\) if and only if \(\limsup_{y\to x}\Phi(y)=\Phi(x)\). (c) If \(\Phi\) is continuous at \(x\), then \(\liminf_{y\to x}\Phi(y)=\limsup_{y\to x}\Phi(y)\). Conversely, equality of these limits together with local boundedness of \(\Phi\) at \(x\) implies continuity at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed-valued multifunction, lower semicontinuity is equivalent to equality of the inner limit and the reference value, while closedness is equivalent to equality of the outer limit and the reference value. Continuity makes the two limits equal; conversely, equal limits imply continuity when the map is locally bounded at the point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\Phi\text{ is l.s.c. at }x\iff\liminf_{y\to x}\Phi(y)=\Phi(x)\right],\quad\left[\Phi\text{ is closed at }x\iff\limsup_{y\to x}\Phi(y)=\Phi(x)\right],\quad\Phi\text{ continuous at }x\Rightarrow\liminf_{y\to x}\Phi(y)=\limsup_{y\to x}\Phi(y),\quad\left[\liminf_{y\to x}\Phi(y)=\limsup_{y\to x}\Phi(y)\ \land\ \Phi\text{ locally bounded at }x\right]\Rightarrow\Phi\text{ continuous at }x

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\ne\varnothing\) be open in \(\mathbb R^N\). Then \(C_b(D)\) is closed in \(C_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)\), and the induced metric \(\rho_\delta\) is complete on \(\mathcal F_b(D)\). If \(D\) is bounded and open, \(C_b(D)\) is closed and compact in \(C(\overline D)\), and the uniform metric \(\rho\) is complete. Furthermore, \(b_A\mapsto(b_A^+,b_A^-,|b_A|)=(d_A,d_{A^c},d_{\partial A})\) is continuous and satisfies \[\max\{\|d_B-d_A\|_{C(D)},\|d_{B^c}-d_{A^c}\|_{C(D)},\|d_{\partial B}-d_{\partial A}\|_{C(D)}\}\le\|b_B-b_A\|_{C(D)}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularity of Sums of Set-Valued Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient conditions for local boundedness, outer semicontinuity, and total continuity of a pointwise sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S_1,S_2:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m. (a) If S_1 and S_2 are locally bounded, then S_1+S_2 is locally bounded. (b) If S_1 and S_2 are outer semicontinuous and (x,y)\mapsto S_1(x)\cap[y-S_2(x)] is locally bounded, then S_1+S_2 is outer semicontinuous; the auxiliary boundedness condition holds if either summand is locally bounded. (c) At \bar x, suppose S_1 and S_2 are totally continuous, [S_1(\bar x)\times S_2(\bar x)]^\infty=S_1(\bar x)^\infty\times S_2(\bar x)^\infty, and S_1(\bar x)^\infty\cap[-S_2(\bar x)^\infty]=\{0\}. Then S_1+S_2 is totally continuous at \bar x. Both horizon conditions hold if either mapping is locally bounded at \bar x; the product-horizon equality also holds when S_1(\bar x) and S_2(\bar x) are convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise sum of two set-valued mappings preserves local boundedness when both mappings are locally bounded. It preserves outer semicontinuity when both mappings are outer semicontinuous and the decompositions of nearby sum values are locally bounded; local boundedness of either summand suffices for this auxiliary condition. Total continuity at a point follows from total continuity of both summands, the stated product-horizon equality, and the absence of nonzero opposite horizon directions. Local boundedness of either mapping at the point ensures both horizon conditions, while convexity of both values ensures the product-horizon equality.
assumptions_latex: \text{For (b): }S_1,S_2\text{ are outer semicontinuous and }(x,y)\mapsto S_1(x)\cap[y-S_2(x)]\text{ is locally bounded}
[S_1(\bar x)\times S_2(\bar x)]^\infty=S_1(\bar x)^\infty\times S_2(\bar x)^\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_1+S_2\text{ has the corresponding local boundedness, outer-semicontinuity, or total-continuity property under the stated conditions.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to any infinite sequence generated by Algorithm 11.5.1 under the stated mixed-\(P_0\) and centering assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H:\mathbb R_+^{2n}\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^{n+m}\) be continuous, continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb R_{++}^{2n}\times\mathbb R^m\), and suppose \(JH(x,y,z)\) has the mixed \(P_0\) property throughout that open domain. If, for every \(\delta,\eta>0\), the set \[\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R_{++}^{2n}\times\mathbb R^m:\delta\le \|H(x,y,z)\|+x^Ty\le\eta\}\] is bounded, then \(x^k\circ y^k\to0\) and \(H(x^k,y^k,z^k)\to0\); if additionally \(H\) is affine, (11.1.3) has a solution. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stability of Perturbed Convex Inequality Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The vector inequalities \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\varepsilon\to+0\) are componentwise; \((t)_+=\max\{t,0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be convex, let \(S=\{x:g_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) be convex and bounded, and assume \(S\subset\operatorname{int}D(g_i)\) for every \(i\). Define \(S_\varepsilon=\{x:g_i(x)\le\varepsilon_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). For every componentwise \(\varepsilon>0\), \(S_\varepsilon\) is nonempty and bounded, and \(\Delta(S_\varepsilon,S)\to0\) as \(\varepsilon\to+0\). If there exist \(x^0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that \(g_i(x^0)\le-\delta\) for all \(i\), then \(S_\varepsilon\) is nonempty and bounded whenever \(\varepsilon_i\ge g_i(x^0)\) for all \(i\), and every \(x_\varepsilon\in S_\varepsilon\) satisfies \[\operatorname{dist}(x_\varepsilon,S)\le \frac{1}{\delta}\max_{x\in S}\|x-x^0\|\left(\max_{1\le i\le m}\varepsilon_i\right)_+.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive right-hand-side relaxations of a bounded convex inequality system give nonempty bounded feasible sets converging to the original set in Hausdorff distance. A uniformly strict feasible point also gives the stated distance error bound and permits the specified wider perturbation range.
assumptions_latex: S=\{x:g_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\text{ is convex and bounded}.
\text{For the error bound and extended range, }\exists x^0,\delta>0:\ g_i(x^0)\le-\delta\quad\forall i.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varepsilon>0\Rightarrow S_\varepsilon\ne\varnothing,\ S_\varepsilon\text{ bounded},\ \Delta(S_\varepsilon,S)\to0;\quad \varepsilon_i\ge g_i(x^0)\Rightarrow \operatorname{dist}(x_\varepsilon,S)\le\delta^{-1}\max_{x\in S}\|x-x^0\|\left(\max_i\varepsilon_i\right)_+.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local boundedness of a set-valued mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes pointwise and global local boundedness, boundedness of the range, an equivalent ball formulation, and the vacuous case outside the domain closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mapping \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) is locally bounded at \(\bar x\) if some neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar x\) has bounded image \(S(V)\). Equivalently, there exist \(\delta,\rho>0\) such that \(\|x-\bar x\|\le\delta\) and \(u\in S(x)\) imply \(\|u\|\le\rho\), or \(S(\mathbb B(\bar x,\delta))\subset\mathbb B(0,\rho)\). It is locally bounded on \(\mathbb R^n\) if this holds at every point, and bounded on \(\mathbb R^n\) if \(\operatorname{rge}S\) is bounded. In particular, it is locally bounded at every \(\bar x\notin\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{dom}S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is locally bounded at a point when all values over some neighborhood lie in one bounded set. This is equivalent to a uniform norm bound on nearby values. Local boundedness on the whole domain means the condition holds at every point, whereas global boundedness means the entire range is bounded. Local boundedness holds vacuously outside the closure of the domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is locally bounded at }\bar x\iff \exists\delta,\rho>0\ \forall x,u:\ (\|x-\bar x\|\le\delta\land u\in S(x))\Rightarrow\|u\|\le\rho.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \[d(x_0,F_n)\longrightarrow\infty,\] then for every \(R<\infty\) there exists \(N_R\) such that \[F_n\cap B_R(x_0)=\varnothing\qquad\text{for every }n\geq N_R.\] Consequently, \(F_n\to\varnothing\) in the Fell topology.

children.title: Local Vanishing
children.top_down_role: Disappearance of sets within each fixed bounded region.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local vanishing means \(F_n\cap K=\varnothing\) eventually for every compact \(K\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact-window criterion for disappearance of a closed-set sequence.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((F_n)\) vanishes locally if \[\text{for every compact }K\subseteq X\text{ there exists }N_K\text{ such that }F_n\cap K=\varnothing\text{ for all }n\geq N_K.\] In a proper metric space this is equivalent to eventual emptiness on every closed bounded ball. For nonempty \(F_n\), it is also equivalent to \(d(x_0,F_n)\to\infty\) for any fixed base point \(x_0\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local vanishing means that every compact observation region is eventually disjoint from the closed sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Vanishing

children.title: Empty-Limit Formation
children.top_down_role: Formation of an empty limiting set.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a locally compact Hausdorff space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\to\varnothing\) in the Fell topology if and only if every compact subset is eventually missed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of convergence to the empty set in the Fell topology.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((F_n)\) converges to \(\varnothing\) in the Fell topology precisely when \[\forall K\subseteq X\text{ compact},\quad \exists N_K\quad \forall n\geq N_K,\quad F_n\cap K=\varnothing.\] The usual hit condition is vacuous for the empty limit, while the displayed compact-miss condition is exactly the remaining Fell convergence requirement. Thus empty-limit formation is the hyperspace manifestation of local vanishing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed-set sequence has empty Fell limit exactly when it eventually misses every compact subset of the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.title: Empty-Limit Formation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness and lower semicontinuity of the feasible-set map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two regularity conclusions for the constraint-generated map K under distinct hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If X is closed and each g_i is lower semicontinuous on X\times Y for i=1,\ldots,k, then K is closed on X. If, for every i and y\in Y, g_i(\cdot,y) is upper semicontinuous on X; for every i and x\in X, g_i(x,\cdot) is strictly quasiconvex and upper semicontinuous on the convex set Y; and for every x\in X there exists y\in Y such that \max_{1\le i\le k}g_i(x,y)<0, then K is lower semicontinuous and convex-valued on X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower semicontinuity of all constraint functions and closedness of the parameter set make the feasible-set map closed. Parameterwise upper semicontinuity, strict quasiconvexity in the decision variable, convexity of its domain, and a strict-feasibility condition make the map lower semicontinuous and convex-valued.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is closed and }g_i\text{ is lower semicontinuous on }X\times Y\ \forall i=1,\ldots,k\quad\text{(closedness branch)}
g_i(\cdot,y)\text{ is upper semicontinuous on }X\ \forall i,\forall y\in Y
Y\text{ is convex and }g_i(x,\cdot)\text{ is strictly quasiconvex and upper semicontinuous on }Y\ \forall i,\forall x\in X
\forall x\in X\ \exists y\in Y:\ \max_{1\le i\le k}g_i(x,y)<0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is closed on }X\text{ under the first branch; under the latter assumptions, }K\text{ is lower semicontinuous and convex-valued on }X.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Duality Between Limits of Closed Convex Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here \(K^*\) denotes the polar cone of \(K\), and the lower limit is taken as \(y\to x\) with \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S:\mathbb{R}^k\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^k\), and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^k\). If \(S(y)\) is a closed convex cone for every \(y\), then
\[
\liminf_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in C}}S(y)=\left[\limsup_{y\to x}S(y)^*\right]^*.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a set-valued mapping whose values are closed convex cones, the lower limit along C equals the polar of the upper limit of the polar cones.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence of closed cones \(K_n\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) converges to a closed cone \(K\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense when \[\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}K_n=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}K_n=K.\]

children.title: Polar-Cone Limits
children.top_down_role: Limiting behavior of polar cones.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_n^\circ\to K^\circ\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuity of negative polarity for closed convex cones in Euclidean space.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a cone \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), define its negative polar by \[K^\circ=\bigl\{y\in\mathbb{R}^d:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }x\in K\bigr\}.\] If closed convex cones \(K_n\) converge in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense to a closed convex cone \(K\), then \[\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}K_n^\circ=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}K_n^\circ=K^\circ.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For closed convex cones in finite dimensions, taking the negative polar commutes with Painlevé–Kuratowski limits.
knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Cone Limits

children.title: Polarity Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility of polarity with cone limits.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_n\to K\iff K_n^\circ\to K^\circ\), and \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed-convex polarity as an involutive convergence duality.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every closed convex cone \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), negative polarity is involutive: \[K^{\circ\circ}=K.\] For closed convex cones \(K_n,K\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), \[K_n\to K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K_n^\circ\to K^\circ,\] where both convergences are Painlevé--Kuratowski convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On closed convex cones, negative polarity is involutive, and convergence of cones is equivalent to convergence of their negative polar cones.
knowledge_statements.title: Polarity Compatibility

children.title: Duality Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where limiting operations fail to preserve polar duality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(C_n\to C\), one has \(C_n^\circ\not\to C^\circ\).

notation.meaning: nonconic singleton sequence and its limit

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure after removing the cone hypothesis.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb{R}\), let \(C_n=\{1/n\}\) and \(C=\{0\}\). Then \(C_n\to C\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense, whereas \[C_n^\circ=(-\infty,0]\quad\text{for every }n,\qquad C^\circ=\mathbb{R}.\] Consequently, \(C_n^\circ\to(-\infty,0]\neq C^\circ\). Thus polarity compatibility can fail when the cone hypothesis is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity need not commute with set limits outside the cone class: positive singletons converge to zero, while their polars do not converge to the polar of zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Duality Failure Boundary

children.title: Horizon-Recession Limit Pair
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic set behavior carried by directions escaping bounded regions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Horizon-cone convergence means \(C_n^\infty\to C^\infty\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional horizon cones and their Painlevé--Kuratowski convergence.

source_refs.locator: F. Horizon Limits p. 122

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), its horizon cone is \[C^\infty=\bigl\{w\in\mathbb{R}^d:\text{there exist }x_k\in C\text{ and }t_k\downarrow0\text{ with }t_kx_k\to w\bigr\}.\] The horizon cones of \(C_n\) converge to the horizon cone of \(C\) when \[\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}C_n^\infty=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}C_n^\infty=C^\infty.\] For closed convex \(C\), the horizon cone equals the recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horizon-cone convergence requires the horizon cones of the sets to converge in the Painlevé–Kuratowski sense to the horizon cone of the limiting set.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizon-Cone Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: F. Horizon Limits p. 122

assumptions_latex: \(C_n	o C\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is recession-sensitive precisely when \(C_n^\infty	o C^\infty\).

notation.meaning: horizon cone, equal to the recession cone for closed convex sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set convergence augmented by exact convergence of asymptotic directions.

source_refs.locator: F. Horizon Limits p. 122

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convergent sequence \(C_n	o C\) lies in a recession-sensitive stable regime when its ordinary set limit and its asymptotic-direction limit are simultaneously exact:
\[
\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n	o\infty}C_n^\infty
=
\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n	o\infty}C_n^\infty
=C^\infty.
\]
The outer equality excludes asymptotic directions persisting along subsequences without belonging to \(C^\infty\); the inner equality requires every direction in \(C^\infty\) to be approximable by directions from all sufficiently late \(C_n^\infty\). For closed convex sets, the same condition can be written using recession cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recession-sensitive stable regime combines ordinary set convergence with exact convergence of horizon, or convex recession, cones.
knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Sensitive Limit Regimes

children.title: Loss of Asymptotic Directions
children.top_down_role: Disappearance of previously present directions in the limit.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_n\to\{0\}\), but \(C_n^\infty=[0,\infty)\) while \(\{0\}^\infty=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: closed set with an escaping unbounded component

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvex escaping-component example of lost horizon directions.

source_refs.locator: F. Horizon Limits p. 122

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), let \[C_n=\{0\}\cup[n,\infty)\subset\mathbb{R}.\] Then \(C_n\to\{0\}\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense, but \[C_n^\infty=[0,\infty)\quad\text{for every }n,\qquad \bigl(\{0\}\bigr)^\infty=\{0\}.\] Thus the positive asymptotic directions of the escaping unbounded component are absent from the limit set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbounded component can escape while the sets converge, causing all of its positive horizon directions to disappear from the limit.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(C_n=[0,n]\subset\mathbb{R}\). Then \[C_n\to C=[0,\infty)\] in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense. Moreover, \[C_n^\infty=\{0\}\quad\text{for every }n,\qquad C^\infty=[0,\infty).\] Hence \[\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}C_n^\infty=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}C_n^\infty=\{0\}\neq C^\infty.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expanding compact intervals converge to a ray, creating positive asymptotic directions absent from every approximating horizon cone.

children.title: Asymptotic-Direction Stability
children.top_down_role: Regimes preserving directional behavior through set convergence.

assumptions_latex: \(C_n	o C\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Asymptotic directions are stable iff \(\operatorname*{Limsup}_n C_n^\infty=\operatorname*{Liminf}_n C_n^\infty=C^\infty\).

notation.meaning: distance from a point to a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact criterion excluding both loss and creation of horizon directions.

source_refs.locator: F. Horizon Limits p. 122

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Asymptotic directions are stable along \(C_n	o C\) precisely when
\[
\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n	o\infty}C_n^\infty
=
\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n	o\infty}C_n^\infty
=C^\infty.
\]
Equivalently, every convergent subsequence \(w_{n_k}	o w\) with \(w_{n_k}\in C_{n_k}^\infty\) satisfies \(w\in C^\infty\), and every \(w\in C^\infty\) satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(w,C_n^\infty)	o0\). The first requirement prevents persistent directions from being lost; the second prevents directions from appearing only after passage to the limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Asymptotic-direction stability holds exactly when outer exclusion and inner recovery make the horizon cones converge to the limit set’s horizon cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic-Direction Stability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence of Convex Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three preservation regimes for ordinary or total convergence under convex-hull formation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The following hold.

(a) If K^\nu\to K for cones K,K^\nu\subset\mathbb R^n and K is pointed, then
\[
\operatorname{con}K^\nu\to\operatorname{con}K.
\]

(b) If C^\nu\to C and all C^\nu are contained in one bounded region of \mathbb R^n, then
\[
\operatorname{con}C^\nu\to\operatorname{con}C.
\]

(c) If C^\nu\overset{\mathrm t}{\to}C for C,C^\nu\subset\mathbb R^n, with C\ne\varnothing and C^\infty pointed, then
\[
\operatorname{con}C^\nu\overset{\mathrm t}{\to}\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{con}C)
=\operatorname{con}C+\operatorname{con}C^\infty.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex-hull formation preserves convergence for cones with a pointed limiting cone and for uniformly bounded set families. It also preserves total convergence for a nonempty limiting set with pointed horizon cone, with limit equal to the closed convex hull, represented as the convex hull of the set plus that of its horizon cone.

children.title: Infinite Union Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Instability introduced by unrestricted or nonuniform unions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every fixed \(j\), \(A_n^j\to\{0\}\), but \(\bigcup_{j=1}^{\infty}A_n^j=\{0,1\}\not\to\bigcup_{j=1}^{\infty}\{0\}=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal counterexample showing failure for countably infinite unions.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n,j\in\mathbb{N}\), define \[A_n^j=\begin{cases}\{1\},&j=n,\\\{0\},&j\neq n.\end{cases}\] For every fixed \(j\), \(A_n^j\to A^j=\{0\}\). However, \[\bigcup_{j=1}^{\infty}A_n^j=\{0,1\}\quad\text{for every }n,\qquad \bigcup_{j=1}^{\infty}A^j=\{0\}.\] Thus componentwise convergence of a countably infinite family does not ensure convergence of the corresponding unions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Countably infinite unions are unstable under componentwise set convergence because a moving diagonal component can survive in every union.
knowledge_statements.title: Infinite Union Failure Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Cartesian Product Stability
children.top_down_role: Limit preservation for Cartesian products of varying sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian Product Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Painlevé--Kuratowski product rule, including empty limiting factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A_n,A\subset\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(B_n,B\subset\mathbb{R}^q\) be closed. If \(A_n\to A\) and \(B_n\to B\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense, then
\[
A_n\times B_n\to A\times B.
\]
The assertion also applies when either limiting factor is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence of two set sequences implies convergence of their Cartesian products, including when a limiting factor is empty.
assumptions_latex: \(A_n\to A\) and \(B_n\to B\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_n\times B_n\to A\times B\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Intersection Stability
children.top_down_role: Preservation of set limits under intersections.

assumptions_latex: \(A_n\to A\) and \(B_n\to B\) are closed-set convergences in \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
Near every \(z\in A\cap B\), eventually \(d(x,A_n\cap B_n)\leq\kappa[d(x,A_n)+d(x,B_n)]\) for one local constant \(\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_n\cap B_n\to A\cap B\).

notation.meaning: distance from a point to a set, with distance to the empty set infinite

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient intersection rule under a uniform local linear-regularity estimate.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108
3.3.1 Sequential Normal Compactness of Set Intersections and Inverse Images p. 341
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A_n,B_n,A,B\) be closed subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\), with \(A_n\to A\) and \(B_n\to B\). Suppose that for every \(z\in A\cap B\) there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(z\), \(\kappa>0\), and \(n_0\) such that, for \(n\geq n_0\) and \(x\in U\),
\[
d(x,A_n\cap B_n)\leq\kappa\bigl(d(x,A_n)+d(x,B_n)\bigr).
\]
Then \(A_n\cap B_n\to A\cap B\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersections converge when the individual sets converge and a uniform local error bound prevents their approximating intersections from separating.
knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Stability

children.title: Constraint Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interactions among varying constraint families.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_n\cap B_n=\{x:(x,x)\in A_n\times B_n\}=\delta^{-1}(A_n\times B_n)\), where \(\delta(x)=(x,x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection constraints represented as product constraints coupled through the diagonal.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Set-Valued Mappings p. 148

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For closed sets \(A_n,B_n\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), define the diagonal embedding \(\delta:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^{2d}\) by \(\delta(x)=(x,x)\) and the diagonal \(\Delta=\delta(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Then
\[
A_n\cap B_n=\delta^{-1}(A_n\times B_n),
\]
and, equivalently,
\[
\delta(A_n\cap B_n)=(A_n\times B_n)\cap\Delta.
\]
Thus stability of intersections is precisely stability of an inverse-image constraint, or of the coupling between a product set and the fixed diagonal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An intersection is the inverse image of a product set under the diagonal embedding, exposing intersection stability as a coupled constraint problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Coupling

children.title: Transversality Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric regularity supporting stable intersections.

knowledge_statements.title: Transversality Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative normal-cone transversality for locally convex set pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let closed sets \(A_n,B_n,A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfy \(A_n\to A\) and \(B_n\to B\). A uniform local normal-angle transversality regime at \(z\in A\cap B\) consists of numbers \(r>0\), \(\alpha>0\), and \(n_0\) such that \(A_n\) and \(B_n\) are locally convex on \(\mathbb{B}(z,r)\) for every \(n\geq n_0\), and whenever \(a\in A_n\cap\mathbb{B}(z,r)\), \(b\in B_n\cap\mathbb{B}(z,r)\), \(u\in N_{A_n}(a)\cap\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\), and \(v\in N_{B_n}(b)\cap\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\),
\[
\|u+v\|\geq\alpha.
\]
Under this regime, the pair is locally linearly regular near \(z\), with constants uniform for all sufficiently large \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near each limiting intersection point, uniform separation of opposing unit normals is a quantitative transversality regime yielding eventually uniform local linear regularity.
assumptions_latex: \(A_n,B_n,A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) are closed, with \(A_n\to A\) and \(B_n\to B\).
For each point under consideration \(z\in A\cap B\), the sets \(A_n\) and \(B_n\) are eventually locally convex on a common ball about \(z\).
Nearby unit normals satisfy a common lower bound \(\|u+v\|\geq\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pairs \((A_n,B_n)\) are locally linearly regular near \(z\), uniformly for all sufficiently large \(n\).

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal cone to a locally convex closed set
open Euclidean ball of radius r centered at z

children.title: Feasibility Loss
children.top_down_role: Disappearance of common feasible points under limiting operations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(A_n\to\{0\}\) and \(B_n\to\{0\}\), one has \(A_n\cap B_n=\varnothing\to\varnothing\neq\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary failure of intersection continuity without a coupling qualification.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In \(\mathbb{R}\), set \(A_n=\{0\}\) and \(B_n=\{1/n\}\). Then
\[
A_n\to\{0\},\qquad B_n\to\{0\},
\]
but \(A_n\cap B_n=\varnothing\) for every \(n\). Consequently,
\[
A_n\cap B_n\to\varnothing\neq\{0\}=\bigl(\lim_n A_n\bigr)\cap\bigl(\lim_n B_n\bigr).
\]
Thus separate set convergence does not prevent complete loss of feasibility; an intersection qualification is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two singleton sequences can converge to the same point while remaining disjoint, so their feasible intersections converge to the empty set.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Loss

children.title: Minkowski Sum Limits
children.top_down_role: Limiting behavior of Minkowski sums.

knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski Sum Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact finite-dimensional continuity of Minkowski addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A_n,B_n,A,B\) be nonempty compact subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\), all contained in a common compact set. If \(A_n\to A\) and \(B_n\to B\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense, then
\[
A_n+B_n\to A+B,
\qquad
A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,\ b\in B\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minkowski sums of uniformly bounded compact sets converge when both summand sequences converge.
assumptions_latex: All sets lie in a common compact set, and \(A_n\to A\), \(B_n\to B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_n+B_n\to A+B\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower Limits of Sums and Nonnegative Scalar Multiples
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real liminf calculus, including the indeterminate-sum boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For arbitrary extended-real-valued functions f_1,f_2,
\liminf_{x\to\bar x}(f_1(x)+f_2(x))\geq \liminf_{x\to\bar x}f_1(x)+\liminf_{x\to\bar x}f_2(x),
provided the right-hand sum is not the indeterminate form \infty-\infty. For every extended-real-valued f and every \lambda\geq0,
\liminf_{x\to\bar x}(\lambda f)(x)=\lambda\liminf_{x\to\bar x}f(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The liminf of a sum is at least the sum of the liminfs whenever the latter is well defined rather than infinity minus infinity. Liminf always commutes with multiplication by a nonnegative scalar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \liminf_{x\to\bar x}(f_1+f_2)(x)\geq\liminf_{x\to\bar x}f_1(x)+\liminf_{x\to\bar x}f_2(x),\qquad \liminf_{x\to\bar x}(\lambda f)(x)=\lambda\liminf_{x\to\bar x}f(x)

children.title: Scalar Multiplication Limits
children.top_down_role: Limiting behavior under varying scalar multiplication.

assumptions_latex: \(A_n,A\) are nonempty compact subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) contained in one compact set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_nA_n\to\lambda A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-set multiplication with uniform boundedness, including zero limiting scale.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A_n,A\) be nonempty compact subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\), contained in a common compact set, and suppose \(A_n\to A\). If \(\lambda_n\to\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\), then
\[
\lambda_nA_n\to\lambda A,
\qquad
\lambda A=\{\lambda a:a\in A\}.
\]
Uniform boundedness controls the products when \(\lambda=0\); in particular, every sequence \(\lambda_na_n\) with \(a_n\in A_n\) converges to zero whenever \(\lambda_n\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergent scalar factors preserve set convergence for compact sets sharing a common bound, including when the limiting scalar is zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Multiplication Limits

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Degenerate Scaling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scaling behavior near zero, infinity, or sign changes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_n\to\varnothing\) and \(\lambda_n\to0\), but \(\lambda_nA_n=\{1\}\to\{1\}\neq0\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of scaling continuity at zero when the sets escape to infinity.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In \(\mathbb{R}\), take \(A_n=\{n\}\) and \(\lambda_n=1/n\). The sets escape every bounded region, hence \(A_n\to\varnothing\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense, while \(\lambda_n\to0\). Nevertheless,
\[
\lambda_nA_n=\{1\}\to\{1\}.
\]
Thus the formal limiting expression \(0\varnothing=\varnothing\) does not describe the scaled-set limit. At a zero limiting scale, boundedness or an equivalent control of \(\lambda_nA_n\) is indispensable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When sets escape at the reciprocal rate of a vanishing scalar, their scaled images can retain nonzero points despite an empty set limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Scaling Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Minkowski Cancellation Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of recoverability under Minkowski combination.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A+C=B+C=\{0,1,2,3\}\) although \(A\neq B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-set counterexample to cancellation for Minkowski addition.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
A=\{0,2\},\qquad B=\{0,1,2\},\qquad C=\{0,1\}
\]
in \(\mathbb{R}\). Direct calculation gives
\[
A+C=\{0,1,2,3\}=B+C,
\]
although \(A\neq B\). Hence Minkowski addition by a fixed nonempty compact set is not injective on arbitrary compact sets, and equality or convergence of sums cannot generally be canceled to recover equality or convergence of the summands.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minkowski addition is not cancellative: distinct finite sets can have identical sums with the same compact set.
knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski Cancellation Failure

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.title: Images Under Varying Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniformly convergent mappings acting on uniformly compact set sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^p\) be compact, and let \(A_n,A\subset K\) be nonempty compact sets with \(A_n\to A\). Suppose continuous mappings \(f_n,f:K\to\mathbb{R}^q\) satisfy
\[
\sup_{x\in K}\|f_n(x)-f(x)\|\to0.
\]
Then
\[
f_n(A_n)\to f(A).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform convergence of mappings and compact convergence of their domains imply convergence of the corresponding image sets.
assumptions_latex: \(A_n,A\) are nonempty compact subsets of a common compact set \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^p\), with \(A_n\to A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n(A_n)\to f(A)\).

notation.meaning: image of a set under a mapping

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Total Convergence of Linear Images
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of total set convergence by a fixed linear mapping under a recession-kernel transversality condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m be linear. If
\[
C^\nu\overset{\mathrm t}{\longrightarrow}C
\quad\text{and}\quad
L^{-1}(0)\cap C^\infty=\{0\},
\]
then
\[
L(C^\nu)\overset{\mathrm t}{\longrightarrow}L(C).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed linear mapping preserves total convergence of sets when the kernel of the mapping contains no nonzero recession direction of the limiting set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L(C^\nu)\overset{\mathrm t}{\longrightarrow}L(C)

children.title: Inverse-Image Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior of inverse images under varying mappings or target sets.

assumptions_latex: \(f_n,f:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^q\) are continuous and \(f_n\to f\) locally uniformly; closed sets \(D_n\to D\).
For every \(z\in f^{-1}(D)\), locally and eventually \(d(x,f_n^{-1}(D_n))\leq\kappa d(f_n(x),D_n)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-image convergence under local uniform mapping convergence and metric regularity.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let continuous mappings \(f_n,f:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^q\) satisfy \(f_n\to f\) locally uniformly, and let closed sets \(D_n\to D\). Put \(F_n=f_n^{-1}(D_n)\) and \(F=f^{-1}(D)\). Suppose that for every \(z\in F\) there exist a neighborhood \(U\), \(\kappa>0\), and \(n_0\) such that
\[
d(x,F_n)\leq\kappa d(f_n(x),D_n)
\]
for \(x\in U\) and \(n\geq n_0\). Then \(F_n\to F\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse images converge when mappings and target sets converge and a uniform local error bound supplies feasible recovery points.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Image Limits

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let continuous mappings \(g_n,g:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfy \(g_n\to g\) locally uniformly, and define
\[
F_n=\{x:g_n(x)\leq0\},\qquad F=\{x:g(x)\leq0\},
\]
with componentwise inequalities. Suppose that for every \(z\in F\) there exist a neighborhood \(U\), \(\kappa>0\), and \(n_0\) such that
\[
d(x,F_n)\leq\kappa\|[g_n(x)]_+\|
\]
for \(x\in U\) and \(n\geq n_0\). Then \(F_n\to F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible sets of convergent inequality systems converge when constraint violation uniformly controls distance to feasibility near every limiting feasible point.

children.title: Closure Stability
children.top_down_role: Interaction of closure with set convergence.

assumptions_latex: \((C_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) is a sequence of subsets of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}\overline{C_n}=\liminf_{n\to\infty}C_n\) and \(\limsup_{n\to\infty}\overline{C_n}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}C_n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential Painlevé–Kuratowski limits in a metric space are unchanged by termwise closure.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Termwise closure leaves both sequential set limits unchanged:
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\overline{C_n}=\liminf_{n\to\infty}C_n,
\qquad
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\overline{C_n}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}C_n.
\]
Consequently, \(C_n\xrightarrow{PK}C\) implies \(\overline{C_n}\xrightarrow{PK}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the closure of every set in a sequence leaves its inner and outer Painlevé–Kuratowski limits unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Stability

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Convexification Stability
children.top_down_role: Interaction of convex hull formation with set convergence.

assumptions_latex: \(C_n\) and \(C\) are nonempty compact subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\).
There is a compact set \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\) such that \(C_n\subset K\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\) and \(C\subset K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{co}C_n\xrightarrow{PK}\operatorname{co}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convexification stability under a common compact bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multifunctions, selections, and inner–outer limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the basic objects associated with a multifunction and its limiting sets at a point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multifunction is a mapping $F:X\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n$. Its domain, range, and graph are $\operatorname{dom}F=\{x\in X:F(x)\neq\varnothing\}$, $F(X)=\bigcup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}F}F(x)$, and $\operatorname{gph}F=\bigcup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}F}\{x\}\times F(x)$. A selection is a function $f:\operatorname{dom}F\to\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfying $f(x)\in F(x)$ for every $x$. For $x^*\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{dom}F)$, $y\in\limsup_{x\to x^*}F(x)$ iff there exist $x_k\to x^*$ and $y_k\to y$ with $y_k\in F(x_k)$. Moreover, $y\in\liminf_{x\to x^*}F(x)$ when there is a selection $f$ near $x^*$ such that $f(x)\to y$ as $x\to x^*$. Always $\liminf_{x\to x^*}F(x)\subseteq\limsup_{x\to x^*}F(x)$; if equality holds, their common value is $\lim_{x\to x^*}F(x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction assigns a subset of Euclidean space to each point. Its domain consists of points with nonempty values; its range and graph are the corresponding unions. A selection chooses one member of every nonempty value. At a closure point of the domain, the outer limit consists of limits of convergent point-value sequences, while the inner limit consists of limits attained by selections. The inner limit is contained in the outer limit, and equality defines the set limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \liminf_{x\to x^*}F(x)\subseteq\limsup_{x\to x^*}F(x),\quad \liminf_{x\to x^*}F(x)=\limsup_{x\to x^*}F(x)\Longrightarrow \lim_{x\to x^*}F(x)\text{ exists}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semicontinuity, cuscos, and monotone multifunctions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and basic properties for finite-dimensional set-valued mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset E\), let \(Y\) be Euclidean, and let \(\Omega:K\rightrightarrows Y\). It is upper semicontinuous at \(x\in K\) if, for every open \(U\supset\Omega(x)\), there is a relative neighborhood \(N\) of \(x\) such that \(\Omega(z)\subset U\) for all \(z\in N\cap K\). It is lower semicontinuous if, for every \(x\in K\), \(y\in\Omega(x)\), and neighborhood \(V\) of \(y\), one has \(V\cap\Omega(z)\ne\varnothing\) for every \(z\in K\) sufficiently close to \(x\). The sets \(\Omega(x)\) are its images. A cusco is upper semicontinuous with nonempty compact convex images, and every cusco is locally bounded. Clarke subdifferentials of locally Lipschitz functions are cuscos. A multifunction \(\Phi:E\rightrightarrows E\) is monotone when \(\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\ge0\) for all \(u\in\Phi(x)\) and \(v\in\Phi(y)\). It is maximal monotone if no proper graph enlargement remains monotone. Positive-semidefinite linear operators and convex subdifferentials are monotone; subdifferentials of closed proper convex functions are maximal monotone; and every monotone multifunction is contained in a maximal monotone multifunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper and lower semicontinuity describe, respectively, outer containment and persistent intersection of nearby multifunction images. A cusco is upper semicontinuous with nonempty compact convex images and is locally bounded. Monotonicity is defined by the nonnegative pairing inequality, maximality means that the graph admits no proper monotone enlargement, and every monotone multifunction has a maximal monotone extension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Omega\text{ is a cusco}\Rightarrow\Omega\text{ is locally bounded},\qquad \forall\Phi\text{ monotone}\;\exists\widetilde\Phi\supseteq\Phi\text{ maximal monotone}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multifunction objects, convex processes, LSC, and openness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for multifunctions between Euclidean spaces and their pointwise continuity properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a multifunction \(\Phi:\mathbf E\rightrightarrows\mathbf Y\), define \(D(\Phi)=\{x\in\mathbf E:\Phi(x)\neq\varnothing\}\), \(\Phi(C)=\bigcup_{x\in C}\Phi(x)\), \(R(\Phi)=\Phi(\mathbf E)\), \(G(\Phi)=\{(x,y):y\in\Phi(x)\}\), and \(x\in\Phi^{-1}(y)\iff y\in\Phi(x)\). The multifunction has nonempty images if \(D(\Phi)=\mathbf E\), is surjective if \(R(\Phi)=\mathbf Y\), and is convex, closed, or polyhedral when its graph has that property. It is a process when its graph is a cone. At \((x_0,y)\in G(\Phi)\), it is LSC if every neighborhood \(V\) of \(y\) intersects \(\Phi(x)\) for all sufficiently near \(x\); equivalently, for every \(x_n\to x_0\), there exist \(y_n\in\Phi(x_n)\) with \(y_n\to y\). This entails \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}D(\Phi)\). It is LSC at \(x_0\) when this holds for every \(y\in\Phi(x_0)\). At \((x,y_0)\in G(\Phi)\), it is open if \(y_0\in\operatorname{int}\Phi(U)\) for every neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\); equivalently, for every \(y_n\to y_0\), there exist \(x_n\to x\) such that \(y_n\in\Phi(x_n)\) for all \(n\). This entails \(y_0\in\operatorname{int}R(\Phi)\). It is open at \(y_0\) when this holds for every \(x\in\Phi^{-1}(y_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is specified through its domain, images, range, graph, and inverse relation. Graph properties define convex, closed, and polyhedral multifunctions, while a conic graph defines a process. Lower semicontinuity tracks nearby image points for nearby inputs; openness tracks nearby preimages for nearby outputs.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf E\text{ and }\mathbf Y\text{ are Euclidean spaces}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The displayed conditions define the basic multifunction objects, processes, pointwise LSC, and pointwise openness.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localization of a finite polyhedral graph decomposition around a domain point.

children.title: Graph Closures
children.top_down_role: Closure constructions applied to multifunction graphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}\overline F=\operatorname{cl}_{X\times Y}(\operatorname{gph}F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure is taken jointly in arguments and values, not separately in each fiber.

source_refs.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graph closure of \(F\) is the multifunction \(\overline F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) uniquely specified by \[\operatorname{gph}\overline F:=\operatorname{cl}_{X\times Y}(\operatorname{gph}F).\] Equivalently, \(\overline F(x):=\{y\in Y:(x,y)\in\operatorname{cl}_{X\times Y}(\operatorname{gph}F)\}\). In general, this joint closure can contain values generated by nearby arguments and need not equal \(\operatorname{cl}_Y F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph closure is obtained by closing the entire graph in the product topology and then taking its vertical sections.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Closures

children.title: Closed-Graph Representations
children.top_down_role: Representation of multifunction behavior through closed graphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) has closed graph if and only if limits of convergent graph sequences remain in its graph.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential and closure representations agree in metric product spaces.

source_refs.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following conditions are equivalent: \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is closed in \(X\times Y\); \(F=\overline F\); and, whenever \(x_k\to x\), \(y_k\to y\), and \(y_k\in F(x_k)\) for every \(k\), one has \(y\in F(x)\). Hence a closed-graph multifunction is exactly one represented by a closed incidence set in the product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction has closed graph exactly when every convergent sequence of its argument–value pairs has its limit in the graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Graph Representations

source_witnesses.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^{-1}(y)=\{x\in X:y\in F(x)\}\) and \(\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The inverse reverses the graph incidence relation and is generally set-valued.

source_refs.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inverse multifunction \(F^{-1}:Y\rightrightarrows X\) is defined by \[F^{-1}(y):=\{x\in X:y\in F(x)\}.\] Thus \(x\in F^{-1}(y)\) if and only if \(y\in F(x)\), and its graph is the coordinate transpose \[\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}=\tau(\operatorname{gph}F)=\{(y,x)\in Y\times X:(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse multifunction assigns to each value all arguments whose images contain that value; its graph is the transposed original graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Multifunctions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric regularity at a graph point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines metric regularity with an explicit local rate constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multifunction \(\Psi:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((x_0,y_0)\in\operatorname{gph}\Psi\) with rate \(c\) if, for every \((x,y)\) in some neighborhood of \((x_0,y_0)\), \[\operatorname{dist}\bigl(x,\Psi^{-1}(y)\bigr)\le c\,\operatorname{dist}\bigl(y,\Psi(x)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is metrically regular at a graph point with rate c when, locally, the distance from x to the inverse image of y is at most c times the residual distance from y to the image of x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists U\ni(x_0,y_0)\ \forall(x,y)\in U:\ \operatorname{dist}(x,\Psi^{-1}(y))\le c\operatorname{dist}(y,\Psi(x))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric regularity under a Lipschitz perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers metric regularity between the multifunctions associated with two nearby mappings and gives the perturbed rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:X\to Y\) be continuous. Suppose \(\mathcal F_G\) is metrically regular at \((x_0,y_0)\) with rate \(c>0\), and let \(D(x):=G(x)-H(x)\) be Lipschitz near \(x_0\) with modulus \(\kappa<c^{-1}\). Then \(\mathcal F_H\) is metrically regular at \((x_0,y_0-D(x_0))\) with rate \[c(\kappa)=\frac{c}{1-c\kappa}.\] Equivalently, for all \((x,y)\) sufficiently close to \((x_0,y_0-D(x_0))\), \[\operatorname{dist}\bigl(x,\mathcal F_H^{-1}(y)\bigr)\le c(\kappa)\operatorname{dist}\bigl(y,\mathcal F_H(x)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the multifunction associated with G is metrically regular with rate c and G-H is locally Lipschitz with modulus kappa less than 1/c, then the multifunction associated with H remains metrically regular at the shifted graph point, with rate c divided by 1-c kappa.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal F_G\text{ is metrically regular at }(x_0,y_0)\text{ with rate }c>0
D(x):=G(x)-H(x)\text{ is Lipschitz near }x_0\text{ with modulus }\kappa<c^{-1}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F_H\text{ is metrically regular at }(x_0,y_0-D(x_0))\text{ with rate }c(\kappa)=c(1-c\kappa)^{-1}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper-Lipschitz sufficient conditions for calmness of a conic linear problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Calmness derived from uniform or directional upper-Lipschitz stability of the associated solution multifunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach spaces and let $\Psi$ be the multifunction defined for the conic linear problem. Let \(\Omega\subset [S,T]\times\mathbb R^n\) be relatively open, let \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\), let \(X:[S,T]\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) be closed with \(\operatorname{Gr}X\subset\Omega\), and let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\) be closed. Define

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Graph and Upper Semicontinuity Implications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two directional implications under distinct topological hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X,U be Hausdorff topological spaces and F:U\rightrightarrows X. \text{ If }X\text{ is compact and }\operatorname{gph}F\text{ is closed, then }F\text{ is upper semicontinuous. Conversely, if }F\text{ is closed-valued and upper semicontinuous and every neighborhood of each point of }X\text{ contains a closed neighborhood, then }\operatorname{gph}F\text{ is closed.}
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a multifunction between Hausdorff spaces, a closed graph implies upper semicontinuity when the range space is compact. Conversely, closed values and upper semicontinuity imply a closed graph when the range space has the closed-neighborhood property.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ and }U\text{ are Hausdorff topological spaces}
\text{For the forward implication, }X\text{ is compact and }\operatorname{gph}F\text{ is closed}
\text{For the converse, }F\text{ is closed-valued and upper semicontinuous, and every point-neighborhood in }X\text{ contains a closed neighborhood}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[X\text{ compact}\land\operatorname{gph}F\text{ closed}\bigr]\Rightarrow F\text{ upper semicontinuous};\qquad \bigl[F\text{ closed-valued and upper semicontinuous}\land X\text{ has the closed-neighborhood property}\bigr]\Rightarrow\operatorname{gph}F\text{ closed}

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rge}F=\bigcup_{x\in X}F(x)=\operatorname{dom}F^{-1}\).

source_refs.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The range of \(F\) is \[\operatorname{rge}F:=\{y\in Y:\exists x\in X,\ y\in F(x)\}=\bigcup_{x\in X}F(x).\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{rge}F=\operatorname{dom}F^{-1}\), because a value is attained by \(F\) exactly when its inverse fiber is nonempty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cellina Approximate Selection Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-close continuous approximation of an upper-semicontinuous convex-valued multifunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K\subset\mathbf{E} be compact and let \Omega:K\rightrightarrows\mathbf{Y} be upper semicontinuous with nonempty convex values. For every \epsilon>0, there exists a continuous map f:K\to\mathbf{Y} such that d_{G(\Omega)}((x,f(x)))<\epsilon for every x\in K. Moreover, f(K)\subset\operatorname{conv}(\Omega(K)), where \Omega(K)=\bigcup_{x\in K}\Omega(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If Ω is an upper-semicontinuous multifunction on a compact set K with nonempty convex values, then for every positive ε there is a continuous map whose graph lies strictly within ε of the graph of Ω at every point. Its range is contained in the convex hull of the range of Ω.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists f\in C(K,\mathbf{Y})\quad (\forall x\in K)\ d_{G(\Omega)}((x,f(x)))<\epsilon,\qquad f(K)\subset\operatorname{conv}(\Omega(K)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Selections and Pointwise Continuous Selection under Inner Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a selection and states the local selection consequence and its neighborhood-level limitation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A selection of \(S:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) is a map \(s:\operatorname{dom}S\to\mathbb R^m\) satisfying \(s(x)\in S(x)\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}S\). If \(S\) is inner semicontinuous at \(\bar x\) relative to \(\operatorname{dom}S\), then for every \(\bar u\in S(\bar x)\) there exists a selection \(s\) continuous at \(\bar x\) relative to \(\operatorname{dom}S\) with \(s(\bar x)=\bar u\). Inner semicontinuity on a neighborhood alone does not in general guarantee a selection continuous throughout a neighborhood; additional structure such as convex-valuedness is needed for global continuous-selection results.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selection chooses one value from every value set. Inner semicontinuity at a point permits a selection continuous at that point through any prescribed value there, but inner semicontinuity on a neighborhood alone does not ensure a selection continuous throughout the neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is isc at }\bar x\text{ relative to }\operatorname{dom}S
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists s:\operatorname{dom}S\to\mathbb R^m:\ s(x)\in S(x)\ \forall x,\ s(\bar x)=\bar u,\text{ and }s\text{ is continuous at }\bar x\text{ relative to }\operatorname{dom}S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multifunction and Pointwise Value Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued mappings between Banach spaces, allowing empty values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach spaces and $V\subset X$. A multifunction $\Gamma:V\rightrightarrows Y$ assigns to each $x\in V$ a set $\Gamma(x)\subset Y$, which may be empty. It is closed-valued, compact-valued, or nonempty-valued, respectively, when $\Gamma(x)$ is closed, compact, or nonempty for every $x\in V$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction assigns a possibly empty subset of Y to every point in its domain. It is closed-valued, compact-valued, or nonempty-valued when every one of its values has the corresponding property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Gamma\text{ is }P\text{-valued}\iff (\forall x\in V)\;\Gamma(x)\text{ has property }P,\quad P\in\{\text{closed, compact, nonempty}\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Michael Representation of an Inner-Semicontinuous Multifunction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Countable continuous-selection representation under closed convex values and a sigma-compact domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) be inner semicontinuous relative to \(\operatorname{dom}S\), closed-convex-valued, and suppose \(\operatorname{dom}S\) is \(\sigma\)-compact. Then \(S\) has a continuous selection. Moreover, there is a countable family \(\{s_i\}_{i\in I}\) of selections continuous relative to \(\operatorname{dom}S\) such that \(S(x)=\operatorname{cl}\{s_i(x):i\in I\}\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inner-semicontinuous, closed-convex-valued multifunction on a sigma-compact domain has a continuous selection and is pointwise the closure of the values of countably many continuous selections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ countable }\{s_i\}_{i\in I}:\ S(x)=\operatorname{cl}\{s_i(x):i\in I\}\ \forall x\in\operatorname{dom}S,\quad s_i\text{ continuous selections}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extension of a Continuous Selection from a Closed Subset
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative continuous-selection extension for inner-semicontinuous convex-valued multifunctions on sigma-compact domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) be inner semicontinuous relative to \(\operatorname{dom}S\) and convex-valued, with \(\operatorname{dom}S\) \(\sigma\)-compact. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an inner-semicontinuous convex-valued multifunction on a sigma-compact domain, every continuous selection prescribed on a closed subset extends to a continuous selection on the whole domain.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists s:\operatorname{dom}S\to\mathbb R^m:\ s(x)\in S(x)\ \forall x,\ s|_X=\bar s,\text{ and }s\text{ is continuous relative to }\operatorname{dom}S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz continuity, strict continuity, and Lipschitz modulus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued mappings between finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, including continuity relative to a subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m and X\subset D. The map F is Lipschitz continuous on X if there is \kappa\ge0 such that \lVert F(x')-F(x)\rVert\le\kappa\lVert x'-x\rVert for all x,x'\in X. For \bar x\in X, define \operatorname{lip}_X F(\bar x):=\limsup_{\substack{x,x'\to\bar x,\ x,x'\in X\\x\ne x'}}\frac{\lVert F(x')-F(x)\rVert}{\lVert x'-x\rVert}; F is strictly continuous at \bar x relative to X exactly when this modulus is finite. If \bar x\in\operatorname{int}D, \operatorname{lip}F(\bar x) is defined analogously without restricting x,x' to X. Strict continuity relative to X means strict continuity at every \bar x\in X and, for single-valued F, is equivalent to local Lipschitz continuity on X. Moreover, \operatorname{lip}_X F(\bar x)\le\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x) whenever the latter is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map is Lipschitz on a set when one finite constant controls every pair of function values there. Its relative Lipschitz modulus at a point is the limiting upper bound of nearby difference quotients, and finiteness of this modulus defines strict continuity. For single-valued mappings, strict continuity relative to a set is exactly local Lipschitz continuity on that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is strictly continuous at }\bar x\text{ relative to }X\iff\operatorname{lip}_X F(\bar x)<\infty\iff F\text{ is Lipschitz on }X\cap V\text{ for some neighborhood }V\text{ of }\bar x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nowhere-Dense and Meager Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-topology definitions and the dense-complement property in open or closed Euclidean subspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\subset X\subset\mathbb R^n\), \(A\) is nowhere dense in \(X\) when \(\operatorname{int}_X(\operatorname{cl}_X A)=\varnothing\), and it is meager in \(X\) when it is a countable union of nowhere-dense subsets of \(X\). Subsets of meager sets are meager. If \(X\) is open or closed in \(\mathbb R^n\), every meager \(A\subset X\) has dense complement in \(X\): \(\operatorname{cl}(X\setminus A)\supset X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset is nowhere dense relative to X when its relative closure has empty relative interior, and is meager when it is a countable union of such sets. Subsets of meager sets are meager. In an open or closed Euclidean subspace, every meager set has dense complement.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is open or closed in }\mathbb R^n\text{ for the dense-complement conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{int}_X(\operatorname{cl}_X A)=\varnothing\text{ characterizes nowhere density, and if }A\text{ is meager then }\operatorname{cl}(X\setminus A)\supset X

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper Semicontinuity of a Multifunction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric epsilon-delta definition for finite-dimensional set-valued mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $V\subset\mathbb{R}^k$, let $\Gamma:V\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^l$, and let $x\in V$. The multifunction $\Gamma$ is upper semicontinuous at $x$ if, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta>0$ such that, for every $x'\in V$ satisfying $\|x'-x\|<\delta$, one has $\Gamma(x')\subset\{z+h:z\in\Gamma(x),\ \|h\|<\varepsilon\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is upper semicontinuous at x if, for every positive epsilon, every value at a sufficiently nearby domain point lies in the open epsilon-neighborhood of the value at x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall\varepsilon>0)(\exists\delta>0)(\forall x'\in V)\;\|x'-x\|<\delta\Longrightarrow\Gamma(x')\subset\Gamma(x)+B_{\varepsilon}(0).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Robinson–Ursescu stability theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives an interior-range characterization and a quantitative local regularity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Psi:X\rightrightarrows Y\) be closed and convex and let \((x_0,y_0)\in\operatorname{gph}\Psi\). Then \(\Psi\) is metrically regular at \((x_0,y_0)\) if and only if \(y_0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{range}\Psi)\). More precisely, if \(y_0+\eta B_Y\subseteq\Psi(x_0+vB_X)\) for \(\eta,v>0\), then whenever \(\|x-x_0\|<v/2\) and \(\|y-y_0\|<\eta/8\), \[\operatorname{dist}\bigl(x,\Psi^{-1}(y)\bigr)\le \frac{4v}{\eta}\operatorname{dist}\bigl(y,\Psi(x)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex multifunction, metric regularity at a graph point is equivalent to the output lying in the interior of the range. A ball-image inclusion with radii eta and v yields rate 4v/eta on the stated smaller neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Psi\text{ is metrically regular at }(x_0,y_0)\iff y_0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{range}\Psi),\quad \|x-x_0\|<v/2,\ \|y-y_0\|<\eta/8\Rightarrow \operatorname{dist}(x,\Psi^{-1}(y))\le(4v/\eta)\operatorname{dist}(y,\Psi(x))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic definitions and properties of multifunctions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and elementary consequences for a set-valued mapping between Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a multifunction \(\Psi:X\rightrightarrows Y\), \(\operatorname{dom}\Psi=\{x\in X:\Psi(x)\ne\varnothing\}\), \(\operatorname{range}\Psi=\{y\in Y:\exists x\in X,\ y\in\Psi(x)\}\), \(\operatorname{gph}\Psi=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:y\in\Psi(x)\}\), and \(\Psi^{-1}(y)=\{x\in X:y\in\Psi(x)\}\). Thus \((\Psi^{-1})^{-1}=\Psi\) and \(\operatorname{dom}\Psi=\operatorname{range}(\Psi^{-1})\). The mapping is closed at \(x\) if \(x_n\to x\), \(y_n\in\Psi(x_n)\), and \(y_n\to y\) imply \(y\in\Psi(x)\); it is closed iff \(\operatorname{gph}\Psi\) is closed. It is convex iff \(\operatorname{gph}\Psi\) is convex, equivalently \(t\Psi(x_1)+(1-t)\Psi(x_2)\subseteq\Psi(tx_1+(1-t)x_2)\) for all \(x_1,x_2\in X\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). If \(\Psi\) is convex and \(S\subseteq X\) is convex, then \(\Psi(S)=\bigcup_{x\in S}\Psi(x)\) is convex. Finally, \(\Psi\) is upper Lipschitzian at \(\bar x\) with modulus \(c>0\) if \(\Psi(x)\subseteq\Psi(\bar x)+c\|x-\bar x\|\widetilde B_Y\) for every \(x\) in some neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The domain, range, graph, and graph inverse of a multifunction are defined by membership in its values. Graph inversion is involutive and exchanges domain with range. Closedness is sequential graph closedness, convexity is graph convexity and has an equivalent value-set inclusion, convex multifunctions map convex sets to convex sets, and upper Lipschitzness is a local one-sided value-set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\Psi^{-1})^{-1}=\Psi,\quad \operatorname{dom}\Psi=\operatorname{range}(\Psi^{-1}),\quad \Psi\text{ closed}\iff\operatorname{gph}\Psi\text{ closed},\quad \Psi\text{ convex}\iff t\Psi(x_1)+(1-t)\Psi(x_2)\subseteq\Psi(tx_1+(1-t)x_2).
