knowledge_statements.statement_title: Openness at a linear rate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform local covering property around a graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces. A multifunction \(\Psi:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is open at \((x_0,y_0)\in\operatorname{gph}\Psi\) at linear rate \(\gamma>0\) if there exist \(t_{\max}>0\) and a neighborhood \(N\) of \((x_0,y_0)\) such that, for every \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}\Psi\cap N\) and every \(t\in[0,t_{\max}]\), \[y+t\gamma B_Y\subseteq\Psi(x+tB_X).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is open at a graph point with linear rate gamma when, uniformly at all nearby graph points and all sufficiently small nonnegative radii, the image of the input ball contains an output ball whose radius is gamma times the input radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists t_{\max}>0\ \exists N\ni(x_0,y_0)\ \forall(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}\Psi\cap N\ \forall t\in[0,t_{\max}],\quad y+t\gamma B_Y\subseteq\Psi(x+tB_X).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cosmic continuity and cosmic outer semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines sequential cosmic continuity and records the global closed-graph characterization of cosmic outer semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\operatorname{csm}\mathbb{R}^m and \bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n. The mapping S is cosmically continuous at \bar x when, for every sequence x^\nu\to\bar x, one has S(x^\nu)\xrightarrow{c}S(\bar x); cosmic outer and inner semicontinuity are defined analogously using the corresponding cosmic outer and inner limits. Moreover, S is cosmically outer semicontinuous at every x\in\mathbb{R}^n if and only if \operatorname{gph}S is closed in \mathbb{R}^n\times\operatorname{csm}\mathbb{R}^m.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cosmic-set-valued mapping is cosmically continuous at a point if its values converge cosmically along every sequence approaching that point; the outer and inner variants use the corresponding one-sided cosmic limits. Global cosmic outer semicontinuity is equivalent to closedness of its graph in the product with the cosmic-set space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Componentwise criteria for cosmic semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes cosmic outer and inner semicontinuity of a cosmic-set-valued mapping represented by finite and directional components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\operatorname{csm}\mathbb{R}^m have the representation S(x)=C(x)\cup\operatorname{dir}K(x), where C(x)\subset\mathbb{R}^m and K(x)\subset\mathbb{R}^m is a cone. Then S is cosmically outer semicontinuous at \bar x if and only if C(\bar x)\supset\limsup_{x\to\bar x}C(x) and K(\bar x)\supset\limsup_{x\to\bar x}^{\infty}C(x)\cup\limsup_{x\to\bar x}K(x). It is cosmically inner semicontinuous at \bar x if and only if C(\bar x)\subset\liminf_{x\to\bar x}C(x) and K(\bar x)\subset\liminf_{x\to\bar x}^{\infty}C(x)\cup\liminf_{x\to\bar x}K(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a cosmic set represented by an ordinary component C and a directional cone K, cosmic outer semicontinuity is equivalent to the corresponding upper-limit inclusions for C, the horizon limit of C, and K. Cosmic inner semicontinuity is equivalently characterized by the reversed lower-limit inclusions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cosc}_{\bar x}S\Longleftrightarrow\left[C(\bar x)\supset\limsup_{x\to\bar x}C(x),\ K(\bar x)\supset\limsup_{x\to\bar x}^{\infty}C(x)\cup\limsup_{x\to\bar x}K(x)\right],\quad \operatorname{cisc}_{\bar x}S\Longleftrightarrow\left[C(\bar x)\subset\liminf_{x\to\bar x}C(x),\ K(\bar x)\subset\liminf_{x\to\bar x}^{\infty}C(x)\cup\liminf_{x\to\bar x}K(x)\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inner Semicontinuity from Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-valued and graph-convex sufficient or equivalent conditions, plus preservation under pointwise convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m and \bar x\in\mathbb R^n. (a) If S is convex-valued and \operatorname{int}S(\bar x)\ne\varnothing, then S is inner semicontinuous at \bar x relative to \operatorname{dom}S iff, for every u\in\operatorname{int}S(\bar x), there exists W\in\mathcal N(\bar x,u) such that W\cap(\operatorname{dom}S\times\mathbb R^m)\subset\operatorname{gph}S. In particular, S is inner semicontinuous at \bar x iff (\bar x,u)\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{gph}S) for every u\in\operatorname{int}S(\bar x). (b) If \operatorname{gph}S is convex and \bar x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}S), then S is inner semicontinuous at \bar x. (c) If S is inner semicontinuous at \bar x, then T(x)=\operatorname{con}S(x) is inner semicontinuous at \bar x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex-valued multifunction with a nonempty-interior reference value, inner semicontinuity relative to its domain is equivalent to a local graph-neighborhood condition at every interior reference value. A graph-convex multifunction is inner semicontinuous at every interior domain point, and pointwise convexification preserves inner semicontinuity.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is convex-valued and }\operatorname{int}S(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\text{ in part (a)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated local graph conditions characterize or imply inner semicontinuity, and }\operatorname{isc}_{\bar x}S\implies\operatorname{isc}_{\bar x}(x\mapsto\operatorname{con}S(x)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Criteria and sufficient conditions for total continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes total continuity by ordinary continuity plus control of horizon upper limits and gives three regimes where that control is automatic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m. Then S is totally continuous at \bar x if and only if S is continuous at \bar x and \limsup_{x\to\bar x}^{\infty}S(x)\subset S(\bar x)^{\infty}. Consequently, continuity at \bar x implies total continuity whenever S is convex-valued on a neighborhood of \bar x, cone-valued on a neighborhood of \bar x, or locally bounded at \bar x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total continuity is equivalent to ordinary continuity together with an upper-limit condition on horizon sets. For a continuous multifunction, total continuity follows automatically if its nearby values are convex, its nearby values are cones, or it is locally bounded at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is totally continuous at }\bar x\Longleftrightarrow\left[S\text{ is continuous at }\bar x\ \land\ \limsup_{x\to\bar x}^{\infty}S(x)\subset S(\bar x)^{\infty}\right];\quad S\text{ continuous at }\bar x\ \land\ \left[S\text{ locally convex-valued, locally cone-valued, or locally bounded at }\bar x\right]\Longrightarrow S\text{ totally continuous at }\bar x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Total continuity and total semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines total continuity through ordinary and horizon set limits and distinguishes its outer and inner one-sided forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m. The mapping S is totally continuous at \bar x if S(x)\xrightarrow{t}S(\bar x) whenever x\to\bar x, equivalently if \lim_{x\to\bar x}S(x)=S(\bar x) and \lim_{x\to\bar x}^{\infty}S(x)=S(\bar x)^{\infty}. It is totally outer semicontinuous at \bar x if \limsup_{x\to\bar x}S(x)\subset S(\bar x) and \limsup_{x\to\bar x}^{\infty}S(x)\subset S(\bar x)^{\infty}. At \bar x\in\operatorname{dom}S, the analogous total inner conditions are S(\bar x)\subset\liminf_{x\to\bar x}S(x) and S(\bar x)^{\infty}\subset\liminf_{x\to\bar x}^{\infty}S(x); the first inclusion always implies the second, so total inner semicontinuity is equivalent to ordinary inner semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total continuity requires convergence of both the values and their horizon behavior. Total outer semicontinuity requires the corresponding two upper-limit inclusions. For a point in the domain, the proposed horizon condition for total inner semicontinuity follows automatically from ordinary inner semicontinuity, so the two inner notions coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S(x)\xrightarrow{t}S(\bar x)\Longleftrightarrow\left[\lim_{x\to\bar x}S(x)=S(\bar x)\ \land\ \lim_{x\to\bar x}^{\infty}S(x)=S(\bar x)^{\infty}\right],\qquad \operatorname{tisc}_{\bar x}S\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{isc}_{\bar x}S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuity of the Minimum Value and Closedness of the Argmin Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-form Berge theorem for a continuous, nonempty, compact-valued feasible multifunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(\Phi:\mathcal O\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) be continuous, nonempty-valued, and compact-valued, and let \(f:\mathbb R^{n+m}\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. Then \(\theta(x):=\min_{y\in\Phi(x)}f(x,y)\) is finite-valued and continuous on \(\mathcal O\). Moreover, \(S(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\Phi(x)}f(x,y)\) is compact-valued, and for every closed \(C\subseteq\mathcal O\), the restriction \(S|_C\) has a closed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the feasible-set multifunction is continuous with nonempty compact values and the objective is continuous, then the parametric minimum is finite and continuous. The optimizer map has compact values, and its restriction to every closed subset of the parameter domain has a closed graph.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi:\mathcal O\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) is continuous, nonempty-valued, and compact-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta(x)=\min_{y\in\Phi(x)}f(x,y)\) is finite-valued and continuous on \(\mathcal O\); \(S(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\Phi(x)}f(x,y)\) is compact-valued, and \(S|_C\) has a closed graph for every closed \(C\subseteq\mathcal O\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((F_n)\) converges imagewise in the Kuratowski sense to \(F\) when, for every fixed \(x\in X\), \[\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}F_n(x)=F(x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}F_n(x).\] Equivalently, every \(y\in F(x)\) is the limit of some sequence \(y_n\in F_n(x)\), while every convergent subsequence \(y_{n_k}\in F_{n_k}(x)\) has its limit in \(F(x)\). The base point remains fixed throughout both tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each fixed base point, the images converge to the limiting image through matching inner and outer Kuratowski limits.

assumptions_latex: F_n,F:X\rightrightarrows Y\text{ have nonempty compact values}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defined for nonempty compact-valued multifunctions using the Hausdorff metric on each image.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((F_n)\) converges pointwise in Hausdorff distance to \(F\) if, for every fixed \(x\in X\), \[d_H(F_n(x),F(x))\longrightarrow0,\] where \[d_H(A,B):=\max\left\{\sup_{a\in A}d(a,B),\ \sup_{b\in B}d(b,A)\right\}.\] Thus the convergence is tested separately on each image and imposes no uniformity in \(x\). For compact subsets of \(Y\), Hausdorff convergence implies Kuratowski convergence of the corresponding fixed-base images.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every fixed base point, the compact images approach the limiting image in Hausdorff distance, without uniformity across base points.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Hausdorff Convergence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A moving-spike counterexample separating pointwise image convergence from graphical convergence.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F(x):=\{0\}\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), and define \[F_n(x):=\begin{cases}\{1\},&x=1/n,\\\{0\},&x\ne 1/n.\end{cases}\] Then, for every fixed \(x\in\mathbb R\), \(F_n(x)\) converges to \(F(x)\) in Hausdorff distance, whereas \[\operatorname{gph}F_n\xrightarrow{K}\operatorname{gph}F\cup\{(0,1)\}\ne\operatorname{gph}F.\] Thus pointwise image convergence does not imply graphical convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spike moving toward the origin disappears at every fixed base point but produces an additional graphical limit point at (0,1).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For multifunctions \(F_n:X\rightrightarrows Y\), the graphical inner limit is the multifunction whose graph is the Painlevé-Kuratowski inner limit of the graphs. Explicitly, \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}(\operatorname{g\!\!-liminf}_{n\to\infty}F_n)\) exactly when there are points \((x_n,y_n)\in\operatorname{gph}F_n\), for every sufficiently large \(n\), such that \((x_n,y_n)\to(x,y)\). Equivalently, \(d((x,y),\operatorname{gph}F_n)\to0\), with distance to the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For multifunctions \(F_n:X\rightrightarrows Y\), the graphical outer limit is the multifunction whose graph is the Painlevé-Kuratowski outer limit of the graphs. Explicitly, \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}(\operatorname{g\!\!-limsup}_{n\to\infty}F_n)\) exactly when some strictly increasing sequence \((n_k)\) and points \((x_k,y_k)\in\operatorname{gph}F_{n_k}\) satisfy \((x_k,y_k)\to(x,y)\). Thus it records every cluster point obtainable along a subsequence of graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graphical outer limit contains precisely the limits of graph points selected along subsequences of the multifunction sequence.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((F_n)\) converges graphically to \(F\), written \(F_n\xrightarrow{g}F\), when its graphical inner and outer limits coincide with \(F\). Equivalently, every \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\) is approximated by points \((x_n,y_n)\in\operatorname{gph}F_n\), while every convergent subsequence \((x_k,y_k)\in\operatorname{gph}F_{n_k}\) has its limit in \(\operatorname{gph}F\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-sided graphical convergence means that the inner and outer set limits of the graphs both equal the graph of the limit multifunction.

children.title: Inverse Multifunction Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Symmetry between a multifunction and its inverse.

notation.meaning: Inverse multifunction from Y to X

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued inversion without injectivity or surjectivity assumptions.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(y\in Y\), define the inverse value by \(F^{-1}(y)=\{x\in X:y\in F(x)\}\). Then inversion is involutive: for every \(x\in X\), \((F^{-1})^{-1}(x)=F(x)\). Moreover, \(y\in F(x)\) if and only if \(x\in F^{-1}(y)\). These identities hold for arbitrary set-valued mappings, including mappings with empty values, and require neither single-valuedness nor any regularity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set-valued inversion exchanges inputs and outputs and is involutive, even when values are empty or contain multiple points.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Multifunction Symmetry

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

children.title: Graph Transposition
children.top_down_role: Coordinate transposition of multifunction graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(T:X\times Y\to Y\times X\) is defined by \(T(x,y)=(y,x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}=T(\operatorname{gph}F)=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph identity induced by exchanging product coordinates.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every multifunction \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), the graph of its inverse is the coordinate transpose of its graph: \(\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}=T(\operatorname{gph}F)=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}\). The transposition map \(T\) is bijective and involutive, with \(T^{-1}=T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse multifunction's graph is exactly the original graph with its input and output coordinates exchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Transposition

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

children.title: Convergence Invariance
children.top_down_role: Preservation of graphical convergence under inversion or transposition.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, and \(F_n,F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
Both product spaces carry compatible product metrics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_n\xrightarrow{g}F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F_n^{-1}\xrightarrow{g}F^{-1}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance of two-sided graphical convergence under multifunction inversion.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166
Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:X\times Y\to Y\times X\) be given by \(T(x,y)=(y,x)\). Then \(\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}F_n^{-1}=T(\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}F_n)\) and \(\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}F_n^{-1}=T(\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}F_n)\). In particular, \(F_n\xrightarrow{g}F\) if and only if \(F_n^{-1}\xrightarrow{g}F^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphical inner limits, outer limits, and two-sided graphical convergence are invariant under inversion because the associated graphs are coordinate transposes.
knowledge_statements.title: Convergence Invariance

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166
Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Inverse-Symmetry Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Settings where related non-graphical convergence modes lose inverse symmetry.

assumptions_latex: For \(n\ge1\), define \(F_n:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) by \(F_n(1/n)=\{0\}\) and \(F_n(x)=\varnothing\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_n(x)\to F(x)\text{ for every fixed }x,\qquad F_n^{-1}(0)=\{1/n\}\to\{0\}\ne F^{-1}(0).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise convergence lacks the inversion symmetry enjoyed by graphical convergence.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each fixed \(x\in\mathbb R\), one has \(F_n(x)=\varnothing\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), so the values converge pointwise to \(F(x)=\varnothing\). At \(y=0\), however, \(F_n^{-1}(0)=\{1/n\}\), whose set limit is \(\{0\}\), whereas \(F^{-1}(0)=\varnothing\). Hence inversion need not preserve pointwise set convergence. The missing hypothesis is convergence of the entire graphs, which detects the moving points \((1/n,0)\to(0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise set convergence is not invariant under inversion: moving graph points can disappear at every fixed input but persist after inversion.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Symmetry Failure Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

children.title: Localized Graph Convergence
children.top_down_role: Graph convergence observed on bounded or local regions.

assumptions_latex: \((Z,\rho)\) is a metric space with base point \(z_0\), and \(G_n,G\subset Z\) are closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[G_n\to_{m loc}G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sup_{z\in B_r}\left|\min\{1,d(z,G_n)\}-\min\{1,d(z,G)\}\right|\to0\quad\forall r>0.\]

notation.meaning: Closed metric ball of radius r about z_0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local uniform convergence of truncated distance functions for closed graphs.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For closed sets \(G_n,G\subset Z\), localized convergence means uniform convergence on every bounded observation ball of their truncated distance functions. With the convention \(d(z,\varnothing)=+\infty\), this definition also permits empty sets. For multifunctions \(F_n,F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) having closed graphs, localized graph convergence is defined by applying this criterion in \(Z=X\times Y\) to \(G_n=\operatorname{gph}F_n\) and \(G=\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed graphs converge locally when their truncated distance functions converge uniformly on every bounded observation ball.

assumptions_latex: \((Z,\rho)\) is a metric space with base point \(z_0\), and \(G,H\subset Z\) are closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D(G,H)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-m}\delta_m(G,H),\qquad G_n\to_{\rm loc}G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D(G_n,G)\to0.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A summable metric representation of local closed-graph convergence.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(D(G,H)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-m}\delta_m(G,H)\). On the family of closed subsets of \(Z\), including the empty set, \(D\) is a metric. For closed sets \(G_n,G\subset Z\), \(D(G_n,G)\to0\) if and only if \(\delta_m(G_n,G)\to0\) for every integer \(m\ge1\), equivalently \(G_n\to_{\rm loc}G\). Applied to closed graphs, \(D\) metrizes localized graph convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted sum of bounded-window distance-function discrepancies is a metric that metrizes localized convergence of closed graphs.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Graph Convergence

children.title: Bounded-Window Graph Metrics
children.top_down_role: Graph metrics formed through bounded observation windows.

assumptions_latex: \((Z,\rho)\) is a metric space with base point \(z_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\delta_r(G,H)=\sup_{\rho(z,z_0)\le r}\left|\min\{1,d(z,G)\}-\min\{1,d(z,H)\}\right|\in[0,1].\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truncated distance-function discrepancy on a bounded observation window.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For radius \(r>0\), the bounded-window discrepancy between closed sets \(G\) and \(H\) is the uniform difference of their truncated distance functions over \(B_r(z_0)\). Use \(d(z,\varnothing)=+\infty\), so \(\min\{1,d(z,\varnothing)\}=1\). The quantity \(\delta_r\) is symmetric, nonnegative, bounded by \(1\), and satisfies the triangle inequality, although a single fixed window may fail to distinguish sets whose distance functions agree throughout that window.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-window graph discrepancy compares truncated distances to two closed graphs only from points within a fixed observation ball.

children.title: Graph-Convergence Globalization Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of passing from localized graph convergence to global convergence.

assumptions_latex: Localized convergence is measured by bounded-window truncated distance discrepancies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[G_n\to_{\rm loc}G,\qquad d_H(G_n,G)=n\not\to0.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local graph convergence does not control graph components escaping to infinity.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(r>0\). Whenever \(n>2r\), every \(z\in[-r,r]\) is at least as close to \(0\) as to \(n\), hence \(d(z,G_n)=d(z,G)\) and \(\delta_r(G_n,G)=0\). Thus \(G_n\to_{\rm loc}G\). Nevertheless, the global Hausdorff excess of \(G_n\) over \(G\) equals \(d(n,G)=n\), so \(d_H(G_n,G)=n\). Local convergence globalizes only with additional control preventing graph points from escaping beyond all bounded windows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local convergence ignores components escaping to infinity, so it need not imply global Hausdorff convergence without a uniform boundedness condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Convergence Globalization Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise-localized equivalences relative to a set, including the additional graphical characterization when the limit is locally finite.

Let \(f^
u:\mathbb{R}^n	o\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), and \( ar x\in X\). The following are equivalent at \( ar x\) relative to \(X\): (a) \(f^

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes continuous convergence relative to a set and gives a local continuity consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f^
u:\mathbb{R}^n	o\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) and \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\). Then \(f^
u\) converges continuously to \(f\) relative to \(X\) if and only if \(f\) is continuous relative to \(X\) and \(f^
u\) converges uniformly to \(f\) on every compact subset of \(X\). Moreover, if \(f^
u\) converges continuously to \(f\) at \( ar x\in X\) relative to \(X\) and converges pointwise to \(f\) on a relative neighborhood of \( ar x\), then \(f\) is continuous at \( ar x\) relative to \(X\).

Locally, continuous convergence plus pointwise convergence on a relative neighborhood forces continuity of the limit at the point.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space and \((Y,d_Y)\) is a metric space.
\(F_n,F:X\to\mathcal K(Y)\), where \(\mathcal K(Y)\) denotes the nonempty compact subsets of \(Y\).

notation.meaning: Hausdorff distance induced by the metric on Y

source_refs.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sequence \((F_n)\) converges compact-uniformly to \(F\) if, for every compact set \(K\subset X\),
\[
\sup_{x\in K}d_H\bigl(F_n(x),F(x)\bigr)\longrightarrow 0.
\]
The empty compact set imposes no condition, with its supremum conventionally equal to \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact-uniform convergence means that the Hausdorff error between the multifunction values tends uniformly to zero on every compact subset of the domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Uniform Convergence

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space and \((Y,d_Y)\) is a metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\to F\) locally uniformly exactly when every point admits a neighborhood satisfying the displayed uniform estimate.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local uniformity is measured by Hausdorff distance between values.

source_refs.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sequence \((F_n)\) converges locally uniformly to \(F\) if, for every \(x\in X\), there exists a neighborhood \(U_x\) of \(x\), independent of \(n\), such that
\[
\sup_{u\in U_x}d_H\bigl(F_n(u),F(u)\bigr)\longrightarrow 0.
\]
The neighborhood may depend on \(x\), while the convergence is uniform over all points of that neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local uniform convergence requires uniform Hausdorff convergence on some fixed neighborhood of each domain point.
knowledge_statements.title: Locally Uniform Convergence

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local uniform convergence implies compact-uniform convergence; exhaustion convergence characterizes compact-uniform convergence, and local compactness makes the local and compact-uniform modes equivalent.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(F_n\to F\) locally uniformly, then \(F_n\to F\) compact-uniformly. Moreover,
\[
F_n\to F\text{ compact-uniformly}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sup_{x\in K_m}d_H\bigl(F_n(x),F(x)\bigr)\to0
\text{ for every }m.
\]
If, in addition, every point of \(X\) has a compact neighborhood, then compact-uniform convergence also implies locally uniform convergence; hence the two modes coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local uniform convergence implies compact-uniform convergence. A cofinal compact exhaustion tests compact-uniform convergence, and local compactness makes the two notions equivalent.

\[

For each nonempty closed graph define \(\delta_F(z)=d(z,\operatorname{gph}F)\). The graph-distance metric
\[
D_{\mathrm{gd}}(F,G)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-m}\min\!\left\{1,\sup_{z\in B_m}|\delta_F(z)-\delta_G(z)|\right\}
\]
is finite and vanishes exactly when \(\operatorname{gph}F=\operatorname{gph}G\). Thus graph convergence can be represented as \(D_{\mathrm{gd}}(F_n,F)\to0\), equivalently as uniform convergence of the graph-distance functions on every bounded ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted sum of local sup-norm differences between graph-distance functions defines a metric for closed multifunction graphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat d_r\) is a finite symmetric graph discrepancy at radius \(r\), and its zero value records mutual inclusion inside the truncation ball.

notation.meaning: Closed radius-r ball centered at the base point

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With \(e(\varnothing,B)=0\), the radius-\(r\) truncated-graph discrepancy is
\[
\widehat d_r(F,G)=\max\!\left\{e\bigl(\operatorname{gph}F\cap B_r,\operatorname{gph}G\bigr),e\bigl(\operatorname{gph}G\cap B_r,\operatorname{gph}F\bigr)\right\}.
\]
Unlike the Hausdorff distance between two separately truncated graphs, each truncated portion is compared with the full opposing graph, avoiding artificial discrepancies caused solely by cutting near the boundary of \(B_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The truncated-graph discrepancy symmetrizes excesses from each graph inside a bounded ball to the full opposing graph.

children.title: Truncation-Radius Dependence
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of metric descriptions to the chosen truncation scale.

assumptions_latex: \((Z,d)\) is a metric space with base point \(z_0\).
\(F_n,F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) have nonempty closed graphs in \(Z=X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convergence of every fixed-radius discrepancy is equivalent to convergence along any unbounded increasing sequence of radii.

notation.meaning: Symmetric truncated-graph discrepancy at radius r
An unbounded increasing sequence of truncation radii

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radius monotonicity makes any unbounded radius exhaustion convergence-determining.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The truncated discrepancy is monotone in its radius:
\[
0<r\le s\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \widehat d_r(F,G)\le\widehat d_s(F,G).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\widehat d_r(F_n,F)\to0\text{ for every }r>0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\widehat d_{r_j}(F_n,F)\to0\text{ for every }j.
\]
Thus the resulting convergence mode does not depend on the particular unbounded increasing radius sequence used to test it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Truncated-graph discrepancies increase with radius, so convergence can be tested on any fixed unbounded sequence of radii.
knowledge_statements.title: Truncation-Radius Dependence

children.title: Image-Excess Profiles
children.top_down_role: Directional excess measurements for images of multifunctions.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d_X)\) and \((Y,d_Y)\) are metric spaces, with base point \(x_0\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The profile \(E_r(F\mid G)\) records the worst directed image excess over inputs in the radius-\(r\) ball.

notation.meaning: Excess of A over B in Y
Closed radius-r ball in X centered at x_0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed, radius-indexed discrepancy between multifunction images.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181
C. Pompeiu-Hausdorff Distance p. 117

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(r>0\), the directed image-excess profile of \(F\) relative to \(G\) is
\[
E_r(F\mid G)=\sup_{x\in B_X(r)}e_Y\bigl(F(x),G(x)\bigr),
\qquad
e_Y(A,B)=\sup_{a\in A}\inf_{b\in B}d_Y(a,b).
\]
The profile is nondecreasing in \(r\), need not be symmetric in \(F,G\), and may take the value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An image-excess profile gives, at each domain radius, the largest directed excess of one multifunction’s values over another’s.

children.title: Hausdorff Image Profiles
children.top_down_role: Symmetric Hausdorff measurements across domain-indexed images.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d_X)\) and \((Y,d_Y)\) are metric spaces, with base point \(x_0\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The profile \(H_r(F,G)\) is the pointwise symmetrization of the two directed image-excess profiles.

notation.meaning: Hausdorff distance on nonempty compact subsets of Y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric image profile for compact-valued multifunctions.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181
C. Pompeiu-Hausdorff Distance p. 117

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(r>0\), define
\[
H_r(F,G)=\sup_{x\in B_X(r)}d_H\bigl(F(x),G(x)\bigr).
\]
Since \(d_H(A,B)=\max\{e_Y(A,B),e_Y(B,A)\}\), one has the exact representation
\[
H_r(F,G)=\max\bigl\{E_r(F\mid G),E_r(G\mid F)\bigr\}.
\]
Thus \(H_r\) is symmetric and nondecreasing in \(r\), and \(H_r(F_n,F)\to0\) expresses uniform Hausdorff convergence on \(B_X(r)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hausdorff image profile is exactly the maximum of the two oppositely directed image-excess profiles.
knowledge_statements.title: Hausdorff Image Profiles

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hausdorff Continuity at a Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise epsilon–delta continuity of a set-valued mapping in Hausdorff distance. The extract does not impose nonempty, closed, or bounded values, so well-definedness and finiteness of the Hausdorff distance require appropriate conventions or value restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set-valued mapping \(G:\mathbb{R}^n\to 2^{\mathbb{R}^m}\) is Hausdorff continuous at \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) if
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists\delta>0\;\forall y\in B(x;\delta),\qquad d_H\bigl(G(y),G(x)\bigr)<\varepsilon.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued mapping is Hausdorff continuous at x if, for every positive tolerance, all sufficiently nearby points have images within that tolerance of G(x) in Hausdorff distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists\delta>0\;\forall y\in B(x;\delta),\ d_H\bigl(G(y),G(x)\bigr)<\varepsilon

children.top_down_role: Relations between one-sided image excess and symmetric image distance.

assumptions_latex: \(F,G:X\to\mathcal K(Y)\), where \(X,Y\) are metric spaces and \(x_0\in X\).
\(E_m(F\mid G)\) and \(H_m(F,G)\) are the radius-\(m\) directed and symmetric image profiles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The symmetric profile metric lies between the maximum and the sum of its two directional counterparts.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative comparison of integrated directional and symmetric image profiles.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
D^{\to}(F,G)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-m}\min\{1,E_m(F\mid G)\},
\qquad
D^H(F,G)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-m}\min\{1,H_m(F,G)\}.
\]
Then
\[
\max\{D^{\to}(F,G),D^{\to}(G,F)\}
\le D^H(F,G)
\le D^{\to}(F,G)+D^{\to}(G,F).
\]
Hence convergence in the symmetric profile metric is equivalent to convergence in both directional profile discrepancies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric image-profile metric is equivalent to requiring both directional excess-profile discrepancies to vanish.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional-Derivative and Subdifferential Upper Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-dimensional result for pointwise convergence on an open convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] be convex, let C\subset\mathbb{R}^n be open and convex with f finite on C, and let (f_i) be convex functions finite on C such that f_i(u)\to f(u) for every u\in C. If x_i\in C, x_i\to x\in C, and y_i\to y\in\mathbb{R}^n, then \limsup_{i\to\infty}f_i'(x_i;y_i)\le f'(x;y). Moreover, for every \varepsilon>0 there exists i_0 such that \partial f_i(x_i)\subseteq\partial f(x)+\varepsilon B for all i\ge i_0, where B is the Euclidean unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex functions finite on a common open convex set and converging there pointwise, directional derivatives along convergent base points and directions have an upper-limit bounded by the limiting directional derivative. The corresponding subdifferentials are eventually contained in any prescribed Euclidean enlargement of the limiting subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is open and convex, and }f\text{ is finite on }C
f_i\text{ is convex and finite on }C\text{ for every }i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential selection properties of a set-valued mapping at a parameter point and at a graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Gamma:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\). It is inner semicompact at \(\bar z\) if, for every sequence \(z^k\to\bar z\), there exist \(\alpha^k\in\Gamma(z^k)\) such that \((\alpha^k)\) contains a convergent subsequence. It is inner semicontinuous at \((\bar z,\bar\alpha)\in\operatorname{gph}\Gamma\) if, for every sequence \(z^k\to\bar z\), there exist \(\alpha^k\in\Gamma(z^k)\) satisfying \(\alpha^k\to\bar\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inner semicompactness permits selections along every convergent parameter sequence that have a convergent subsequence. Inner semicontinuity at a graph point permits selections converging to the specified graph value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Gamma\text{ satisfies the corresponding sequential selection property.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise convergence is imposed on a common open convex finiteness region, with base points allowed to vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K and K_i be concave in u and convex in v, all finite on an open convex set C\times D, with K_i\to K pointwise on C\times D. For every \(x\in X\), the set \(\{F_n(x):n\ge1\}\) has compact closure in \((\mathcal K(Y),d_H)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A subsequence converges compact-uniformly in Hausdorff distance to a continuous compact-valued multifunction.

notation.meaning: Hausdorff metric on nonempty compact subsets of Y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential Arzelà–Ascoli theorem in the Hausdorff hyperspace.

source_refs.locator: F. Equicontinuity of Sequences p. 173
G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist indices \(n_1<n_2<\cdots\) and a continuous mapping \(F:X\to\mathcal K(Y)\) such that, for every compact set \(K\subset X\),
\[
\sup_{x\in K}d_H\bigl(F_{n_j}(x),F(x)\bigr)\longrightarrow0
\quad\text{as }j\to\infty.
\]
Equivalently, every equicontinuous, pointwise relatively compact sequence of continuous \(\mathcal K(Y)\)-valued mappings is sequentially relatively compact for compact-uniform convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equicontinuity and pointwise relative compactness yield a subsequence converging uniformly on compact sets to a continuous compact-valued multifunction.
knowledge_statements.title: Arzelà–Ascoli-Type Multifunction Compactness

source_witnesses.locator: F. Equicontinuity of Sequences p. 173
G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Set-Valued Arzelà–Ascoli Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A compactness theorem for asymptotically equicontinuous sequences of multifunctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If (S^\nu) is a sequence of mappings S^\nu:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m that is asymptotically equicontinuous relative to X\subset\mathbb R^n, then it has a subsequence converging uniformly on every compact subset of X to a mapping S:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m that is continuous relative to X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every asymptotically equicontinuous sequence of multifunctions relative to X has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact subsets of X to a multifunction continuous relative to X.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists(\nu_k),\ \exists S:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m:\ S^{\nu_k}\to S\text{ uniformly on every compact }K\subset X,\quad S\text{ continuous relative to }X.

children.title: Generic Continuity Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Convergence consequences involving residual or generic continuity behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Baire metric space and \(Y\) is a compact metric space.
\(F:X\to\mathcal K(Y)\) is Baire-one for the Hausdorff metric on nonempty compact subsets of \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in X:F\text{ is Hausdorff-continuous at }x\}\) is residual in \(X\).

notation.meaning: Hausdorff distance induced by the metric of Y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Baire-one compact-valued version of generic continuity.

source_refs.locator: J.* Generic Continuity and Selections p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Baire metric space, let \(Y\) be a compact metric space, and equip \(\mathcal K(Y)\) with the Hausdorff metric \(d_H\). If \(F:X\to\mathcal K(Y)\) is the pointwise Hausdorff limit of continuous mappings \(F_k:X\to\mathcal K(Y)\), then the set of points \(x\in X\) at which \(d_H(F(x'),F(x))\to0\) whenever \(x'\to x\) is a dense \(G_\delta\) subset of \(X\). Thus a Baire-one compact-valued multifunction admits a residual interface on which ordinary sequential limits and value-set limits agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact-valued multifunction that is a pointwise limit of continuous multifunctions is Hausdorff-continuous on a residual set of its Baire domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Generic Continuity Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: J.* Generic Continuity and Selections p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generic Continuity from Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic relative continuity of closed-valued multifunctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) be closed-valued and let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\). If \(S\) is outer semicontinuous relative to \(X\), or inner semicontinuous relative to \(X\), then \(\{x\in X:S\text{ is not continuous at }x\text{ relative to }X\}\) is meager in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed-valued multifunction that is either outer or inner semicontinuous relative to X is continuous relative to X except on a meager subset of X.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is osc relative to }X\text{ or isc relative to }X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x\in X:S\text{ fails to be continuous relative to }X\}\text{ is meager in }X

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generic boundary continuity of the normal-cone mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Baire-category generic continuity relative to the boundary of an arbitrary finite-dimensional set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every C\subset\mathbb R^n, the set \{\bar x\in\operatorname{bdry}C:N_C\text{ is not continuous at }\bar x\text{ relative to }\operatorname{bdry}C\} is meager in \operatorname{bdry}C. Hence the points where N_C is continuous relative to \operatorname{bdry}C are dense in \operatorname{bdry}C.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space, discontinuity points of its normal-cone mapping form a meager subset of the boundary. Thus relative continuity points are dense in the boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{\bar x\in\operatorname{bdry}C:N_C\text{ fails to be continuous relative to }\operatorname{bdry}C\}\text{ is meager in }\operatorname{bdry}C;\quad \{\bar x\in\operatorname{bdry}C:N_C\text{ is relatively continuous}\}\text{ is dense in }\operatorname{bdry}C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generic Continuity of Semicontinuous Extended-Real Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Function-valued specialization of generic continuity from semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\). If \(f\) is lower semicontinuous relative to \(X\), or upper semicontinuous relative to \(X\), then \(\{x\in X:f\text{ is not continuous at }x\text{ relative to }X\}\) is meager in \(X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior Upper Semicontinuity of Directional Derivatives and Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded local continuity result for a proper convex function on the interior of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] is proper and convex, then (x,y)\mapsto f'(x;y) is upper semicontinuous on \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\times\mathbb{R}^n. Moreover, for every x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f) and every \varepsilon>0, there exists \delta>0 such that \partial f(z)\subseteq\partial f(x)+\varepsilon B for every z\in x+\delta B, where B is the Euclidean unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function, the directional derivative is jointly upper semicontinuous in the base point and direction when the base point lies in the interior of the effective domain. Nearby subdifferentials are contained in any prescribed enlargement of the subdifferential at an interior point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x,y)\mapsto f'(x;y)\text{ is upper semicontinuous on }\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\times\mathbb{R}^n,\quad \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0\ \forall z\in x+\delta B:\ \partial f(z)\subseteq\partial f(x)+\varepsilon B.

children.title: Selection-Limit Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Limit behavior of selected trajectories or selected single-valued representatives.

assumptions_latex: Graph convergence means Painlevé-Kuratowski convergence in \(X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F_n\to\operatorname{gph}F\) exactly when the outer and inner selection conditions both hold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization of graphical convergence in metric spaces.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graphical convergence \(\operatorname{gph}F_n\to\operatorname{gph}F\) is equivalent to the following two selection-limit interfaces. First, whenever \(n_k\uparrow\infty\), \(x_k\to x\), \(y_k\to y\), and \(y_k\in F_{n_k}(x_k)\), one has \(y\in F(x)\). Second, for every \(x\in X\) and \(y\in F(x)\), there exist \(x_n\to x\) and \(y_n\to y\) such that \(y_n\in F_n(x_n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). The first condition controls all convergent selected subsequences, while the second supplies recovery selections for every limiting graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphical convergence is equivalent to an outer closedness rule for convergent selections plus a recovery-selection rule for every point of the limiting graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Limit Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Selection-Theory Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundary between convergence questions retained here and selection theory owned elsewhere.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is paracompact, \(E\) is a Banach space, and \(F:X\rightrightarrows E\) is lower semicontinuous.
The values of \(F\) are nonempty and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity guarantees a continuous selection, whereas closed nonconvex values need not do so.

notation.meaning: Unit circle in the complex plane
Square-root multifunction on the unit circle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-valued continuous-selection boundary with a circle counterexample.

source_refs.locator: J.* Generic Continuity and Selections p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every value \(F(x)\) is convex, then the lower semicontinuous multifunction \(F:X\rightrightarrows E\) has a continuous selection \(f:X\to E\) satisfying \(f(x)\in F(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). Closedness without convexity is insufficient: the compact-valued multifunction \(R:\mathbb S^1\rightrightarrows\mathbb S^1\), defined by \(R(z)=\{w\in\mathbb S^1:w^2=z\}\), is continuous and has nonempty finite closed values but has no continuous selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower semicontinuous multifunction with nonempty closed convex values has a continuous selection, while closed nonconvex values do not suffice, as shown by the square-root multifunction on the circle.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Theory Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: J.* Generic Continuity and Selections p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Escape to the horizon
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bounded-region avoidance condition for a sequence of set-valued mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sequence S^
u:\mathbb R^nightrightarrows\mathbb R^m escapes to the horizon if, for every bounded C\subset\mathbb R^n and bounded D\subset\mathbb R^m, there exists an infinite index set N\subset\mathbb N such that S^
u(x)\cap D=\varnothing for every 
u\in N and every x\in C.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction sequence escapes to the horizon when, for every bounded set of arguments and every bounded set of values, an infinite subsequence has no values in the bounded value set at any argument in the bounded argument set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall C,D\text{ bounded},\ \exists N\subset\mathbb N\text{ infinite}:\ \forall\nu\in N,\ \forall x\in C,\ S^\nu(x)\cap D=\varnothing.

children.title: Inverse-Multifunction Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior under inversion of set-valued mappings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n^{-1}\to F^{-1}\) graphically in \(Y\times X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphical limits under inversion of a multifunction.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(n\), define \(F_n^{-1}:Y\rightrightarrows X\) by \(F_n^{-1}(y)=\{x\in X:y\in F_n(x)\}\), and define \(F^{-1}\) analogously. If \(F_n\to F\) graphically in \(X\times Y\), then \(F_n^{-1}\to F^{-1}\) graphically in \(Y\times X\). This limit rule requires no local boundedness or compactness hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphical convergence is preserved by multifunction inversion, with no additional boundedness or compactness hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Multifunction Limits

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Transposed-Graph Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior under coordinate transposition of graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces and \(C_n,C\subset X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_n^{\mathsf T}\to C^{\mathsf T}\) in \(Y\times X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set convergence under transposition of graph coordinates.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a relation \(C\subset X\times Y\), define \(C^{\mathsf T}=\{(y,x)\in Y\times X:(x,y)\in C\}\). If \(C_n\to C\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense, then \(C_n^{\mathsf T}\to C^{\mathsf T}\). Transposition commutes with both the outer and inner set limits and requires no auxiliary compactness hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transposing each relation by swapping its coordinates preserves Painleve-Kuratowski convergence without an additional compactness hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.title: Transposed-Graph Limits

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Inversion–Transposition Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The convergence interface linking inverse mappings with transposed graphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}(F^{-1})=(\operatorname{gph}F)^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact identification of inversion with graph transposition.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every multifunction \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), define \(F^{-1}:Y\rightrightarrows X\) by \(x\in F^{-1}(y)\) if and only if \(y\in F(x)\). Its graph representation is
\[\operatorname{gph}(F^{-1})=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}=(\operatorname{gph}F)^{\mathsf T}.\]
Both operations are involutive: \((F^{-1})^{-1}=F\) and \(((\operatorname{gph}F)^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T}=\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multifunction inversion is represented exactly by graph transposition, and both operations are involutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Inversion–Transposition Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Multifunction Sum Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior of pointwise set-valued sums.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is metric and \(Y\) is a finite-dimensional normed space.
The sets \(H_n(x')\) are locally uniformly bounded near each \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n+G_n\to F+G\) graphically.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sum rule using joint graphical convergence.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_n:X\rightrightarrows Y\times Y\) be given by \(H_n(x)=F_n(x)\times G_n(x)\), and suppose \(H_n\to H\) graphically with \(H(x)=F(x)\times G(x)\). Assume that for every \(x\in X\) there are a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\), a bounded set \(B\subset Y\times Y\), and \(n_0\) such that \(H_n(x')\subset B\) for \(x'\in U\) and \(n\ge n_0\). Then the continuous addition map \(a(y,z)=y+z\) yields graphical convergence \(a\circ H_n\to a\circ H\), equivalently \(F_n+G_n\to F+G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint graphical convergence of the two summands, together with local uniform boundedness, passes through addition and yields convergence of their pointwise sums.
knowledge_statements.title: Multifunction Sum Limits

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Multifunction Product Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior of product-valued mapping constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is metric, \(Y_1,Y_2,Z\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces, and \(b:Y_1\times Y_2\to Z\) is continuous bilinear.
The joint values are locally uniformly bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b(F_n,G_n)\to b(F,G)\) graphically.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous bilinear-product rule with bounded joint factors.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(H_n(x)=F_n(x)\times G_n(x)\) and \(H(x)=F(x)\times G(x)\). Suppose \(H_n\to H\) graphically and, locally in \(x\), all sufficiently late values of \(H_n\) lie in one bounded subset of \(Y_1\times Y_2\). For the multifunction \(P_n:X\rightrightarrows Z\) defined by \(P_n(x)=\{b(y,z):y\in F_n(x),\ z\in G_n(x)\}\), one then has \(P_n\to P\) graphically, where \(P(x)=\{b(y,z):y\in F(x),\ z\in G(x)\}\). The boundedness prevents factor pairs with finite products from escaping to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous bilinear operation preserves joint graphical convergence when the factor pairs are locally uniformly bounded, preventing hidden products from escaping factors.
knowledge_statements.title: Multifunction Product Limits

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Cartesian-Construction Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior of Cartesian products of values or graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(F_n:X_1\rightrightarrows Y_1\) and \(G_n:X_2\rightrightarrows Y_2\) converge graphically to \(F\) and \(G\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\boxtimes G_n\to F\boxtimes G\) graphically.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Cartesian products of independently convergent graphs.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \((F_n\boxtimes G_n)(x_1,x_2)=F_n(x_1)\times G_n(x_2)\) and define \(F\boxtimes G\) analogously. If \(F_n\to F\) and \(G_n\to G\) graphically, then \(F_n\boxtimes G_n\to F\boxtimes G\) graphically. Under the canonical regrouping of coordinates,
\[\operatorname{gph}(F_n\boxtimes G_n)=\operatorname{gph}F_n\times\operatorname{gph}G_n.\]
No compactness assumption is required for this finite independent Cartesian construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite Cartesian products of independently graph-convergent multifunctions converge graphically, with no additional compactness assumption.
knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian-Construction Limits

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Product-Compactness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Compactness restrictions affecting product and Cartesian limit preservation.

assumptions_latex: Set convergence is Painleve-Kuratowski convergence in Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without bounded factor pairs, convergence of sets need not pass to their product images.

notation.meaning: A sequence of two-point factor sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Escaping-factor obstruction for product-image convergence.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(A_n=\{(n,1/n),(0,1)\}\) and \(A=\{(0,1)\}\). Then \(A_n\to A\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense. For the continuous multiplication map \(m:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\), one has \(m(A_n)=\{0,1\}\) for every \(n\), while \(m(A)=\{0\}\). Thus \(m(A_n)\) does not converge to \(m(A)\), exhibiting failure of product-image convergence when factor pairs may escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sets consisting of an escaping factor pair and a fixed pair converge, but their multiplication images do not, demonstrating the need to control unbounded factor pairs.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Compactness Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Direct Composition Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence of ordinary compositions of set-valued mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y,Z\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces and \(F_n:X\rightrightarrows Y\), \(G_n:Y\rightrightarrows Z\) converge graphically to \(F\) and \(G\), respectively.
Whenever \(n_k\uparrow\infty\), \(x_k\to x\), \(z_k\to z\), and \(z_k\in(G_{n_k}\circ F_{n_k})(x_k)\), there are bounded witnesses \(y_k\in F_{n_k}(x_k)\) satisfying \(z_k\in G_{n_k}(y_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\limsup_n\operatorname{gph}(G_n\circ F_n)\subset\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer-limit theorem for compositions with bounded intermediate witnesses.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H_n=G_n\circ F_n\) and \(H=G\circ F\). Assume that whenever \(n_k\uparrow\infty\), \(x_k\to x\), \(z_k\to z\), and \(z_k\in H_{n_k}(x_k)\), there exist witnesses \(y_k\in F_{n_k}(x_k)\) such that \(z_k\in G_{n_k}(y_k)\) and the sequence \((y_k)\) is bounded. Then
\[\limsup_n\operatorname{gph}H_n\subset\operatorname{gph}H.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every convergent outer sequence for the compositions has a bounded choice of intermediate witnesses, graphical convergence of the component multifunctions yields the outer graphical limit inclusion for their compositions.
knowledge_statements.title: Direct Composition Limits

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Implicit Composition Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence of compositions mediated by latent variables or relational constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y,Z\) are metric spaces and \(F_n:X\rightrightarrows Y\), \(G_n:Y\rightrightarrows Z\).
Every \((x,z)\in\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F)\) admits a witness \(y\in F(x)\) with \(z\in G(y)\) and a compatible recovery sequence through \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F)\subset\liminf_n\operatorname{gph}(G_n\circ F_n)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatible-lifting condition for the inner composition limit.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H_n=G_n\circ F_n\) and \(H=G\circ F\). A compatible-lifting condition is that, for every \(x\in X\) and \(z\in H(x)\), there exist \(y\in F(x)\) with \(z\in G(y)\) and sequences \(x_n\to x\), \(y_n\to y\), and \(z_n\to z\) such that \(y_n\in F_n(x_n)\) and \(z_n\in G_n(y_n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Under this condition,
\[\operatorname{gph}H\subset\liminf_n\operatorname{gph}H_n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inner composition limit follows when every point of the limiting composition graph has one intermediate witness admitting compatible recovery sequences through both component multifunctions.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Composition Limits

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Intermediate-Variable Compactness
children.top_down_role: Compactness requirements for variables eliminated during composition.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y,Z\) are metric spaces and \(F_n:X\rightrightarrows Y\), \(G_n:Y\rightrightarrows Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\limsup_n\operatorname{gph}(G_n\circ F_n)\subset\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential compactness condition supporting the outer-limit calculus for compositions of multifunctions.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that whenever \(x_{n_k}\to x\), \(z_{n_k}\to z\), and \(z_{n_k}\in(G_{n_k}\circ F_{n_k})(x_{n_k})\), there exist intermediate points \(y_k\in F_{n_k}(x_{n_k})\) with \(z_{n_k}\in G_{n_k}(y_k)\) such that \((y_k)\) has a convergent subsequence. Then every outer graphical cluster point \((x,z)\) of the compositions has an intermediate point \(y\) satisfying \(y\in F(x)\) and \(z\in G(y)\). Consequently, \[\limsup_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}(G_n\circ F_n)\subset\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer graphical limits pass through composition when every convergent input-output sequence admits a subsequentially convergent sequence of intermediate variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate-Variable Compactness

children.title: Qualification Failures
children.top_down_role: Limit mismatches caused by missing compatibility or regularity conditions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_n\cap B_n=\varnothing\) for every \(n\), although \(A_n\to B\) and \(B_n\to B\) with \(B\cap B=B\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary intersection counterregime illustrating why operation qualifications cannot be omitted.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_n=\mathbb R\times\{1/n\}\), \(B_n=B=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\), and use Painleve-Kuratowski convergence. Then \(A_n\to B\) and \(B_n\to B\), but \(A_n\cap B_n=\varnothing\) for every \(n\). Hence \[\lim_{n\to\infty}(A_n\cap B_n)=\varnothing\ne B=(\lim_{n\to\infty}A_n)\cap(\lim_{n\to\infty}B_n).\] Thus convergence of the operands alone does not justify passing a limit through intersection; a qualification preventing asymptotically incompatible contact is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two convergent set sequences can have empty intersections even though their limits coincide, so intersection calculus requires an additional qualification.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualification Failures

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

children.title: Compactness Failures
children.top_down_role: Limit mismatches caused by escaping or nonprecompact intermediate objects.

assumptions_latex: \(F_n,G_n:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) are the multifunctions specified below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F_n\to\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{gph}G_n\to\varnothing\), while \(\operatorname{gph}(G_n\circ F_n)=\{(0,0)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Escaping intermediate variables destroy the expected outer-limit inclusion for composition.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F_n(0)=\{n\}\), \(F_n(x)=\varnothing\) for \(x\ne0\), and \(G_n(n)=\{0\}\), \(G_n(y)=\varnothing\) for \(y\ne n\). Both graphs escape every bounded region, so \(\operatorname{gph}F_n\to\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{gph}G_n\to\varnothing\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense. Nevertheless, \[(G_n\circ F_n)(0)=\{0\},\qquad \operatorname{gph}(G_n\circ F_n)=\{(0,0)\}.\] The composition retains a finite limit point solely through the unbounded intermediate variable \(n\), demonstrating failure without intermediate-variable compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component graphs may escape while their compositions retain finite points because unbounded intermediate variables cancel the escape.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Failures

children.title: Operation-Specific Counterregimes
children.top_down_role: Failure patterns specific to inversion, products, sums, or composition.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_n\to\varnothing\) and \(B_n\to\varnothing\), but \(A_n+B_n=\{0\}\) for every \(n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minkowski addition has an escape-cancellation counterregime distinct from intersection and composition failures.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_n=\{n\}\) and \(B_n=\{-n\}\). In \(\mathbb R\), both sequences converge in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense to the empty set because their unique points escape to infinity. However, their Minkowski sums satisfy \[A_n+B_n=\{n-n\}=\{0\}\quad\text{for every }n.\] Hence \(A_n+B_n\to\{0\}\), whereas the sum of the operand limits is empty. This operation-specific failure is caused by cancellation between two unbounded selections and is excluded by suitable boundedness or no-cancellation hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minkowski sums can retain finite points through cancellation of unbounded operands even when both operand sequences converge to the empty set.
knowledge_statements.title: Operation-Specific Counterregimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), define its epigraph by \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\le r\}.\] The sequence \((f_n)\) converges epigraphically to \(f\), written \(f_n\xrightarrow{e}f\), when the epigraphs converge in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense in the product metric space: \[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{epi}f_n=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{epi}f_n=\operatorname{epi}f.\] Equivalently, the lower and upper set limits of the epigraphs agree with the epigraph of the limiting function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Function generated by an upper-stable set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes empty, full, and proper nonempty vertical fibers and possible omission of boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\) is upper stable if \((x,\mu)\in\Omega\) and \(\mu'\ge\mu\) imply \((x,\mu')\in\Omega\). Define \(\varphi:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) by \(\varphi(x)=\inf\{\mu:(x,\mu)\in\Omega\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). An empty vertical fiber gives \(\varphi(x)=+\infty\), a full vertical fiber gives \(\varphi(x)=-\infty\), and every proper nonempty fiber has a threshold \(\lambda=\varphi(x)\) such that all \(\mu>\lambda\) belong to the fiber and all \(\mu<\lambda\) do not. Consequently, \(\operatorname{epi}\varphi\) can differ from \(\Omega\) only at boundary points \((x,\varphi(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper-stable set is closed upward along every vertical line. Taking the infimum of each vertical fiber generates an extended-real function whose epigraph agrees with the set except possibly at threshold points on the graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi(x)=\inf\{\mu:(x,\mu)\in\Omega\},\qquad \operatorname{epi}\varphi\triangle\Omega\subseteq\{(x,\varphi(x)):x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \varphi(x)\in\mathbb R\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hypographical convergence is Painleve-Kuratowski convergence of hypographs, equivalently epigraphical convergence after negating the functions.

children.title: Level-Set Convergence

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space, \(f_n,f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_\alpha(f_n)\to L_\alpha(f)\) is level-set convergence at \(\alpha\).

source_refs.locator: C. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 250

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the level set of \(f\) at \(\alpha\) by \[L_\alpha(f)=\{x\in X:f(x)=\alpha\}.\] The sequence \((f_n)\) has level-set convergence to \(f\) at \(\alpha\) when \[\liminf_{n\to\infty}L_\alpha(f_n)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}L_\alpha(f_n)=L_\alpha(f).\] In sequential terms, every limit of points \(x_{n_k}\in L_\alpha(f_{n_k})\) belongs to \(L_\alpha(f)\), and each \(x\in L_\alpha(f)\) is approached by some sequence \(x_n\in L_\alpha(f_n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Level-set convergence means that the exact equality sets at a fixed threshold converge in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Set Convergence

children.title: Sublevel-Set Convergence

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space, \(f_n,f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_\alpha(f_n)\to S_\alpha(f)\) is sublevel-set convergence at \(\alpha\).

notation.meaning: closed sublevel set at threshold alpha

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-sublevel convergence at one fixed finite threshold.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the closed sublevel set of \(f\) at \(\alpha\) by \[S_\alpha(f)=\{x\in X:f(x)\le\alpha\}.\] The sequence \((f_n)\) has sublevel-set convergence to \(f\) at \(\alpha\) when \[\liminf_{n\to\infty}S_\alpha(f_n)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}S_\alpha(f_n)=S_\alpha(f).\] Thus every cluster point of points satisfying \(f_n(x_n)\le\alpha\) must satisfy \(f(x)\le\alpha\), and every point of \(S_\alpha(f)\) must admit approximating points in the corresponding sublevel sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sublevel-set convergence is Painleve-Kuratowski convergence of the sets on which each function does not exceed a fixed threshold.

children.top_down_role: Threshold values where set-limit representations change or cease to agree.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(f_n\xrightarrow{e}f\), where \(f_n,f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\{f<\alpha\}}\subset\liminf_n S_\alpha(f_n)\subset\limsup_n S_\alpha(f_n)\subset\{f\le\alpha\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold regularity boundary for deriving sublevel convergence from epigraphical convergence.

source_refs.locator: C. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 250

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite threshold \(\alpha\), epigraphical convergence yields the sandwich \[\overline{\{x:f(x)<\alpha\}}\subset\liminf_{n\to\infty}S_\alpha(f_n)\subset\limsup_{n\to\infty}S_\alpha(f_n)\subset\{x:f(x)\le\alpha\}.\] Therefore, if \(\overline{\{f<\alpha\}}=\{f\le\alpha\}\), then \(S_\alpha(f_n)\to S_\alpha(f)\). Thresholds for which this density equality fails are exceptional: epigraphical convergence alone need not recover boundary points lying in \(\{f=\alpha\}\) but outside \(\overline{\{f<\alpha\}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epi-convergence gives sublevel convergence at thresholds where strict sublevels are dense in closed sublevels; failure of this density identifies exceptional thresholds.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold-Exceptional Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gamma convergence and its fundamental stability properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential definition of Gamma convergence, stability of minima and minimizers, continuous perturbations, and the stated Modica–Mortola example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $F_n:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ on a metric space $X$, define $$F^-(x)=\inf_{x_n\to x}\liminf_{n\to\infty}F_n(x_n),\qquad F^+(x)=\inf_{x_n\to x}\limsup_{n\to\infty}F_n(x_n).$$ One has $F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F$ when $F^-=F^+=F$. A family $F_\varepsilon$ Gamma-converges as $\varepsilon\to0$ when every sequence $\varepsilon_n\to0$ has the same Gamma-limit. If $F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F$ and a compact $K\subset X$ satisfies $\inf_XF_n=\inf_KF_n$ for every $n$, then $F$ attains its minimum and $\inf F_n\to\min F$. Every convergent subsequence of minimizers of $F_n$ converges to a minimizer of $F$, and $F_n+G\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F+G$ for continuous $G:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. For $$F_\varepsilon(u)=\begin{cases}\varepsilon^{-1}\int_\Omega W(u)\,dx+\varepsilon\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,dx,&u\in H^1(\Omega),\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}$$ if $W(0)=W(1)=0$ and $W(t)>0$ for $t\ne0,1$, then $F_\varepsilon$ Gamma-converges in $L^1(\Omega)$ to $$F(u)=\begin{cases}c\operatorname{Per}(S),&u=\mathbb1_S\text{ and }S\text{ has finite perimeter},\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad c=2\int_0^1\sqrt{W(t)}\,dt.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gamma-liminf and Gamma-limsup optimize sequential liminf and limsup values over all sequences approaching a point; their equality defines Gamma convergence. The extract also states stability of minimum values, cluster points of minimizers, continuous additive perturbations, and the Modica–Mortola convergence from diffuse-interface energy to perimeter.
assumptions_latex: $X$ is a metric space and $F_n:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$.
Minimum-value convergence assumes a compact $K\subset X$ with $\inf_XF_n=\inf_KF_n$ for every $n$.
The minimizer conclusion assumes a convergent subsequence of minimizers.
The perturbation conclusion assumes that $G$ is continuous.
For the phase-field example, $W(0)=W(1)=0$ and $W(t)>0$ for every $t\ne0,1$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed formulas define Gamma convergence and imply the stated stability properties; the displayed phase-field energies Gamma-converge to the perimeter functional with $c=2\int_0^1\sqrt{W(t)}\,dt$.

children.title: Continuous-Convergence Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Interfaces involving continuous convergence of functions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(f_n,f:X\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\) converges continuously to \(f\) if and only if \(f_n\xrightarrow{e}f\) and \(f_n\xrightarrow{h}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential continuous convergence compared with simultaneous epi- and hypographical convergence for finite-valued functions.

source_refs.locator: C. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 250

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Continuous convergence means that for every \(x\in X\) and every sequence \(x_n\to x\), \[f_n(x_n)\to f(x).\] This holds if and only if \((f_n)\) converges both epigraphically and hypographically to the same finite-valued function \(f\): \[f_n\xrightarrow{e}f\quad\text{and}\quad f_n\xrightarrow{h}f.\] The epigraphical limit supplies the lower inequality along every moving sequence, while the hypographical limit supplies the upper inequality. In particular, continuous convergence implies pointwise convergence and forces \(f\) to be continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite-valued functions, continuous convergence is equivalent to simultaneous epigraphical and hypographical convergence to the same limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Convergence Comparisons

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a compact metric space, let \(f_n:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. Then \[\sup_{x\in X}|f_n(x)-f(x)|\longrightarrow0\] if and only if, for every \(x\in X\) and every sequence \(x_n\to x\), \[f_n(x_n)\longrightarrow f(x).\] Under either condition, \((f_n)\) converges pointwise, epigraphically, and hypographically to \(f\).

u\} is equi-lsc (respectively equi-usc) at  ar x relative to X when the corresponding uniform lower- (respectively upper-) semicontinuity condition holds there, and is equicontinuous when both hold. A property holds relative to X when it holds at every  ar x\in X. Its asymptotic version requires the uniform condition only for indices

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Narrow convergence and convergence-determining classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the definition and the stated sufficient test-class and Lipschitz-approximation criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sequence $(\mu_n)\subset\mathcal P(X)$ converges narrowly to $\mu\in\mathcal P(X)$ iff $\int_X f\,d\mu_n	o\int_X f\,d\mu$ for every $f\in C_b^0(X)$. It suffices to verify convergence on a class $\mathcal C_0\subset C_b^0(X)$ whenever a class $\mathcal C$ has uniformly dense linear span in $C_b^0(X)$ and, for every $f\in\mathcal C$ and $
u\in\mathcal P(X)$, $\int f\,d
u=\sup_{h\in\mathcal C_0,\,h\le f}\int h\,d
u=\inf_{h\in\mathcal C_0,\,h\ge f}\int h\,d
u$. Bounded Lipschitz functions form such a determining class; indeed $f_k(x):=\inf_y\{f(y)+k d(x,y)\}$ increases pointwise to each bounded continuous $f$. If $X$ is separable, a countable family of bounded Lipschitz functions, closed under finite infima and rational scaling as described, is convergence determining.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Narrow convergence means convergence of integrals against every bounded continuous function. It can be checked on any class that approximates a uniformly dense test class from both below and above. Bounded Lipschitz functions suffice, and on a separable metric space a countable bounded-Lipschitz determining family exists.
assumptions_latex: $(X,d)$ is a separable metric space for the countable-family assertion.
$\operatorname{span}(\mathcal C)$ is uniformly dense in $C_b^0(X)$, and $\mathcal C_0$ has the stated integral approximation properties for the determining-class criterion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epi-Convergence of Maxima of Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An epi-limsup bound and an epi-convergence preservation result for pointwise maxima under a domain qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_1^\nu,f_2^\nu,f_1,f_2:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be convex and satisfy
\[
f_i\geq \operatorname{e\!\!-limsup}_{\nu}f_i^\nu\quad(i=1,2).
\]
If \(\operatorname{dom}f_1\) and \(\operatorname{dom}f_2\) cannot be separated, equivalently
\[
0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f_1-\operatorname{dom}f_2),
\]
then
\[
\operatorname{e\!\!-limsup}_{\nu}\max\{f_1^\nu,f_2^\nu\}\leq\max\{f_1,f_2\}.
\]
Consequently, if \(f_i^\nu\xrightarrow{e}f_i\) for \(i=1,2\), then
\[
\max\{f_1^\nu,f_2^\nu\}\xrightarrow{e}\max\{f_1,f_2\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex functions whose limiting domains satisfy the stated nonseparation qualification, the epi-limsup of the pointwise maxima is bounded above by the maximum of the limiting functions. Thus, componentwise epi-convergence implies epi-convergence of the maxima.
