knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal Function Principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional marginalization for a lower-semicontinuous extended-real-valued function, using limiting and horizon subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be lower semicontinuous and let (\bar x,\bar u)\in\operatorname{dom}F. Suppose there is a bounded K\subset\mathbb{R}^n such that \operatorname{dom}F(\cdot,u)\subset K for every u\in\mathbb{R}^m, and \bar x is the unique minimizer of F(\cdot,\bar u). Define V(u):=\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}F(x,u). Then V is lower semicontinuous and \partial V(\bar u)\subset\{\xi:(0,\xi)\in\partial F(\bar x,\bar u)\},\qquad \partial^\infty V(\bar u)\subset\{\xi:(0,\xi)\in\partial^\infty F(\bar x,\bar u)\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every parameterized effective domain is contained in one bounded set and the reference parameter has a unique minimizing point, then the marginal value function is lower semicontinuous. Every limiting or horizon subgradient of the value function at the reference parameter lifts to the corresponding subgradient of the original function with zero component in the minimized variable.
assumptions_latex: \bar x\text{ is the unique minimizer of }F(\cdot,\bar u)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V\text{ is lower semicontinuous},\quad \partial V(\bar u)\subset\{\xi:(0,\xi)\in\partial F(\bar x,\bar u)\},\quad \partial^\infty V(\bar u)\subset\{\xi:(0,\xi)\in\partial^\infty F(\bar x,\bar u)\}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and nonattainment-sensitive representation of the epigraph of an infimal projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $p(u)=\inf_x f(x,u)$ for $f:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, and let $E$ be the image of $\operatorname{epi}f$ under $(x,u,\alpha)\mapsto(u,\alpha)$. children.title: Eliminated-Variable Compactness
children.top_down_role: Compactness regimes controlling variable elimination in these operations.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces and \(F_n:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bounded marginal values along \(x_n\to x\) force associated eliminated variables to have convergent subsequences.

notation.meaning: sublevel section in the eliminated variable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential local uniform level-boundedness in the eliminated variable.

source_refs.locator: B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Write \(L_n(x,\alpha):=\{y\in Y:F_n(x,y)\leq\alpha\}\). The sequence is locally uniformly level-bounded in the eliminated variable if, for every \(x\in X\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\), a sequentially compact set \(K\subset Y\), and \(N\in\mathbb N\) such that
\[L_n(x',\alpha)\subset K\quad\text{for all }x'\in U\text{ and }n\geq N.\]
Equivalently in proper metric spaces, any \(x_n\to x\) and \(y_n\) with \(\sup_nF_n(x_n,y_n)<+\infty\) have an eliminated-variable subsequence converging in \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminated-variable compactness requires uniformly bounded sublevel sections near each retained variable, preventing bounded-value witnesses from escaping.
knowledge_statements.title: Eliminated-Variable Compactness

source_witnesses.locator: B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

assumptions_latex: Functions take values in \(\overline{\mathbb R}\) on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Epi-convergence is not preserved by pointwise addition without a common-recovery qualification.

notation.meaning: indicator taking zero on the set and positive infinity outside

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of epi-continuity for addition through incompatible recovery sequences.

source_refs.locator: B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_n:=\delta_{\{0\}}\) and \(g_n:=\delta_{\{1/n\}}\) on \(\mathbb R\). Then \(f_n\xrightarrow{e}\delta_{\{0\}}\) and \(g_n\xrightarrow{e}\delta_{\{0\}}\). However, the two finite domains are disjoint for every \(n\), so
\[f_n+g_n\equiv+\infty,\]
whereas \(\delta_{\{0\}}+\delta_{\{0\}}=\delta_{\{0\}}\). Hence \(f_n+g_n\) does not epi-converge to the sum of the epi-limits. The failure is precisely the absence of a sequence that simultaneously recovers both limiting values at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two epi-convergent indicator sequences can have disjoint finite domains, making every approximating sum infinite although the sum of their limits is finite.

children.title: Gamma-Convergence
children.top_down_role: The calculus-of-variations organization of topological variational convergence, compactness, and asymptotic minimization.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Gamma-convergence and K-convergence; comparison with pointwise convergence; convergence of minima and minimizers

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space and \(F_n:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\) topologically Gamma-converges to \(F\) exactly when its neighborhood Gamma-liminf and Gamma-limsup both equal \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood definition valid without assuming first countability.

source_refs.locator: B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in X\), define
\[(\Gamma\!\operatorname{-liminf}_nF_n)(x):=\sup_{U\in\mathcal N(x)}\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{y\in U}F_n(y),\]
and define \(\Gamma\!\operatorname{-limsup}_nF_n\) by replacing \(\liminf\) with \(\limsup\). The sequence topologically Gamma-converges to \(F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), written \(F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\), when
\[\Gamma\!\operatorname{-liminf}_nF_n=F=\Gamma\!\operatorname{-limsup}_nF_n\]
pointwise on \(X\). This neighborhood formulation remains meaningful when convergent sequences do not determine the topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Topological Gamma-convergence means that the neighborhood-based Gamma-liminf and Gamma-limsup coincide pointwise with the limiting functional.
knowledge_statements.title: Topological Gamma-Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The neighborhood formula is mathematically plausible, but the cited epi-convergence section does not establish support for the claimed arbitrary-topological-space Gamma formulation. A source treating topological Gamma-limits beyond sequential or metrizable settings is required.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a first-countable topological space and \(F_n,F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\) sequentially if and only if the liminf and recovery-sequence conditions hold at every point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization on first-countable spaces.

source_refs.locator: B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sequence \(F_n\) sequentially Gamma-converges to \(F\) if, for every \(x\in X\), both conditions hold: first, every sequence \(x_n\to x\) satisfies
\[F(x)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}F_n(x_n);\]
second, there exists a recovery sequence \(x_n\to x\) satisfying
\[F(x)\geq\limsup_{n\to\infty}F_n(x_n).\]
Together these inequalities force convergence of the recovery values whenever \(F(x)\) is finite. First countability ensures equivalence with the neighborhood definition of topological Gamma-convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential Gamma-convergence consists of a liminf inequality along every convergent sequence and a matching limsup inequality along at least one recovery sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Gamma-Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential liminf and recovery conditions are standard, but the cited source locator does not reliably support the stated equivalence with neighborhood Gamma-convergence on every first-countable topological space. A source with that exact topological scope is required.

children.title: Gamma-Type Functional Convergence
children.top_down_role: Functional convergence viewed through Gamma-type variational limits.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(F_n,F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Gamma-type convergence predicate is the conjunction of the universal liminf inequality and pointwise recovery.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional inequalities underlying Gamma-convergence in metric spaces.

source_refs.locator: B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Gamma-type functional convergence to \(F\) requires, at every \(x\in X\),
\[F(x)\leq\inf_{x_n\to x}\liminf_{n\to\infty}F_n(x_n)\]
and
\[F(x)\geq\inf_{x_n\to x}\limsup_{n\to\infty}F_n(x_n).\]
The first inequality is equivalent to the liminf inequality along every sequence converging to \(x\); the second asserts existence of arbitrarily accurate recovery sequences and, in metric spaces, may be realized by one diagonal recovery sequence. Equality of the resulting Gamma-lower and Gamma-upper limits with \(F\) is Gamma-convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gamma-type convergence compares function values along all converging sequences for the lower bound and along a selected recovery sequence for the upper bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Gamma-Type Functional Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower-Semicontinuous Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real functionals bounded below on metric spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $F:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}$ be bounded below. Its relaxation $\bar F$ is the greatest lower-semicontinuous functional satisfying $\bar F\le F$. For every $x\in X$,\[\bar F(x)=\inf\left\{\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(x_n):x_n\to x\right\},\]and $\inf_XF=\inf_X\bar F$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded-below extended-real functional on a metric space, its relaxation is the greatest lower-semicontinuous minorant. Its value at a point is the infimum of the liminf values along all sequences converging to that point, and relaxation preserves the global infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar F=\max\{G:G\text{ is lower semicontinuous and }G\le F\},\qquad \bar F(x)=\inf_{x_n\to x}\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(x_n),\qquad \inf_XF=\inf_X\bar F.

children.title: Kuratowski-Type Functional Convergence
children.top_down_role: Functional convergence represented through Kuratowski limits of associated sets.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(F_n,F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Kuratowski-type functional convergence is Painleve–Kuratowski convergence of \(\operatorname{epi}F_n\) to \(\operatorname{epi}F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional convergence encoded by Kuratowski limits of epigraphs.

source_refs.locator: B. Painleve-Kuratowski Convergence p. 111
B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Equip \(X\times\mathbb R\) with the product topology. Kuratowski-type functional convergence of \(F_n\) to \(F\) means
\[\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{epi}F_n\subseteq\operatorname{epi}F\subseteq\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{epi}F_n.\]
Equivalently, the outer and inner Painleve–Kuratowski limits of the epigraphs both equal \(\operatorname{epi}F\). The outer inclusion excludes limiting epigraph points below \(F\), while the inner inclusion requires every point of the limiting epigraph to be approximated by points in the epigraphs of \(F_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kuratowski-type functional convergence means that the inner and outer set limits of the epigraphs coincide with the epigraph of the limit function.
knowledge_statements.title: Kuratowski-Type Functional Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: B. Painleve-Kuratowski Convergence p. 111
B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

children.title: Functional–Set Limit Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The representation bridge between functional limits and associated set limits.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(F_n,F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\) if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}F_n\to\operatorname{epi}F\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-space equivalence between Gamma-convergence and epigraph set convergence.

source_refs.locator: B. Epi-Convergence p. 240
B. Painleve-Kuratowski Convergence p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following are equivalent: \(F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\); and \(\operatorname{epi}F_n\to\operatorname{epi}F\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense in \(X\times\mathbb R\). More explicitly, the sequential Gamma-liminf condition corresponds to \(\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{epi}F_n\subseteq\operatorname{epi}F\), and the recovery condition corresponds to \(\operatorname{epi}F\subseteq\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{epi}F_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In metric spaces, Gamma-convergence of lower-semicontinuous functions is equivalent to Painleve-Kuratowski convergence of their epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.title: Functional–Set Limit Correspondence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Helly selection lemma for non-increasing functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential pointwise compactness of extended-real monotone functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(\varphi_n)$ be non-increasing functions $\varphi_n:[0,T]\to[-\infty,+\infty]$. Then there exist a subsequence $(\varphi_{n(k)})$ and a non-increasing function $\varphi:[0,T]\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ such that $\lim_{k\to\infty}\varphi_{n(k)}(t)=\varphi(t)$ for every $t\in[0,T]$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every sequence of non-increasing extended-real-valued functions on a compact interval has a subsequence converging pointwise at every time to a non-increasing extended-real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,n(k)\uparrow\infty,\ \exists\,\varphi:[0,T]\to[-\infty,+\infty]\text{ non-increasing}:\quad \varphi_{n(k)}(t)\to\varphi(t)\ \forall t\in[0,T].

children.title: Gamma-Compactness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Precompact families under Gamma-type convergence.

assumptions_latex: \(F_n:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is a sequence of extended-real-valued functionals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist indices \(n_k\uparrow\infty\) and \(F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) such that \(F_{n_k}\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\); under equicoercivity, \(F\) is coercive and almost-minimizers are relatively compact.

notation.meaning: Gamma-convergence in the metric topology of X
Every bounded-energy sequence lies eventually in a common relatively compact set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential compactness in the Gamma topology, with equicoercivity supplying compactness of bounded-energy sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X\) is separable and metrizable, every sequence \((F_n)\) with \(F_n:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) has a subsequence \((F_{n_k})\) and a functional \(F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) such that \(F_{n_k}\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\). If, additionally, for every \(t\in\mathbb R\) there is a relatively compact \(K_t\subset X\) with \(\{x:F_n(x)\le t\}\subset K_t\) for all \(n\), then \(F\) has relatively compact sublevel sets. Moreover, any sequence \((x_k)\) satisfying \(F_{n_k}(x_k)-\inf_XF_{n_k}\to0\) has cluster points, and every cluster point minimizes \(F\), provided the infima are finite and uniformly bounded above.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a separable metric space, functionals admit a Gamma-convergent subsequence. Equicoercivity makes the limit coercive and gives compactness and consistency of almost-minimizers.
knowledge_statements.title: Gamma-Compactness Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the Gamma-compactness-regimes leaf and is mathematically plausible, but the broad subsequence compactness theorem and the equicoercive almost-minimizer conclusions require an inspectable authoritative citation with a specific theorem or section locator.

children.title: Subsequence Gamma-Limits
children.top_down_role: Variational limits obtained along selected subsequences.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The subsequence has Gamma-limit \(F\) exactly when its sequential Gamma-liminf and Gamma-limsup both equal \(F\) at every \(x\in X\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sequential Gamma-liminf and Gamma-limsup definition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential metric-space definition along a fixed increasing index subsequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(x\in X\), define
\[(\Gamma\!\operatorname{-liminf}_{k}F_{n_k})(x)=\inf_{x_k\to x}\liminf_{k\to\infty}F_{n_k}(x_k),\qquad (\Gamma\!\operatorname{-limsup}_{k}F_{n_k})(x)=\inf_{x_k\to x}\limsup_{k\to\infty}F_{n_k}(x_k).\]
The subsequence \((F_{n_k})\) Gamma-converges to \(F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) when, for every \(x\in X\), both displayed quantities equal \(F(x)\). Equivalently, every sequence \(x_k\to x\) satisfies \(F(x)\le\liminf_kF_{n_k}(x_k)\), and at least one recovery sequence \(x_k\to x\) satisfies \(F(x)\ge\limsup_kF_{n_k}(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subsequence Gamma-converges when its variational lower and upper limits coincide pointwise, equivalently when the lower-bound and recovery-sequence conditions both hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Subsequence Gamma-Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition, quantifiers, and sequential Gamma-liminf/Gamma-limsup formulas are consistent with the metric-space setting and fit the leaf. No source reference with a specific locator is attached, so the stated equivalence cannot yet pass citation review.

children.title: Limit Identification Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings used to distinguish or identify subsequential Gamma-limits.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every subsequence of \((F_n)\) contains a further subsequence Gamma-converging to \(F\), then \(F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\).

notation.meaning: An arbitrary increasing subsequence of indices

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: subsequence characterization of convergence in the sequential Gamma topology
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subsequence criterion for identifying a unique Gamma-limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that for every increasing sequence \((n_k)\) there is a further subsequence \((n_{k_j})\) such that \(F_{n_{k_j}}\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\), with the same functional \(F\) independent of the chosen subsequence. Then the full sequence satisfies \(F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\). Consequently, after Gamma-compactness has supplied subsequential limits, it suffices to identify every such limit with one candidate \(F\). Identification may be established by matching the Gamma-liminf lower bound and constructing recovery sequences for that candidate on every extracted subsequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full sequence Gamma-converges to a candidate if every subsequence has a further subsequence with that same Gamma-limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Limit Identification Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subsequence identification principle fits the terminal container and is correctly formulated with a common limit independent of the extracted subsequence. An inspectable source for the Gamma-convergence subsequence criterion is still required.

children.title: Integral-Representation Interfaces for Gamma-Limits
children.top_down_role: Detailed localization and integral-representation theory belongs to the integral-functionals chapter.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) has the displayed local integral representation on \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At Lebesgue points, the integrand is recovered by \(f(x,\xi)=\lim_{\rho\downarrow0}F(\ell_{x,\xi},Q_\rho(x))/|Q_\rho(x)|\).

notation.meaning: Cube centered at x with side length ρ

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface only: localization identifies an already-established integral Gamma-limit; existence hypotheses are deferred.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume a localized Gamma-limit \(F\) satisfies
\[F(u,A)=\int_A f(x,\nabla u(x))\,dx\]
for every open \(A\subset\Omega\) and \(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), where \(f\) has suitable measurable dependence on \(x\) and continuous dependence on the gradient variable. For \(\xi\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\), set \(\ell_{x,\xi}(y)=\xi(y-x)\). At every Lebesgue point \(x\) of \(y\mapsto f(y,\xi)\), the density is identified by
\[f(x,\xi)=\lim_{\rho\downarrow0}\frac{F(\ell_{x,\xi},Q_\rho(x))}{|Q_\rho(x)|}.\]
The separate integral-representation theorem must establish locality, measure structure, growth, and lower semicontinuity sufficient for the assumed representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once a Gamma-limit is known to be a local integral functional, its density is identified by normalized energies of affine maps on shrinking cubes.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Representation Interfaces for Gamma-Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record appropriately presents a localization interface rather than an integral-representation existence theorem, and the shrinking-cube formula follows from the assumed representation at Lebesgue points. A source is needed to verify the precise admissibility and localization hypotheses.

children.title: Mosco Convergence
children.top_down_role: Mixed strong–weak convergence for convex sets, convex functions, and associated operators.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Mosco lower bounds use \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\), while recovery conditions require \(x_n\to x\) in norm.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: defining strong-recovery and weak-liminf geometry of Mosco convergence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reflexive Banach-space geometry underlying Mosco convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Mosco convergence combines two different topologies on \(X\). Its closedness or lower-bound clause is tested against arbitrary weakly convergent sequences \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\), whereas its attainability or recovery clause requires a sequence converging strongly, \(x_n\to x\). Since strong convergence implies weak convergence, the recovery requirement is more restrictive topologically, while the weak lower-bound requirement tests more sequences. Reflexivity ensures that norm-bounded sequences have weakly convergent subsequences, which makes this strong–weak pairing effective in compactness arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mosco convergence tests lower bounds along weakly convergent sequences but demands norm-convergent recovery sequences; reflexivity supplies weak subsequential compactness for bounded sequences.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong–Weak Topological Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong-recovery/weak-liminf geometry is accurately stated and the principle content kind fits this conceptual leaf. The reflexive compactness assertion and Mosco convention need a cited textbook section or other inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak and strong topologies of a normed space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational weak-topology terminology for normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed space. The weak topology \(\sigma(X,X^*)\) is the weakest topology on \(X\) for which every \(\varphi\in X^*\) is continuous. The original norm topology, denoted \(\sigma(X,\|\cdot\|_X)\), is called the strong topology, and \(\sigma(X,X^*)\subseteq \sigma(X,\|\cdot\|_X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a normed space X, the weak topology is the weakest topology making every continuous linear functional continuous. The norm topology is called the strong topology, and the weak topology is no finer than it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma(X,X^*)\text{ is the weakest topology making all }\varphi\in X^*\text{ continuous, and }\sigma(X,X^*)\subseteq\sigma(X,\|\cdot\|_X).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Opial-Type Weak Convergence Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convergence obtained from convergence of distances to a target set and localization of every weak cluster point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space, let \((x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subset\mathcal H\), and let \(\varnothing\ne C\subset\mathcal H\). If, for every \(z\in C\), the sequence \((\|x_n-z\|)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) converges and every weak sequential cluster point of \((x_n)\) belongs to \(C\), then there exists \(\bar x\in C\) such that \(x_n\rightharpoonup\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the distance from a Hilbert-space sequence to every point of a nonempty set converges and all of its weak subsequential limits lie in that set, then the whole sequence converges weakly to a point of the set.
assumptions_latex: Every weak sequential cluster point of \((x_n)\) belongs to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\bar x\in C:\ x_n\rightharpoonup\bar x.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong topology of a Hilbert space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the strong topology and the default interpretation of unmodified topological notions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space with norm metric \(d(x,y)=\|x-y\|\). The topology induced by \(d\) is the strong (norm) topology. A net \((x_a)_{a\in A}\) converges strongly to \(x\in\mathcal H\), written \(x_a\to x\), if and only if \(\|x_a-x\|\to0\). Unless otherwise qualified, topological notions on \(\mathcal H\) are taken with respect to this topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strong topology of a Hilbert space is its norm topology. A net converges strongly exactly when its norm distance from the limit tends to zero; unqualified topological notions are understood in this topology.
assumptions_latex: \((x_a)_{a\in A}\) is a net in \(\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_a\to x\text{ strongly}\iff \|x_a-x\|\to0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak-topological notions in Hilbert spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects weak openness, convergence, closedness, compactness, continuity, and lower semicontinuity, including the infinite-dimensional unboundedness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space. A set is weakly open iff it is a union of finite intersections of open half-spaces. If \(\dim\mathcal H=\infty\), every nonempty finite intersection of open half-spaces, and hence every nonempty weakly open set, is unbounded. A net \((x_a)\) converges weakly to \(x\), written \(x_a\rightharpoonup x\), iff \(\langle x_a,u\rangle\to\langle x,u\rangle\) for every \(u\in\mathcal H\). A set \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) is weakly closed iff every weak limit of a net in \(C\) lies in \(C\), and weakly compact iff every net in \(C\) has a weak cluster point in \(C\). It is weakly sequentially closed iff every weak limit of a sequence in \(C\) lies in \(C\), and weakly sequentially compact iff every sequence in \(C\) has a weak sequential cluster point in \(C\). If \(D\subseteq\mathcal H\) is nonempty, \(\mathcal K\) is a real Hilbert space, and \(T:D\to\mathcal K\), then \(T\) is weakly continuous iff \(x_a\rightharpoonup x\in D\) implies \(Tx_a\rightharpoonup Tx\) for every net in \(D\). For \(f:\mathcal H\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), weak lower semicontinuity at \(x\) means that every net \(x_a\rightharpoonup x\) satisfies \(f(x)\leq\liminf_a f(x_a)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weakly open sets are unions of finite intersections of open half-spaces; in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space every nonempty weakly open set is unbounded. Weak convergence is pointwise convergence of all inner products. Weak closedness, compactness, their sequential counterparts, weak continuity, and weak lower semicontinuity are characterized by the stated net or sequence conditions.
assumptions_latex: For weak continuity, \(D\subseteq\mathcal H\) is nonempty, \(\mathcal K\) is a real Hilbert space, and \(T:D\to\mathcal K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_a\rightharpoonup x\iff(\forall u\in\mathcal H)\;\langle x_a,u\rangle\to\langle x,u\rangle,\quad f(x)\leq\liminf_a f(x_a)\text{ for weak lower semicontinuity, with the stated net and sequence characterizations of the other weak-topological notions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak and Weak-Star Continuity of Functionals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood characterization using finitely many dual-pairing seminorms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a normed space and $f:X\to\mathbb R$. The functional $f$ is weakly continuous at $x_0\in X$ if, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exist $\delta>0$ and $x_1^*,\ldots,x_n^*\in X^*$ such that $|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $|\langle x-x_0,x_i^*\rangle|<\delta$ for all $i=1,\ldots,n$. Analogously, $g:X^*\to\mathbb R$ is weak-star continuous at $x_0^*$ when the controlling finite family consists of evaluations at elements of $X$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar functional is weakly continuous at a point when each prescribed output tolerance is ensured by controlling finitely many continuous-linear-functional evaluations near that point. Weak-star continuity on the dual is defined analogously using finitely many evaluations at elements of the original space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0\ \exists x_1^*,\ldots,x_n^*\in X^*:\ \bigl(\forall i,\ |\langle x-x_0,x_i^*\rangle|<\delta\bigr)\Rightarrow |f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on a reflexive Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The functions \((f_n)\) Mosco-converge to \(f\), written \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\), if for every \(x\in X\) the following two conditions hold. For every sequence \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\),
\[f(x)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n(x_n).\]
There also exists a sequence \(y_n\to x\) in norm such that
\[f(x)\ge\limsup_{n\to\infty}f_n(y_n).\]
Together the inequalities imply \(f_n(y_n)\to f(x)\) whenever \(f(x)\) is finite. The first clause is the weak lower bound and the second is the strong recovery condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex functions Mosco-converge when weakly convergent sequences satisfy the lower bound and every point admits a norm-convergent recovery sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Mosco Convergence of Convex Functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weak liminf and strong recovery clauses are correctly quantified, and the observation about convergence along a finite-valued recovery sequence follows from the two inequalities. A specific authoritative source locator is absent.

\[\operatorname{s\!\!-Li}S_n=\{x:\exists x_n\in S_n,\ x_n\to x\},\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the graph-based convention, a sequence of set-valued operators \((A_n)\) Mosco-converges to \(A\), written \(A_n\xrightarrow{M}A\), precisely when
\[\operatorname{gra}A_n\xrightarrow{M}\operatorname{gra}A\]
as subsets of the product Hilbert space \(H\times H\). Thus every pair \((x,u)\) satisfying \(u\in A(x)\) is the strong limit of pairs \((x_n,u_n)\) with \(u_n\in A_n(x_n)\), and every weak subsequential limit of such graph pairs satisfies \(u\in A(x)\). This convention must be distinguished from weaker strong graph convergence or resolvent convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the graph-based convention, operators Mosco-converge exactly when their graphs Mosco-converge in the product Hilbert space.

notation.meaning: Resolvent of A at parameter λ

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Theorem transferring graph-level Mosco convergence to pointwise strong resolvent convergence for maximal monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_n\) and \(A\) be maximal monotone operators on \(H\), and suppose \(\operatorname{gra}A_n\xrightarrow{M}\operatorname{gra}A\) in \(H\times H\). For every \(\lambda>0\), maximal monotonicity makes the resolvents \(J_{\lambda A_n}=(I+\lambda A_n)^{-1}\) and \(J_{\lambda A}=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) single-valued on \(H\). Then, for each \(z\in H\), \[J_{\lambda A_n}z\to J_{\lambda A}z\quad\text{strongly in }H.\] Hence graph-level Mosco convergence transfers to pointwise strong convergence of the associated resolvent operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For maximal monotone operators, Mosco convergence of graphs yields pointwise strong convergence of every positive-parameter resolvent.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph–Operator Transfer

There also exists \(y_n^*\in X^*\) with \(\|y_n^*-x^*\|_{X^*}\to0\) and
\[g(x^*)\ge\limsup_{n\to\infty}g_n(y_n^*).\]
Because \(X\) is reflexive, the weak topology on \(X^*\) agrees with its weak-star topology induced by \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a reflexive dual space, Mosco convergence combines weak dual-space lower bounds with recovery sequences converging in the dual norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Space Mosco Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly applies Mosco convergence to the reflexive dual space, and reflexivity justifies identifying its weak and weak-star topologies through the canonical embedding. A specific authoritative source locator is absent.

children.title: Conjugate Mosco Convergence

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n^*\xrightarrow{M}f^*\) on \(H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space Fenchel conjugacy; no nonconvex or nonreflexive extension is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every sequence \(y_n\rightharpoonup y\), one has \(f^*(y)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n^*(y_n)\). For every \(y\in H\), there exists \(y_n\to y\) such that \(f^*(y)\geq\limsup_{n\to\infty}f_n^*(y_n)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stability of integral-functional relaxation under an additive perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The functional F satisfies the hypotheses ensuring F^{**}=\overline F; continuity of G is required only on every sublevel set of F.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume F satisfies the hypotheses under which its convex lower-semicontinuous regularization equals its lower-semicontinuous regularization, and define
\[
S_\lambda=\{u\in L_m^\alpha:F(u)\leq\lambda\}\qquad(\lambda\in\mathbb R).
\]
Let G\in\Gamma_0(L_m^\alpha) and suppose that, for every \lambda\in\mathbb R, the restriction G|_{S_\lambda} is continuous for \sigma(L^\alpha,L^{\alpha'}). Then
\[
(G+F)^{**}=G+F^{**}=\overline{G+F}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If F has coincident convex and lower-semicontinuous relaxations, and a proper convex lower-semicontinuous function G is weakly continuous on every sublevel set of F, then relaxation commutes with adding G and the resulting biconjugate equals the lower-semicontinuous envelope.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ satisfies the hypotheses of the preceding envelope-coincidence theorem}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (G+F)^{**}=G+F^{**}=\overline{G+F}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential definition at a specified graph point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph, closedness, and upper semicontinuity of a multifunction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for arbitrary topological spaces, with the upper-semicontinuity condition specialized to Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a multifunction \(\Gamma:X\rightrightarrows Y\), \(\operatorname{Gr}\Gamma:=\{(x,y):x\in X,\ y\in\Gamma(x)\}\). The multifunction is closed when \(\operatorname{Gr}\Gamma\) is closed in \(X\times Y\) in the specified product topology. If \(X,Y\) are Banach spaces, \(\Gamma\) is upper semicontinuous at \(x\) when \(\forall\varepsilon>0\,\exists\delta>0\,\forall x'\in x+\delta B_X:\ \Gamma(x')\subseteq\Gamma(x)+\varepsilon B_Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction maps each point of X to a subset of Y. Its graph consists of all pairs (x,y) with y in Γ(x), and it is closed when this graph is closed in the product topology. For Banach spaces, it is upper semicontinuous at x if every sufficiently nearby value Γ(x′) lies within an arbitrarily small ball enlargement of Γ(x).
assumptions_latex: X,Y\text{ are topological spaces for graph closedness}
X,Y\text{ are Banach spaces for the stated upper-semicontinuity definition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Gr}\Gamma=\{(x,y):y\in\Gamma(x)\},\quad \Gamma\text{ closed}\iff\operatorname{Gr}\Gamma\text{ closed},\quad \Gamma\text{ u.s.c. at }x\iff \forall\varepsilon>0\,\exists\delta>0:\Gamma(x')\subseteq\Gamma(x)+\varepsilon B_Y\ \forall x'\in x+\delta B_X.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral convergence under measurable chattering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The maps T_i u paste the values u_k using the previously fixed sets B_i^k and exceptional set N.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let u_1,\ldots,u_m:\Omega\to\mathcal E, where \mathcal E is an arbitrary set, and let f:\Omega\times\mathcal E\to\mathbb R satisfy
\[
x\mapsto f(x,u_k(x))\in L^1(\Omega)\qquad(k=1,\ldots,m).
\]
Define
\[
T_i u(x)=\begin{cases}u_k(x),&x\in B_i^k\cap N^c,\\u_1(x),&x\in N\cup\left(\Omega\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^mB_i^k\right).\end{cases}
\]
Then
\[
\int_\Omega f(x,T_i u(x))\,dx\longrightarrow\sum_{k=1}^m\alpha_k\int_\Omega f(x,u_k(x))\,dx.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pasting finitely many arbitrary-set-valued maps according to the chattering partition makes the integral of the composed numerical function converge to the weighted sum of the component integrals, provided every component composition is integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{i\to\infty}\int_\Omega f(x,T_i u(x))\,dx=\sum_{k=1}^m\alpha_k\int_\Omega f(x,u_k(x))\,dx.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local closed-convex-hull identity for epigraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The displayed conclusion is read coherently with the lower-semicontinuous function denoted by \(\varphi\); the extract uses an inconsistent symbol in its epigraph expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((E,d)\) be a metric space and let \(\varphi:E\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be lower semicontinuous. Suppose \(\Phi(|\xi|)\leq \varphi(e,\xi)\) for every \(e\in E\) and \(\xi\in\mathbb R^m\). Then, for every \(\bar e\in E\),
\[
\bigcap_{\varepsilon>0}\overline{\operatorname{co}}\!\left(\bigcup_{d(e,\bar e)\leq\varepsilon}\operatorname{epi}\varphi(e,\cdot)\right)
=\overline{\operatorname{co}}\operatorname{epi}\varphi(\bar e,\cdot).
\]

children.title: Generalized Differentiability Under Epigraphical Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence interfaces between function limits and first- or second-order generalized variational objects.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Derivative Consequences of Subdifferential Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order epi-differentiability and semidifferentiability criteria for an extended-real-valued function at a subdifferentially regular point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be subdifferentially regular at \(\bar x\). Then \(f\) is epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\), its epi-derivative equals \(w\mapsto df(\bar x)(w)\), and this function is sublinear and lower semicontinuous. Moreover, \(f\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\) if and only if \(df(\bar x)(w)<\infty\) for every \(w\). More generally, with \(D=\{w\mid df(\bar x)(w)<\infty\}\), \(f\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\) in direction \(w\) if and only if \(w\in\operatorname{int}D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an extended-real-valued function is subdifferentially regular at a point, it is epi-differentiable there, and its epi-derivative is its lower directional derivative, which is sublinear and lower semicontinuous. It is semidifferentiable in all directions exactly when that derivative is finite everywhere; directionally, semidifferentiability holds exactly on the interior of the cone where the derivative is finite.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is subdifferentially regular at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is epi-differentiable at }\bar x,\quad e'_f(\bar x;w)=df(\bar x)(w)\text{ is sublinear and lsc};\quad f\text{ is semidifferentiable at }\bar x\iff (\forall w)\,df(\bar x)(w)<\infty;\quad f\text{ is semidifferentiable at }\bar x\text{ for }w\iff w\in\operatorname{int}D.

notation.meaning: lower subderivative of f at the base point in direction w

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower subderivative defined by joint directional difference-quotient limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t>0\), define the first-order difference quotient by \[\Delta_t f(\bar x)(w):=\frac{f(\bar x+t w)-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] The lower subderivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(w\) is the extended-real number \[df(\bar x)(w):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\w'\to w}}\Delta_t f(\bar x)(w').\] Equivalently, the limit inferior ranges over all sequences \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(w_k\to w\). The perturbation \(w'\to w\) makes the definition stable under nearby directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower subderivative is the joint lower limit of first-order difference quotients as step sizes vanish and directions approach the target direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Subderivative Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is a plausible finite-dimensional definition of the lower subderivative and definition is an acceptable role for this leaf. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower and Upper Subderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines first-order subderivatives through perturbed-direction difference quotients and their lower epigraphical limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) and let \(\bar x\) satisfy \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\). For every \(\bar w\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the lower subderivative is
\[
df(\bar x)(\bar w):=\liminf_{\substack{\tau\searrow0\\w\to\bar w}}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w)-f(\bar x)}{\tau},
\]
equivalently \(df(\bar x)=\operatorname{e-liminf}_{\tau\searrow0}\Delta_\tau f(\bar x)\). The upper subderivative replaces \(\liminf\) by \(\limsup\) and equals \(-d(-f)(\bar x)\). Moreover, for every \(\tau>0\),
\[
\operatorname{epi}\Delta_\tau f(\bar x)=\frac{\operatorname{epi}f-(\bar x,f(\bar x))}{\tau}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an extended-real-valued function finite at the base point, the lower subderivative in a direction is the lower limit of first-order difference quotients as the step decreases to zero and the trial direction approaches that direction. It is equivalently the lower epigraphical limit of the difference-quotient functions. The upper subderivative uses the upper limit and is obtained as the negative lower subderivative of the negative function. Difference-quotient epigraphs are translated and positively rescaled copies of the original epigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: df(\bar x)(\bar w)=\liminf_{\substack{\tau\searrow0\\w\to\bar w}}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w)-f(\bar x)}{\tau},\quad df(\bar x)=\operatorname{e-liminf}_{\tau\searrow0}\Delta_\tau f(\bar x),\quad d^{+}f(\bar x)=-d(-f)(\bar x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subderivatives as Epigraph Tangents
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the epigraph of the lower subderivative with the tangent cone to the function epigraph and specializes the identity to set indicators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) and suppose \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\). Then
\[
\operatorname{epi}df(\bar x)=T_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x)).
\]
In particular, if \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\), then
\[
d\delta_C(\bar x)=\delta_{T_C(\bar x)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every point where an extended-real-valued function is finite, the epigraph of its lower subderivative is exactly the tangent cone to its epigraph at the corresponding epigraph point. Consequently, the subderivative of a set indicator at a point of the set is the indicator of the set's tangent cone there.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphical lower limit of first-order difference-quotient functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(t>0\), regard \(\Delta_t f(\bar x):\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) as a function of the direction, with \[\Delta_t f(\bar x)(w):=\frac{f(\bar x+t w)-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] Its epigraphical lower limit satisfies \[\left(\operatorname{e\!\!-\!liminf}_{t\downarrow0}\Delta_t f(\bar x)\right)(w)=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\w'\to w}}\Delta_t f(\bar x)(w')=df(\bar x)(w).\] Thus the lower subderivative is exactly the pointwise value of the epigraphical lower limit of the quotient family.

children.title: Quotient–Subderivative Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Interfaces linking difference-quotient convergence to subderivative limits.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and finite at \(\bar x\).
The functions \(\Delta_t f(\bar x)\) epigraphically converge as \(t\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_e f(\bar x)=\operatorname{e\!\!-\!lim}_{t\downarrow0}\Delta_t f(\bar x)=df(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order epi-differentiability identifies quotient limits with the lower subderivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) when the quotient family has an epigraphical limit as \(t\downarrow0\). In that case its epiderivative is defined by \[d_e f(\bar x):=\operatorname{e\!\!-\!lim}_{t\downarrow0}\Delta_t f(\bar x).\] Because the epigraphical lower limit always has values \(df(\bar x)(w)\), existence of the full epigraphical limit yields, for every \(w\in\mathbb R^d\), \[d_e f(\bar x)(w)=df(\bar x)(w).\] Hence epi-differentiability is precisely the condition under which the quotient-to-subderivative correspondence is realized by a genuine epigraphical limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the first-order quotient family epi-converges, its epigraphical limit is the lower subderivative and is called the epiderivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Quotient–Subderivative Correspondence

children.title: Subgradient Limit Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Variational-limit behavior of subgradient mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(f_n,f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions and \(f_n\xrightarrow{e}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex outer-limit interface with function-value convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(n\), the inclusion \(v_n\in\partial f_n(x_n)\) means \[f_n(y)\ge f_n(x_n)+\langle v_n,y-x_n\rangle\qquad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb R^d.\] Under epigraphical convergence, convergence of the base points, subgradients, and attained function values passes this inequality to the limit along recovery sequences. The limiting inequality is \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb R^d,\] which is equivalent to \(v\in\partial f(x)\). Thus value-attentive graphical outer limits of convex subgradients remain subgradients of the epigraphical limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex epi-convergent functions, convergent subgradients remain subgradients of the limit when the associated points and function values also converge.
knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Limit Interfaces

The sequence \(f_n\) epi-converges to \(f\) if and only if
\[\operatorname{gph}\partial f_n\to\operatorname{gph}\partial f\]
in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense and there exist \((x_n,v_n)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f_n\) and \((x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) such that \((x_n,v_n)\to(x,v)\) and \(f_n(x_n)\to f(x)\). In particular, epi-convergence implies graphical convergence of the convex subdifferentials; the value condition is required for the converse because subdifferentials do not detect additive constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex epi-convergence yields subdifferential graph convergence; conversely, graph convergence plus one convergent function-value anchor yields epi-convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Subdifferential Graph Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem has the expected finite-dimensional Attouch form and the value anchor addresses additive constants, but no source is supplied to confirm this exact equivalence and anchor formulation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(f_n\to f\) uniformly, \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f_n\) converges to \(\{(x,v):|v-2x|\le1\}\), not to \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f\).

notation.meaning: Subdifferential, equal here to the derivative because each function is smooth.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit smooth oscillatory counterexample verified algebraically
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nonconvex example showing that uniform or epi-convergence does not control subgradient graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Since \(\lvert f_n(x)-f(x)\rvert\le n^{-1}\), the functions converge uniformly, hence epi-converge, to \(f\). Nevertheless,
\[\partial f_n(x)=\{2x+\cos(nx)\},\qquad \partial f(x)=\{2x\}.\]
For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), phase-adjusted sequences \(x_n\to x\) realize every cluster value in \(2x+[-1,1]\), and no other cluster values occur. Consequently,
\[\operatorname{gph}\partial f_n\to\{(x,v)\in\mathbb{R}^2:|v-2x|\le1\}\ne\operatorname{gph}\partial f.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing oscillations in function values can leave order-one gradient oscillations, so nonconvex epi-convergence alone does not imply subdifferential graph convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Subdifferential Graph Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit calculation is internally correct and the counterexample content kind is appropriate: the graph limit is the stated strip even though the functions converge uniformly. A standard-field rationale alone does not provide the requested inspectable citation for this nontrivial graph-limit claim.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convex normal-cone mappings converge graphically: \(\operatorname{gph}N_{C_n}\to\operatorname{gph}N_C\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional closed-convex specialization of Mosco and Attouch convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed-convex normal-cone convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(n\), let \(N_{C_n}=\partial\delta_{C_n}\), and similarly let \(N_C=\partial\delta_C\). Painlevé--Kuratowski convergence of nonempty closed convex sets in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is equivalent to epi-convergence of their indicators. Therefore
\[\operatorname{gph}N_{C_n}=\operatorname{gph}\partial\delta_{C_n}\longrightarrow\operatorname{gph}\partial\delta_C=\operatorname{gph}N_C.\]
Equivalently, every convergent sequence of normal pairs has a normal limiting pair, and every pair in \(\operatorname{gph}N_C\) admits approximating pairs from \(\operatorname{gph}N_{C_n}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence of nonempty closed convex sets in finite dimensions entails graphical convergence of their convex normal-cone mappings.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Graph Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional closed-convex specialization is mathematically plausible and correctly placed as a theorem, but the passage from set convergence through indicator epi-convergence to normal-cone graph convergence needs a specific authoritative source locator.

children.title: Subdifferential Graph-Convergence Tests
children.top_down_role: Representation-based diagnostic families for graph convergence.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Graphical convergence \(A_n\to A\) is equivalent to pointwise convergence \(J_{\lambda A_n}x\to J_{\lambda A}x\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of a maximal monotone operator.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: resolvent characterization of maximal-monotone graph convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional maximal-monotone resolvent criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the everywhere single-valued resolvents
\[J_{\lambda A_n}=(I+\lambda A_n)^{-1},\qquad J_{\lambda A}=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}.\]
Then
\[\operatorname{gph}A_n\to\operatorname{gph}A\]
in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense if and only if \(J_{\lambda A_n}(z)\to J_{\lambda A}(z)\) for every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^d\). The test reconstructs a graph pair through \(x=J_{\lambda A}(z)\) and \(v=(z-x)/\lambda\), so the resolvent limit simultaneously controls primal and operator coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximal monotone graphs converge exactly when their resolvents at one fixed positive parameter converge pointwise everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent-Based Tests

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition has the correct role for a resolvent-based test and states the standard finite-dimensional maximal-monotone criterion. No inspectable source is supplied for the exact equivalence between Painleve--Kuratowski graph convergence and pointwise resolvent convergence at one fixed parameter.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The functions \(f_n\) epi-converge to \(f\) exactly when \(e_\lambda f_n(x)\to e_\lambda f(x)\) for every \(x\) and every \(\lambda>0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Moreau-envelope characterization of finite-dimensional convex epi-convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise envelope test for finite-dimensional convex epi-convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\lambda>0\), define
\[e_\lambda f_n(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{f_n(y)+\frac{\|x-y\|^2}{2\lambda}\right\},\]
and define \(e_\lambda f\) analogously. Then \(f_n\) epi-converges to \(f\) if and only if
\[e_\lambda f_n(x)\to e_\lambda f(x)\]
for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and every \(\lambda>0\). Moreover, where the envelopes are differentiated,
\[\nabla e_\lambda f_n(x)=\lambda^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f_n}(x)\bigr),\]
linking envelope tests to resolvent tests for \(\partial f_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex epi-convergence is equivalent to pointwise convergence of all Moreau envelopes, whose gradients also encode the proximal resolvents.
knowledge_statements.title: Moreau-Envelope Tests

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the Moreau-envelope test container and is internally consistent for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions in finite dimensions. A specific source is still required to confirm the exact quantification over points and parameters.

children.title: Primal–Dual Graph Tests
children.top_down_role: Graph-convergence tests using paired primal and dual data.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal and dual subgradient graph tests are equivalent under the coordinate swap \((x,v)\mapsto(v,x)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Fenchel subgradient inversion and induced graph correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex primal-dual graph inversion test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \((x,v)\in\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d\), Fenchel duality gives
\[v\in\partial f_n(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\partial f_n^*(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f_n(x)+f_n^*(v)=\langle x,v\rangle.\]
Consequently,
\[\operatorname{gph}\partial f_n^*=\{(v,x):(x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f_n\}.\]
Thus graphical convergence of the primal subdifferentials is equivalent to graphical convergence of the dual subdifferentials after swapping coordinates, and candidate graph pairs may be checked on either side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex subgradient pair is simultaneously a dual subgradient pair, so primal and conjugate graph convergence tests coincide after swapping coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Graph Tests

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Fenchel subgradient inversion gives the stated coordinate-swap correspondence, and duality is the correct content kind. The record nevertheless lacks an inspectable authoritative source locator supporting the graph-convergence test.

children.title: Conjugate-Function Tests
children.top_down_role: Graph-convergence tests expressed through convex conjugates.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One has \(f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f\) if and only if \(f_n^*\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f^*\).

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of a proper convex function.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional self-duality of convex epi-convergence under Fenchel conjugation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conjugacy test for convex epi-convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[f_n^*(v)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}\{\langle v,x\rangle-f_n(x)\},\qquad f^*(v)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}\{\langle v,x\rangle-f(x)\}.\]
Then Fenchel conjugation preserves and reflects convex epi-convergence:
\[f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f_n^*\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f^*.\]
Hence convergence may be tested in either the primal or conjugate representation; applying conjugation twice returns the original proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper closed convex functions in finite dimensions, epi-convergence occurs precisely when the Fenchel conjugates epi-converge.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate-Function Tests

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim matches finite-dimensional self-duality of convex epi-convergence and the duality content kind fits the leaf. Because this is a convergence theorem rather than merely the definition of conjugation, a specific authoritative locator is required.

children.title: Duality-Gap Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Diagnostics for mismatches between primal and dual convergence evidence.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Fenchel gap \(G_f(x,v)\) is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when \((x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Fenchel--Young inequality and its equality characterization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Fenchel-gap certificate for convex subgradient graph membership; no quantitative or asymptotic distance-to-graph conclusion is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the Fenchel gap by
\[G_f(x,v)=f(x)+f^*(v)-\langle x,v\rangle.\]
The Fenchel--Young inequality gives \(G_f(x,v)\ge 0\), and
\[G_f(x,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\partial f^*(v).\]
Thus exact vanishing of the gap certifies that \((x,v)\) lies on the primal subdifferential graph and that \((v,x)\) lies on the dual subdifferential graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative Fenchel gap is zero exactly for primal-dual subgradient pairs, so exact zero certifies membership in both corresponding subdifferential graphs.
knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Gap Diagnostics

children.title: Normalization Tests
children.top_down_role: Tests controlling additive or scale ambiguity across function families.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A single convergent value anchor fixes the additive drift left undetermined by subdifferential graph convergence.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: normalization clause in the finite-dimensional Attouch convergence theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value anchoring removes additive indeterminacy in convex subdifferential limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A normalization test requires points \((x_n,v_n)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f_n\) and \((x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) such that
\[(x_n,v_n)\to(x,v),\qquad f_n(x_n)\to f(x).\]
Together with graphical convergence of \(\partial f_n\), this condition identifies \(f\) as the epi-limit. The value test is essential: replacing \(f_n\) by \(f_n+c_n\) leaves \(\partial f_n\) unchanged, while unconverged constants \(c_n\) can prevent convergence to the prescribed normalization of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subdifferential graphs ignore additive constants; convergence of one anchored function value fixes that drift and identifies the convex epi-limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Normalization Tests

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed anchor condition correctly targets the additive indeterminacy invisible to subdifferentials, and condition is the correct content kind. Its sufficiency together with graphical convergence is the normalization clause of an Attouch-type theorem and requires a specific authoritative source locator.

children.title: Anchoring Tests
children.top_down_role: Tests using reference points or reference values to stabilize identification.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convergent triples \((x_n,x_n^*,f_n(x_n))\to(x,x^*,f(x))\) anchor the additive constants.

notation.meaning: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on the Hilbert space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value anchoring for convex subdifferential graph convergence.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An anchoring test is satisfied when there exist \((x,x^*)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) and \((x_n,x_n^*)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f_n\) such that \(x_n\to x\), \(x_n^*\to x^*\), and \(f_n(x_n)\to f(x)\). Because subdifferential graphs are unchanged by additive constants, this value convergence supplies the normalization needed to identify the functional limit rather than merely its subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convergent graph point together with convergence of its function value fixes the additive normalization and identifies the limiting convex function.
knowledge_statements.title: Anchoring Tests

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

children.title: Additive-Drift Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Detection of convergence ambiguity caused by uncontrolled additive constants.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Graphical information alone cannot detect the drift \((c_n)\), since \(\partial(f_n+c_n)=\partial f_n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Detects the additive indeterminacy invisible to subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_n=f_n+c_n\). Then \(\partial g_n=\partial f_n\) for every \(n\), regardless of the behavior of \((c_n)\). Thus identical or graphically convergent subdifferentials do not imply convergence of the functions. For example, if \(f_n=f\) and \(c_n\to+\infty\), then \(\partial g_n=\partial f\), while \(g_n(x)\to+\infty\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). A normalization or anchoring value is therefore necessary to identify a particular functional representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding arbitrary constants leaves every subdifferential unchanged; divergent constants can destroy functional convergence while all subdifferential graphs remain identical.
knowledge_statements.title: Additive-Drift Diagnostics

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The common subdifferential graph identifies the function only modulo an additive constant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional nonidentifiability from an unanchored graphical limit.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Since \(g=f+c\), one has \(\partial g(x)=\partial f(x)\) for every \(x\in H\), and hence \(\operatorname{gph}\partial g=\operatorname{gph}\partial f\). Consequently, a sequence whose subdifferential graphs converges to this common graph does not determine whether the corresponding functional representative is \(f\), \(g\), or another additive translate. Graphical convergence identifies the operator but requires an independent value normalization to identify a function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subdifferential graph cannot distinguish two proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions differing by a constant, so an unanchored graph limit has no unique functional representative.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Limits Without Functional Identification

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is \(\Gamma_0(H)\), whose members have maximal-monotone convex subdifferentials and well-defined proximal resolvents and Moreau envelopes for every positive parameter.

notation.meaning: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions from the Hilbert space to the extended reals

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space convex regime for the Attouch theorem family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex lower-semicontinuous regime consists of functions \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) that are convex, lower semicontinuous in the norm topology, and proper, meaning that \(f(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\in H\) and \(\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\). For \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), the convex subdifferential \(\partial f\) is maximal monotone, and the proximal resolvent and Moreau envelope are everywhere defined for every positive parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relevant regime is proper norm-lower-semicontinuous convex functions on a real Hilbert space, whose subdifferentials are maximal monotone and have everywhere-defined proximal resolvents and Moreau envelopes.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every lower-semicontinuous extended-real-valued function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its minimum.

children.title: Mosco Convergence Route
children.top_down_role: Attouch-type stability organized through Mosco convergence of convex functions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Mosco convergence combines a weak sequential lower bound with a strongly convergent recovery sequence.

notation.meaning: Weak convergence in the Hilbert space
Strong convergence in the Hilbert space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential Hilbert-space definition of Mosco convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((f_n)\) Mosco-converges to \(f\) if both of the following conditions hold: for every sequence \((x_n)\subset H\) with \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\), one has \(f(x)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n(x_n)\); and for every \(x\in H\), there exists a sequence \((x_n)\subset H\) with \(x_n\to x\) such that \(f(x)\geq\limsup_{n\to\infty}f_n(x_n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mosco convergence means that every weakly convergent sequence satisfies the lower bound and every point admits a strongly convergent recovery sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Mosco Convergence Route

children.title: Subdifferential Graph Route
children.top_down_role: Attouch-type stability organized through graphical convergence of subdifferentials.

assumptions_latex: The graphs \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f_n\) converge graphically to \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) in the topology specified by the applicable Attouch theorem.
There exist \((x_n,x_n^*)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f_n\) and \((x,x^*)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) such that \(x_n\to x\), \(x_n^*\to x^*\), and \(f_n(x_n)\to f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the precise Attouch graphical-convergence hypotheses, \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\).

notation.meaning: Graphical convergence of set-valued operators in the topology specified by the cited theorem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse Attouch route with explicit additive anchoring; the exact graphical topology must follow the cited theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f_n\) converges graphically to \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) in the topology required by the applicable Attouch theorem. If there exist \((x_n,x_n^*)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f_n\) and \((x,x^*)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) such that \(x_n\to x\), \(x_n^*\to x^*\), and \(f_n(x_n)\to f(x)\), then \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\). The value condition removes the additive ambiguity left by subdifferential data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the precise graphical-convergence topology in Attouch's theorem, convergence of convex subdifferentials yields Mosco convergence when one convergent graph point also carries a convergent function value.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Graph Route

children.title: Mosco–Graph Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes supporting equivalence between function convergence and subdifferential graph convergence.

assumptions_latex: Graphical convergence is interpreted in the topology specified by the applicable Attouch theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the precise Attouch hypotheses, \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\) is equivalent to anchored graphical convergence of \(\partial f_n\) to \(\partial f\).

notation.meaning: Graphical convergence in the topology specified by the cited theorem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attouch equivalence for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, with the exact graphical topology fixed by the source theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the precise topology and hypotheses of the applicable Attouch theorem, \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\) holds if and only if \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f_n\) converges graphically to \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) and there exist \((x_n,x_n^*)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f_n\) and \((x,x^*)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) such that \(x_n\to x\), \(x_n^*\to x^*\), and \(f_n(x_n)\to f(x)\). The anchoring clause removes the additive ambiguity in the reverse implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the precise topology and hypotheses of Attouch's theorem, Mosco convergence is equivalent to subdifferential graph convergence supplemented by one convergent value anchor.
knowledge_statements.title: Mosco–Graph Equivalence Regimes

children.title: Resolvent Convergence Route
children.top_down_role: Attouch-type convergence characterized through resolvent families.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\), then \(J_\lambda^{f_n}x\to J_\lambda^f x\) strongly for every \(x\in H\).

notation.meaning: Proximal resolvent of the convex subdifferential
Identity operator on the Hilbert space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong pointwise convergence of proximal resolvents under Mosco convergence; any converse requires exact sourcing and additive anchoring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\), then for every \(\lambda>0\) and every \(x\in H\), one has \[J_\lambda^{f_n}x=(I+\lambda\partial f_n)^{-1}x\to(I+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}x=J_\lambda^f x.\] Pointwise resolvent convergence identifies the limiting subdifferential but cannot distinguish additive translates of the functions. Therefore, a value anchor is required in any converse that concludes Mosco convergence to the specified representative \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mosco convergence gives strong pointwise convergence of every proximal resolvent; resolvent data alone cannot fix the additive normalization required by a converse to a specified function.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Convergence Route

children.title: Moreau-Envelope Convergence Route
children.top_down_role: Attouch-type convergence characterized through Moreau-envelope families.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the precise Attouch characterization, Mosco convergence is equivalent to pointwise convergence of the Moreau envelopes for every positive parameter.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau-envelope characterization retaining additive normalization; the one-parameter variant requires an exact theorem source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\lambda>0\), define the Moreau envelope by \[e_\lambda f(x)=\inf_{y\in H}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert x-y\rVert^2\right\}.\] Under the standard Hilbert-space Attouch characterization, \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\) if and only if \(e_\lambda f_n(x)\to e_\lambda f(x)\) for every \(\lambda>0\) and every \(x\in H\). Whether convergence for one fixed positive parameter alone is sufficient must be stated only with the exact hypotheses of the cited theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the standard Hilbert-space characterization, Mosco convergence is equivalent to pointwise convergence of the Moreau envelopes for every positive parameter; a one-parameter variant requires exact sourcing.
knowledge_statements.title: Moreau-Envelope Convergence Route

children.title: Resolvent–Envelope Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Transfer of convergence information between resolvents and Moreau envelopes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proximal resolvent is recovered from the envelope gradient by \(J_\lambda^f=I-\lambda\nabla e_\lambda f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise identity connecting proximal mappings and envelope gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), the minimizer in the Moreau-envelope formula is unique and equals \(J_\lambda^f x\). The envelope is Fréchet differentiable and satisfies \[\nabla e_\lambda f(x)=\frac{1}{\lambda}\bigl(x-J_\lambda^f x\bigr),\qquad J_\lambda^f x=x-\lambda\nabla e_\lambda f(x).\] Thus the resolvent and the envelope gradient determine each other pointwise, while envelope values additionally retain the additive normalization of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Moreau-envelope gradient equals the scaled residual from the proximal point, so the resolvent and gradient determine each other.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent–Envelope Correspondence

children.title: Conjugacy Route
children.top_down_role: Attouch-type convergence transported through convex conjugation.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space identified with its continuous dual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fenchel conjugation preserves and reflects Mosco convergence: \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\) if and only if \(f_n^*\xrightarrow{M}f^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-duality of Mosco convergence under Fenchel conjugation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in H\), define the Fenchel conjugate by \[f^*(u)=\sup_{x\in H}\bigl\{\langle u,x\rangle-f(x)\bigr\}.\] Then \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\) if and only if \(f_n^*\xrightarrow{M}f^*\). Hence a Mosco-convergence problem may be transferred to the conjugate sequence and returned by biconjugation, since every \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\) satisfies \(f^{**}=f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Hilbert space identified with its dual, Fenchel conjugation preserves and reflects Mosco convergence, allowing convergence to be checked on the conjugate functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugacy Route

children.title: Duality Route
children.top_down_role: Attouch-type convergence analyzed through primal–dual representations.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space identified with its continuous dual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conjugation reflects the subdifferential graph: \((x,u)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) if and only if \((u,x)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel duality expressed through inverse subdifferentials and graph reflection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,u\in H\), the following conditions are equivalent: \(u\in\partial f(x)\); \(x\in\partial f^*(u)\); and \[f(x)+f^*(u)=\langle u,x\rangle.\] Consequently, \(\partial f^*=(\partial f)^{-1}\), and the graph of \(\partial f^*\) is obtained from the graph of \(\partial f\) by interchanging the primal and dual coordinates. This reflection transfers graphical-convergence statements between the primal and conjugate subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel equality characterizes mutually dual subgradients, making the conjugate subdifferential the inverse of the primal subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Duality Route

children.title: Biconjugate Closure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Closure regimes affecting recovery across conjugate representations.

assumptions_latex: d4b3 is a Banach space with continuous dual \(X^*\).
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and admits a continuous affine minorant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}_{\|\cdot\|}\!\operatorname{conv}f,\qquad f=f^{**}\iff f\text{ is lower semicontinuous and convex}.\]

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate and biconjugate with respect to the pairing between the Banach space and its continuous dual.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Fenchel–Moreau closure identity under a continuous affine-minorant hypothesis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel–Moreau closure on a Banach space; no topology-dependent Attouch extension is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f^*(x^*)=\sup_{x\in X}\{\langle x^*,x\rangle-f(x)\}\) and \(f^{**}(x)=\sup_{x^*\in X^*}\{\langle x^*,x\rangle-f^*(x^*)\}\). Then the biconjugate is the greatest norm-lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(f\), namely \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}_{\|\cdot\|}\operatorname{conv}f\). Consequently, the biconjugation step closes a conjugacy argument without altering the target precisely when \(f\) is lower semicontinuous and convex; for every proper lower-semicontinuous convex \(f\), one has \(f=f^{**}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Biconjugation produces the lower-semicontinuous convex closure; it leaves a proper function unchanged exactly in the lower-semicontinuous convex regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Biconjugate Closure Regimes
