children.title: Normalization Failures
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of equivalence caused by absent or inconsistent normalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalization Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete loss of a proper epigraphical limit when additive constants are not normalized.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(n\), addition of the constant \(n\) gives \(\partial f_n(x)=\partial q(x)=\{x\}\) at each \(x\in X\). Thus the subdifferential graphs are identical and converge trivially. Nevertheless, for every sequence \(x_n\to x\), one has \(f_n(x_n)=\tfrac12\|x_n\|^2+n\to+\infty\). Hence \(f_n\) epigraphically converges only to the improper function identically equal to \(+\infty\), demonstrating that operator convergence cannot recover a proper potential without normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identical subdifferentials can accompany potentials drifting to positive infinity, so operator convergence alone does not yield a proper epigraphical limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial f_n=\partial q\quad\text{for every }n,\qquad \operatorname*{e\!\!-lim}_{n\to\infty}f_n\equiv +\infty.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct computation using invariance of subgradients under additive constants

children.title: Additive-Drift Regimes
children.top_down_role: Function sequences differing through uncontrolled additive constants.

knowledge_statements.title: Additive-Drift Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of constant vertical drift for a fixed proper convex potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every real constant \(c_n\), vertical translation leaves the subdifferential unchanged: \(\partial(f+c_n)=\partial f\). If \(c_n\to c\in\mathbb R\), then \(f_n\) epigraphically converges to \(f+c\). If \(c_n\to+\infty\), its epigraphical limit is the improper function identically \(+\infty\). If \((c_n)\) has two distinct finite cluster values, the corresponding subsequences have different epigraphical limits, so the full sequence has no epigraphical limit although all subdifferential graphs coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Additive constants are invisible to subdifferentials but determine whether potentials converge, diverge to infinity, or have incompatible subsequential epigraphical limits.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper lower-semicontinuous convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial f_n=\partial f,\qquad c_n\to c\Longrightarrow f_n\xrightarrow{e}f+c,\qquad c_n\to+\infty\Longrightarrow f_n\xrightarrow{e}+\infty.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: additive constants preserve subdifferentials and translate epigraphs vertically

children.title: Converse Failures
children.top_down_role: Regimes where operator-side or regularization-side convergence does not recover the expected function limit.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial f_n=\partial q\text{ for all }n,\qquad (f_n)\text{ has no epigraphical limit}.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: even and odd subsequences are constant sequences with distinct epigraphical limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the unnormalized converse from graphical subdifferential convergence to epigraphical convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(n\) and \(x\in X\), one has \(\partial f_n(x)=\{x\}=\partial q(x)\); hence the subdifferential graphs converge to \(\operatorname{gph}\partial q\). The even subsequence is constantly \(q+1\), whereas the odd subsequence is constantly \(q-1\). These subsequences have distinct epigraphical limits. Therefore \((f_n)\) has no epigraphical limit, showing that graphical convergence of subdifferentials does not imply epigraphical convergence of potentials unless additive constants are anchored.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence may have a fixed subdifferential graph while alternating between two distinct vertical translates, invalidating an unnormalized Attouch converse.
knowledge_statements.title: Converse Failures

children.title: Anchoring Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Failure of reference-value information to identify a unique variational limit.

knowledge_statements.title: Anchoring Breakdown
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An anchor controls normalization only when it remains compatible with the limiting local geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Each \(f_n\) is proper lower-semicontinuous convex and has the normalized minimizer \(a_n=n\), satisfying \(f_n(a_n)=0\) and \(0\in\partial f_n(a_n)\). However, the anchors escape every bounded subset of \(X\). For every convergent sequence \(x_n\to x\), the sequence \((x_n)\) is bounded and \((x_n-n)^2\to+\infty\). Thus \(f_n\) epigraphically converges to the improper function identically \(+\infty\); normalization at escaping points does not anchor a proper local limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero-valued stationary anchors may escape to infinity, leaving every bounded region with an improper infinite epigraphical limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f_n(a_n)=0,\quad 0\in\partial f_n(a_n),\qquad a_n\to+\infty,\quad f_n\xrightarrow{e}+\infty.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct evaluation along bounded sequences and at the escaping minimizers

knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Limits of Implicit Solution Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential graphical convergence in metric parameter and solution spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The outer limit of \(\operatorname{gph}S_n\) consists of all \((p,x)\in P\times X\) for which some subsequence \(n_k\) and points \((p_k,x_k)\in\operatorname{gph}S_{n_k}\) satisfy \((p_k,x_k)\to(p,x)\). The inner limit consists of all \((p,x)\in P\times X\) for which there exist \((p_n,x_n)\in\operatorname{gph}S_n\) eventually satisfying \((p_n,x_n)\to(p,x)\). The maps converge graphically to \(S\) precisely when \(\operatorname*{Liminf}_n\operatorname{gph}S_n=\operatorname*{Limsup}_n\operatorname{gph}S_n=\operatorname{gph}S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphical convergence requires equality of the inner and outer limits of the solution-map graphs; sequentially, all limit solutions persist and no spurious ones appear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}S_n=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}S_n=\operatorname{gph}S.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Loss Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of all solutions through escape to infinity in a noncompact ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every approximating solution set \(S_n=\{n\}\) is nonempty. Any selection \(x_n\in S_n\) satisfies \(x_n=n\) and therefore has no convergent subsequence in \(X\). Hence no point belongs to the outer sequential limit, and \(\operatorname*{Limsup}_n S_n=\varnothing\). The inner limit is also empty. Thus nonemptiness of every approximating solution set does not preserve a solution in the limit without compactness or local boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonempty solution sets can escape to infinity, leaving both their inner and outer limits empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S_n\ne\varnothing\text{ for all }n,\quad \operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}S_n=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}S_n=\varnothing.\]

For every \(n\), the equation \(F_n(x)=0\) has the two solutions \(-n^{-1/2}\) and \(n^{-1/2}\), whereas the limiting equation \(F(x)=0\) has the single solution \(0\). Both branches converge to \(0\), so \(S_n\) converges to \(S=\{0\}\) while the local number of solution branches is not preserved.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Limit Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual convergence without metric regularity need not imply convergence of zero sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each bounded set \(B\subset\mathbb R\), one has \(\sup_{x\in B}|F_n(x)-F(x)|=n^{-1}\sup_{x\in B}|x|\to0\). Nevertheless, \(S_n=\{0\}\) for every \(n\), while every real number solves the limiting equation and hence \(S=\mathbb R\). Therefore the set limit of \((S_n)\) is \(\{0\}\), strictly smaller than the solution set of the limiting residual. The zero-set operation is not continuous without a regularity condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Outer–Inner Limit Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical alternating sequence with distinct outer and inner solution-set limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The even subsequence converges as sets to \(\{0\}\), and the odd subsequence converges as sets to \(\{1\}\). Thus both \(0\) and \(1\) are attainable subsequential limits, giving \(\operatorname*{Limsup}_n S_n=\{0,1\}\). No single sequence \(x_n\in S_n\) converges, because it alternates between \(0\) and \(1\); hence \(\operatorname*{Liminf}_n S_n=\varnothing\). The strict gap shows that the solution sets possess no Painlev–Kuratowski limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternating singleton solution sets have outer limit containing both cluster points but empty inner limit, so no set limit exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}S_n=\varnothing\subsetneq\{0,1\}=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}S_n.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local boundedness and semicontinuity of a multifunction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines valuewise properties, local boundedness, outer and inner semicontinuity, and their closed-valued metric characterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multifunction $F:X\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n$ is bounded-valued, closed-valued, or convex-valued when every value $F(x)$ has the corresponding property. It is locally bounded near $x^*$ if there exist a neighborhood $N$ of $x^*$ and a bounded set $B\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $N\subset\operatorname{dom}F$ and $F(N)\subset B$. Under local boundedness, $F$ is outer semicontinuous at $x^*$ if $\limsup_{x\to x^*}F(x)\subseteq F(x^*)$, inner semicontinuous if $F(x^*)\subseteq\liminf_{x\to x^*}F(x)$, and continuous if both hold. If $F$ is also closed-valued, outer semicontinuity is equivalent to: for every $\varepsilon>0$, $F(x)\subseteq F(x^*)+B(0,\varepsilon)$ for all $x$ sufficiently near $x^*$, equivalently $e(F(x)/F(x^*))\leq\varepsilon$; inner semicontinuity is equivalently characterized by $F(x^*)\subseteq F(x)+B(0,\varepsilon)$, or $e(F(x^*)/F(x))\leq\varepsilon$. For single-valued $F$, both notions reduce to ordinary continuity at $x^*$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction inherits properties such as boundedness, closedness, or convexity value by value. It is locally bounded near a point when all nearby values are defined and lie in one bounded set. Outer semicontinuity requires every outer-limit point to belong to the value at the reference point; inner semicontinuity requires every point of that value to belong to the inner limit. Their conjunction is continuity. For closed-valued, locally bounded mappings, these conditions are equivalently expressed by one-sided set inclusions with arbitrarily small balls, or by the corresponding excess bounds. In the single-valued case they reduce to ordinary continuity.
assumptions_latex: \exists N\ni x^*,\ \exists B\subset\mathbb{R}^n\text{ bounded}:N\subset\operatorname{dom}F,\ F(N)\subset B
F\text{ closed-valued for the ball-inclusion and excess characterizations}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is continuous at }x^*\iff F\text{ is both outer and inner semicontinuous at }x^*.

children.title: Constraint Relaxation
children.top_down_role: Variational limits arising from enlargement or closure of constraint sets.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is the original constraint set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxed constraint is \(\overline C\), and the relaxation of \(I_C\) is \(I_{\overline C}\).

notation.meaning: Metric closure of the constraint set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: closure is the sequential relaxation of a constraint in a metric space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint relaxation is expressed through extended-real indicator functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(I_C:X\to\{0,+\infty\}\) by \(I_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(I_C(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Its lower-semicontinuous relaxation is
\[
\overline{I_C}(x)=I_{\overline C}(x),
\qquad
\overline C=\{x\in X:\exists x_n\in C,\ x_n\to x\}.
\]
Thus relaxing the constraint replaces exact feasibility in \(C\) by sequential attainability from \(C\), without changing the objective values assigned to feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing a constraint in a metric space replaces its feasible set by its closure, equivalently replacing its indicator by the indicator of that closure.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Relaxation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The metric-space closure and indicator-envelope identity is standard and the representation kind fits the leaf, but no inspectable citation or specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Distance-Penalty Constraint Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local exactness of a distance penalty for minimizing a Lipschitz function over a closed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed, and suppose \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) satisfies \(\operatorname{lip}f\le\kappa\) on \(C\). For every \(\lambda>\kappa\), there exists an open set \(O\supset C\) such that \(\operatorname{lip}f<\lambda\) on \(O\) and the distance-penalized problem is exact on \(O\): \(\inf_{x\in O}[f(x)+\lambda d_C(x)]=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\) and \(\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in O}[f(x)+\lambda d_C(x)]=\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a function has Lipschitz modulus at most kappa on a nonempty closed constraint set, then every distance-penalty coefficient strictly larger than kappa is locally exact on some open neighborhood of that set: both the infimum and the minimizer set agree with those of the constrained problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists O\supset C\text{ open}:\ \operatorname{lip}f<\lambda\text{ on }O,\quad \inf_O(f+\lambda d_C)=\inf_C f,\quad \operatorname{argmin}_O(f+\lambda d_C)=\operatorname{argmin}_C f

source_evidence.locator: Lipschitzian Properties / K*. Mollifiers and Extremals / Proposition 9.68

source_refs.locator: Lipschitzian Properties / K*. Mollifiers and Extremals / Proposition 9.68

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Distance-Penalty Constraint Relaxation

source_witnesses.locator: Lipschitzian Properties / K*. Mollifiers and Extremals / Proposition 9.68

directory_assessment.rationale: The similarly named listed Constraint Relaxation node concerns relaxation through variational set limits, not exact distance penalties. Canonical ownership should lie in general penalty and feasibility-globalization theory, with Lipschitzian properties serving only as supporting theory.

children.title: Admissible-Class Relaxation
children.top_down_role: Variational limits arising from enlargement or closure of admissible competitors.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\subset X\) is an admissible class and \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxed admissible class is \(\overline{\mathcal A}\), with attainable cost \(F_{\mathrm{rel}}\) defined by admissible recovery sequences.

notation.meaning: Relaxed cost restricted to admissible sequences

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sequential closure with admissible recovery costs is the standard relaxation construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition couples closure of admissibility with limiting objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The relaxed admissible class and its associated cost are
\[
\mathcal A_{\mathrm{rel}}:=\overline{\mathcal A},
\qquad
F_{\mathrm{rel}}(x):=\inf\left\{\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(x_n):x_n\in\mathcal A,\ x_n\to x\right\}.
\]
The infimum over the empty family is \(+\infty\). Hence \(x\) is relaxed-admissible exactly when it is a limit of original admissible points, while \(F_{\mathrm{rel}}(x)\) records the least asymptotic cost achievable along such points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The admissible class is enlarged to its closure, and each relaxed point receives the least limiting cost of admissible sequences converging to it.
knowledge_statements.title: Admissible-Class Relaxation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition coherently couples sequential closure with admissible limiting costs, but it has no source reference with a specific locator.

children.title: Feasibility-Limit Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interaction between set convergence of feasible regions and relaxed variational limits.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_n\to C\) in the Painlevé–Kuratowski sense if and only if \(I_{C_n}\) epi-converges to \(I_C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence is identified with epi-convergence of indicators.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The feasibility sets converge in the Painlevé–Kuratowski sense precisely when
\[
\operatorname{Li}C_n=C=\operatorname{Ls}C_n.
\]
Equivalently, their indicators epi-converge: for every \(x_n\to x\), \(\liminf_n I_{C_n}(x_n)\geq I_C(x)\), and for every \(x\in X\) there exists \(x_n\to x\) with \(\limsup_n I_{C_n}(x_n)\leq I_C(x)\). The recovery condition at \(x\in C\) is exactly asymptotic feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set convergence of feasible regions is equivalent to epi-convergence of their indicator functions; recovery sequences encode whether each limiting feasible point remains approximable.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Limit Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline F^{\tau_c}\leq\overline F^{\tau_f}\leq F\).

notation.meaning: Lower-semicontinuous envelope relative to topology tau

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: monotonicity follows from the topology-relative maximal-envelope characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares relaxation under nested topologies on the same underlying set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a topology \(\tau\), let
\[
\overline F^{\tau}:=\sup\{G:G\leq F\text{ and }G\text{ is }\tau\text{-lower semicontinuous}\}.
\]
If \(\tau_c\subseteq\tau_f\), every \(\tau_c\)-lower-semicontinuous functional is \(\tau_f\)-lower semicontinuous. Consequently,
\[
\overline F^{\tau_c}(x)\leq\overline F^{\tau_f}(x)\leq F(x)
\qquad\text{for every }x\in X.
\]
Thus a coarser topology generally produces a stronger relaxation because it admits more convergent nets or sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coarser topology imposes stronger lower-semicontinuity requirements, so its relaxed functional cannot exceed the envelope obtained with a finer topology.
knowledge_statements.title: Topology-Dependent Relaxation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The envelope monotonicity under nested topologies is standard, but no inspectable source is supplied. The statement also shifts between general topologies and sequential language without assuming sequential spaces, and it does not specify whether the envelope may take \(-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Approximate minimum values converge to \(\inf_XF\), and cluster points of approximate minimizers minimize \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental minimization consequence of metric Gamma-convergence and equicoercivity.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The relation \(F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\) means that every \(x_n\to x\) satisfies \(F(x)\leq\liminf_nF_n(x_n)\), while every \(x\in X\) admits a recovery sequence \(x_n\to x\) with \(F(x)\geq\limsup_nF_n(x_n)\). If \((F_n)\) is equicoercive and \(x_n\) satisfies
\[
F_n(x_n)\leq\inf_XF_n+\varepsilon_n,
\qquad \varepsilon_n\downarrow0,
\]
then every cluster point of \((x_n)\) minimizes \(F\), and \(\inf_XF_n\to\inf_XF\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equicoercive Gamma-limit is the effective relaxed model: minimum values converge, and cluster points of approximate minimizers solve the limiting problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Gamma-Limits as Relaxed Models

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited chapter-opening page on set convergence is not a sufficiently targeted locator for the fundamental theorem of Gamma-convergence. The record should also state the properness or finite-value hypothesis needed to obtain a uniform upper bound for approximate minima and make the minimization conclusion nondegenerate.

children.title: Penalization Limits
children.top_down_role: Variational limits generated by increasing penalties for constraint violations.

assumptions_latex: \(F,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are lower semicontinuous, \(g\geq0\), and \(F\) is finite wherever needed for recovery.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F+\lambda_ng\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F+I_C\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct Gamma-limit for a fixed nonnegative lower-semicontinuous violation function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed penalty function with a diverging multiplier; approximate penalties require additional scale conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(F_n:=F+\lambda_ng\). Then
\[
F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F+I_C.
\]
Indeed, the limiting functional equals \(F(x)\) when \(g(x)=0\) and \(+\infty\) when \(g(x)>0\). The Gamma-liminf assertion applies to every convergent sequence, while for \(x\in C\) the constant sequence is a recovery sequence. Thus diverging penalization converts positive constraint violation into infinite limiting cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying a fixed nonnegative violation function by a diverging parameter yields the hard-constrained functional as the Gamma-limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Penalization Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-penalty Gamma-limit is plausible under suitable lower-semicontinuity and properness assumptions, but the phrase 'finite wherever needed for recovery' is not a mathematical hypothesis and no source locator is supplied. The statement also includes proof-style justification that should be removed from a knowledge statement.

children.title: Regularization Limits
children.top_down_role: Variational limits generated by vanishing or changing regularization terms.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous and \(R:X\to[0,+\infty)\) is finite and continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F+\varepsilon_nR\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: vanishing nonnegative continuous perturbations preserve the Gamma-limit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing finite continuous regularization of an already lower-semicontinuous functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(F_n:=F+\varepsilon_nR\). For every \(x_n\to x\), nonnegativity of \(R\) and lower semicontinuity of \(F\) give
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}F_n(x_n)\geq F(x).
\]
For each \(x\in X\), the constant sequence satisfies \(F_n(x)=F(x)+\varepsilon_nR(x)\to F(x)\). Hence
\[
F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F.
\]
The regularizer may select among nearly minimizing states for finite \(n\), but it contributes no residual term to this Gamma-limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative finite continuous regularizer multiplied by a vanishing parameter does not change the Gamma-limit of a lower-semicontinuous functional.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularization Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vanishing nonnegative continuous perturbation property is mathematically standard and the property kind fits the leaf, but it lacks an inspectable citation. The liminf and constant-sequence argument is proof text rather than part of the terminal statement.

children.title: Parameter-Scale Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interactions among approximation scales, penalty weights, and regularization parameters.

assumptions_latex: \(F,g,R\) satisfy the hypotheses of the penalization and regularization limits.
\(\lambda_n\to+\infty\), \(\varepsilon_n\downarrow0\), and \(\varepsilon_nR(x_n)\to0\) along every required recovery sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F+\lambda_ng+\varepsilon_nR\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F+I_C\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: scale conditions separate hard-constraint enforcement from recovery-neutral regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient two-scale regime, not a necessary characterization of all coupled limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
F_n(x):=F(x)+\lambda_ng(x)+\varepsilon_nR(x),
\]
a sufficient hard-constraint regime is \(\lambda_n\to+\infty\), together with a recovery-neutral regime for regularization: for every \(x\in C\), there exists \(x_n\to x\) such that \(\lambda_ng(x_n)\to0\), \(\varepsilon_nR(x_n)\to0\), and \(F(x_n)\to F(x)\). Under the corresponding lower-bound hypotheses,
\[
F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F+I_C.
\]
Thus the relevant scale comparison is made along recovery sequences, not solely through the scalar product \(\lambda_n\varepsilon_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Penalty and regularization scales are compatible when constraint and regularization errors both vanish along recovery sequences while the penalty still excludes infeasible limits.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Scale Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record does not state a checkable theorem: 'required recovery sequence,' 'corresponding lower-bound hypotheses,' and the cross-reference to other records leave essential assumptions and quantifiers implicit. A source is needed to fix the intended two-scale result and its precise sufficient conditions.

children.title: Overpenalization Failure
children.top_down_role: Limit distortion caused by penalty scales that suppress relevant admissible behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(F_n(x)=\lambda_n(x^2+\delta_n)\), the Gamma-limit is identically \(+\infty\), not \(I_{\{0\}}\).

notation.meaning: Positive residual error in the penalty

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit scalar counterexample verified directly from the displayed inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure caused by amplification of a vanishing positive penalty residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
F_n(x):=\lambda_n\bigl(x^2+\delta_n\bigr).
\]
Although \(x^2+\delta_n\to x^2\) pointwise, every sequence \(x_n\to x\) satisfies
\[
F_n(x_n)\geq\lambda_n\delta_n\to+\infty.
\]
Consequently, \(F_n\) Gamma-converges to the functional identically equal to \(+\infty\), rather than to the intended hard-constraint indicator \(I_{\{0\}}\). The failure is caused by choosing the penalty scale so large that it amplifies the residual \(\delta_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diverging multiplier can amplify a vanishing positive penalty error, making every limiting state infinitely costly and destroying the intended constrained limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Overpenalization Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar counterexample is mathematically explicit and the counterexample kind is suitable for this failure leaf, but it has no inspectable source. The displayed lower-bound argument is proof text and should not remain in the final knowledge statement.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(X_h\subset X\) are discrete admissible sets.
Every \(x\in X\) has \(x_h\in X_h\) with \(x_h\to x\) and \(F(x_h)\to\overline F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_h\xrightarrow{\Gamma}\overline F\), where \(\overline F\) is the lower-semicontinuous relaxation of \(F\).

notation.meaning: Discrete admissible set at scale h

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract conforming discretization criterion with energy-accurate recovery sequences.

source_refs.locator: 7.1.2 Strong Convergence of Discrete Approximations p. 346
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose every sequence \(x_h\in X_h\) with \(x_h\to x\) satisfies \(\liminf_{h\to0}F(x_h)\geq\overline F(x)\), and every \(x\in X\) admits \(x_h\in X_h\) such that \(x_h\to x\) and \(F(x_h)\to\overline F(x)\). Then
\[
F_h:=F+I_{X_h}\xrightarrow{\Gamma}\overline F
\qquad\text{as }h\to0.
\]
Thus a discretization can converge to the relaxed functional rather than the unrelaxed pointwise model when discrete recovery sequences generate fine-scale oscillation or approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discretization whose discrete points realize the relaxed energy has the lower-semicontinuous envelope, rather than necessarily the original functional, as its Gamma-limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Discretization-Induced Relaxation

source_witnesses.locator: 7.1.2 Strong Convergence of Discrete Approximations p. 346
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited section on strong convergence of discrete approximations does not visibly support this abstract Gamma-convergence criterion. The parameter domain for \(h\to0\) is not specified, and the final explanatory sentence introduces an oscillation claim not implied by the stated assumptions. A directly supporting source and a precise indexing convention are required.

children.top_down_role: Navigation boundaries to the theories that identify or represent relaxed functionals.

children.title: Quasiconvex Envelopes
children.top_down_role: Envelope representations associated with quasiconvex relaxation.

assumptions_latex: \(W:\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and satisfies standard \(p\)-growth and coercivity for some \(1<p<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(QW\) is the greatest quasiconvex function below \(W\), under the stated growth hypotheses.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard cell formula for quasiconvexification under continuity and p-growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Morrey quasiconvexification for finite continuous integrands with standard polynomial growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quasiconvex envelope of \(W\) is represented by the cell formula
\[
QW(A):=\inf_{\varphi\in W^{1,p}_0(Q;\mathbb R^m)}
\int_Q W\bigl(A+\nabla\varphi(y)\bigr)\,dy,
\qquad A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}.
\]
Under the stated continuity and growth hypotheses, \(QW\leq W\), \(QW\) is quasiconvex, and every quasiconvex \(V:\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(V\leq W\) also satisfies \(V\leq QW\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quasiconvex envelope is obtained by minimizing the average density over zero-boundary microscopic gradient perturbations; it is the greatest quasiconvex minorant of the integrand.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvex Envelopes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the quasiconvex-envelope leaf, but the one-cell Sobolev formula and greatest-minorant conclusion require a source stating the exact continuity and p-growth hypotheses. 'Standard p-growth and coercivity' is too imprecise to validate the claimed formula without that citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Divergence-free cell formula for the quasiconvex envelope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quasiconvex-envelope representation governing the relaxation of the conductivity integrand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relaxation of the right-hand side of (3.101) is (3.100), and the relaxed integrand is the quasiconvex envelope of \(F\), given for \(Y=(0,1)^N\) by \[QF(\tau)=\inf_{\substack{\eta\in L_{\mu/k}(Y;\mathbb{R}^{nN})\\-\operatorname{div}\eta=0\text{ in }Y\\\int_Y\eta\,dx=0}}\int_Y F\bigl(\tau+\eta(x)\bigr)\,dx.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relaxed conductivity integrand is the quasiconvex envelope of F. It is represented by a unit-cell infimum over admissible divergence-free, zero-mean perturbations of the field, and this envelope gives the stated relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: QF(\tau)=\inf_{\substack{\eta\in L_{\mu/k}(Y;\mathbb{R}^{nN})\\-\operatorname{div}\eta=0\text{ in }Y\\\int_Y\eta\,dx=0}}\int_YF(\tau+\eta(x))\,dx,\quad\text{and this }QF\text{ gives the relaxation of (3.101).}

children.title: Lower-Semicontinuous Envelopes
children.top_down_role: Envelope representations associated with lower-semicontinuous relaxation.

assumptions_latex: \(W:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is bounded below by a finite constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W^{\mathrm{lsc}}\leq W\), and every lower-semicontinuous \(g\leq W\) satisfies \(g\leq W^{\mathrm{lsc}}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean lower-semicontinuous regularization of an extended-real integrand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The lower-semicontinuous envelope of \(W\) is the function
\[
W^{\mathrm{lsc}}(F):=\sup\{g(F):g:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is lower semicontinuous and }g\leq W\}.
\]
Equivalently, because \(\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is metrizable,
\[
W^{\mathrm{lsc}}(F)=\lim_{r\downarrow0}\inf\{W(G):|G-F|<r\}=\inf_{F_j\to F}\liminf_{j\to\infty}W(F_j).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-semicontinuous envelope is the greatest lower-semicontinuous function below the integrand, equivalently its local sequential liminf regularization.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Semicontinuous Envelopes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and sequential characterization are mathematically standard in the stated finite-dimensional metrizable setting, and the content kind fits the leaf. However, no inspectable source with a section, definition, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Envelope Coincidence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings where the relevant envelope constructions agree.

assumptions_latex: \(W:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) admits both a quasiconvex envelope and a lower-semicontinuous envelope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(QW=W^{\mathrm{lsc}}\) on \(\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\).

notation.meaning: Greatest quasiconvex minorant of the integrand.
Greatest lower-semicontinuous minorant of the integrand.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract coincidence criterion; concrete growth hypotheses depend on the relaxation theorem used.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quasiconvex and lower-semicontinuous envelopes are in a coincidence regime precisely when
\[
QW(F)=W^{\mathrm{lsc}}(F)\qquad\text{for every }F\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}.
\]
Equivalently, \(QW\) is lower semicontinuous and every lower-semicontinuous minorant \(g\leq W\) satisfies \(g\leq QW\). Thus the two envelope constructions select the same maximal minorant, even though their defining admissible classes differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coincidence occurs when the greatest quasiconvex minorant and greatest lower-semicontinuous minorant agree at every matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Coincidence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly describes coincidence as equality of the two specified maximal minorants, and condition is an appropriate content kind. A source is still required to establish the precise quasiconvex-envelope convention under which the equivalence is asserted.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex–Quasiconvex Envelope Coincidence for Plane Stress
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise coincidence and formulation-restriction result for three-dimensional plane stress with one zero and two nonzero eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\tau$ be a three-dimensional plane stress with eigenvalues $\tau_1,\tau_2,\tau_3$ satisfying $\tau_1=0$, $\tau_2\neq0$, and $\tau_3\neq0$. Then $QF(\tau)=CF(\tau)$, and the two-dimensional convexified formulation (5.51) is the plane-stress restriction of the three-dimensional true relaxed formulation (5.22).

The cited two-dimensional convexified formulation is the plane-stress restriction of the cited three-dimensional relaxed formulation.

children.title: Envelope Separation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings where quasiconvex and lower-semicontinuous envelope constructions differ.

assumptions_latex: \(W:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) has well-defined quasiconvex and lower-semicontinuous envelopes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{F:QW(F)\neq W^{\mathrm{lsc}}(F)\}\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise diagnostic for failure of envelope coincidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The envelope pair is in a separation regime when there exists \(F_0\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) such that
\[
QW(F_0)\neq W^{\mathrm{lsc}}(F_0).
\]
The separation set is
\[
S_W:=\{F\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}:QW(F)\neq W^{\mathrm{lsc}}(F)\}.
\]
Separation is strict on a set \(E\) when either \(QW<W^{\mathrm{lsc}}\) throughout \(E\) or \(W^{\mathrm{lsc}}<QW\) throughout \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separation occurs wherever the quasiconvex and lower-semicontinuous envelopes take different values; its direction must be stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Separation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise separation criterion matches the terminal container and is stated consistently, but it depends on envelope conventions for which no inspectable source is supplied. Concrete strict-separation directions likewise require sourced examples or hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(QW(F)=\inf_{\nu\in\mathcal{GY}_p(F)}\int W(A)\,d\nu(A)\).

notation.meaning: Homogeneous gradient p-Young measures with barycenter F.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous gradient Young-measure representation under standard coercive growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(F\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), let \(\mathcal{GY}_p(F)\) contain the homogeneous probability Young measures generated by \(L^p\)-bounded gradients and satisfying
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}}A\,d\nu(A)=F.
\]
Then the relaxed density is represented by
\[
QW(F)=\inf_{\nu\in\mathcal{GY}_p(F)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}}W(A)\,d\nu(A).
\]
The Dirac measure \(\delta_F\) is admissible, so \(QW(F)\leq W(F)\); non-Dirac measures encode oscillatory gradient microstructure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relaxed density minimizes the average original energy over homogeneous gradient Young measures having the prescribed matrix as barycenter.
knowledge_statements.title: Young-Measure Relaxation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits Young-Measure Relaxation and representation is the correct content kind. Its validity depends on the exact definition of homogeneous gradient p-Young measures, generation conditions, and growth/equi-integrability hypotheses; no authoritative locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of a Convex Superlinear Integrability Gauge
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted integrability bound for the measurable finite decomposition used in relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the measurable weights \(\bar c_i\) and selections \(\bar q_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,m+1\), arising in the relaxation construction, there exists an increasing convex function \(\psi:[0,+\infty)\to\overline{\mathbb R}_+\) such that \(\lim_{t\to\infty}\psi(t)/t=+\infty\) and \(\int_\Omega\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\bar c_i(x)\,\psi(g(x,\bar q_i(x)))\,dx<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite relaxed mixture admits an increasing convex gauge growing faster than linearly for which the weighted gauge integral of the component controls is finite.
assumptions_latex: (\bar c_i,\bar q_i)_{i=1}^{m+1}\text{ are the measurable mixture data of the relaxation construction.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,\psi\text{ increasing and convex},\quad \frac{\psi(t)}{t}\to+\infty,\quad \int_\Omega\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\bar c_i\,\psi\!\circ g(x,\bar q_i)\,dx<+\infty.

children.title: Rank-One Convexity Interface
children.top_down_role: Connections between variational limits, rank-one convex envelopes, and admissible microstructures.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W((1-t)F+tG)\leq(1-t)W(F)+tW(G)\) whenever \(\operatorname{rank}(F-G)\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued rank-one convexity for matrix integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The integrand \(W\) is rank-one convex if, for every \(F,G\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(F-G)\leq1\), the function
\[
t\longmapsto W((1-t)F+tG)
\]
is convex on \([0,1]\). Equivalently, for every \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
W((1-t)F+tG)\leq(1-t)W(F)+tW(G).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrand is rank-one convex when its restriction to every line in a rank-one matrix direction is convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-One Convexity Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-valued rank-one convexity condition is standard, internally consistent, and appropriate for the leaf. It lacks the required authoritative source and specific locator.

children.title: Quasiconvexity Interface
children.top_down_role: Connections between set convergence, quasiconvex relaxation, and oscillatory minimizing behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(W:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}\) is Borel measurable and locally bounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W(F)\leq |D|^{-1}\int_D W(F+\nabla\varphi(x))\,dx\) for every admissible perturbation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Morrey quasiconvexity tested by compactly supported gradient perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The integrand \(W\) is quasiconvex if, for every bounded Lipschitz domain \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), every \(F\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and every \(\varphi\in W^{1,\infty}_0(D;\mathbb{R}^m)\),
\[
W(F)\leq\frac{1}{|D|}\int_D W(F+\nabla\varphi(x))\,dx.
\]
It suffices, under the usual domain-independence hypotheses, to test this inequality on one fixed cube.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasiconvexity says that no zero-boundary gradient oscillation can lower the average energy below the value at the mean gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvexity Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed inequality is a standard quasiconvexity formulation, but the admissible test space, integrability convention, quantification over domains, and fixed-cube reduction require source support. No citation is supplied.

children.title: Polyconvexity Interface
children.top_down_role: Connections between variational limits, polyconvex representations, and relaxed energies.

assumptions_latex: \(W:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is an extended-real matrix integrand.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W=g\circ\mathcal{M}\) for some convex lower-semicontinuous \(g\).

notation.meaning: Vector of all minors of F, including first-order minors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard minors-based representation of polyconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{M}(F)\) denote the vector consisting of all minors of \(F\) of orders \(1,\ldots,\min\{m,n\}\). The integrand \(W\) is polyconvex if there exists a convex lower-semicontinuous function
\[
g:\mathbb{R}^{N(m,n)}\to(-\infty,+\infty]
\]
such that
\[
W(F)=g(\mathcal{M}(F))\qquad\text{for every }F\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix integrand is polyconvex when it is a convex function of all matrix minors.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyconvexity Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minors representation fits the leaf, but requiring the representing convex function to be lower semicontinuous is convention-sensitive, especially for extended-real integrands. An authoritative source is needed to determine whether this is the intended definition or an overstated regularity requirement.

children.title: Convexity Implication Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Navigation across implication relations among the three convexity notions.

assumptions_latex: \(W:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite-valued and the four notions use their standard matrix-integrand definitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{Convex}\Rightarrow\mathrm{Polyconvex}\Rightarrow\mathrm{Quasiconvex}\Rightarrow\mathrm{RankOneConvex}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical implication chain for finite-valued matrix integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite-valued integrands on \(\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), the generalized convexity notions satisfy
\[
W\text{ convex}\Longrightarrow W\text{ polyconvex}\Longrightarrow W\text{ quasiconvex}\Longrightarrow W\text{ rank-one convex}.
\]
Consequently, failure of rank-one convexity rules out all three stronger properties, while rank-one convexity alone does not supply any reverse implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity implies polyconvexity, which implies quasiconvexity, which in turn implies rank-one convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Implication Hierarchy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implication direction is the classical one and theorem is the correct mathematical role for this leaf. The precise value-range and regularity conventions, particularly those inherited from the polyconvexity record, need an authoritative theorem locator.

children.title: Strict Separation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where the convexity notions yield distinct envelopes or relaxation outcomes.

assumptions_latex: \(m,n\in\mathbb{N}\) are fixed, and \(\mathcal{C}_{m,n},\mathcal{P}_{m,n},\mathcal{Q}_{m,n},\mathcal{R}_{m,n}\) are, under identical value-range and regularity conventions, the convex, polyconvex, quasiconvex, and rank-one convex integrands on \(\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Witnesses in \(\mathcal{P}_{m,n}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{m,n}\), \(\mathcal{Q}_{m,n}\setminus\mathcal{P}_{m,n}\), and \(\mathcal{R}_{m,n}\setminus\mathcal{Q}_{m,n}\) certify \(\mathcal{C}_{m,n}\subsetneq\mathcal{P}_{m,n}\subsetneq\mathcal{Q}_{m,n}\subsetneq\mathcal{R}_{m,n}\).

notation.meaning: Convex, polyconvex, quasiconvex, and rank-one convex integrand classes on the fixed matrix space, respectively.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Witness certificate for strict adjacent inclusions on one fixed matrix space and under common regularity conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(m,n\), strictness of the complete implication hierarchy is certified by integrands \(W_1,W_2,W_3\) satisfying
\[
W_1\in\mathcal{P}_{m,n}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{m,n},\qquad W_2\in\mathcal{Q}_{m,n}\setminus\mathcal{P}_{m,n},\qquad W_3\in\mathcal{R}_{m,n}\setminus\mathcal{Q}_{m,n}.
\]
When these witnesses exist under the same value-range and regularity conventions,
\[
\mathcal{C}_{m,n}\subsetneq\mathcal{P}_{m,n}\subsetneq\mathcal{Q}_{m,n}\subsetneq\mathcal{R}_{m,n}.
\]
A witness in another matrix dimension certifies only the corresponding dimension-specific separation and cannot establish this entire fixed-dimension chain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For one fixed matrix dimension and common regularity conventions, witnesses in each successive larger class certify that convex, polyconvex, quasiconvex, and rank-one convex integrands form a strictly increasing chain.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Separation Regimes

assumptions_latex: \(X\subset Y\) are nonempty admissible classes, \(\mathcal{F}:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and both infima \(\inf_{u\in X}\mathcal{F}(u)\) and \(\inf_{u\in Y}\mathcal{F}(u)\) are finite real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(\mathcal{F};X,Y):=\inf_{u\in X}\mathcal{F}(u)-\inf_{u\in Y}\mathcal{F}(u)>0\).

notation.meaning: Finite difference between the two variational infima.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of energy approximation between a more regular admissible class and a larger ambient class, with finite variational infima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The functional \(\mathcal{F}\) exhibits a Lavrentiev gap between \(X\) and \(Y\) when
\[
L(\mathcal{F};X,Y):=\inf_{u\in X}\mathcal{F}(u)-\inf_{u\in Y}\mathcal{F}(u)>0.
\]
Here both infima are assumed finite, so the difference is well defined. Typically, \(X\) is a more regular subclass of \(Y\); the strict inequality records failure of approximation in energy by elements of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lavrentiev gap is a positive, well-defined difference between finite energy infima over a regular admissible class and a larger ambient class.
knowledge_statements.title: Lavrentiev Gap

children.title: Approximation Limit
children.top_down_role: Approximation-driven limiting behavior prior to variational relaxation.

assumptions_latex: \((Z,\tau)\) is a metrizable topological space and \(\mathcal{F}_\varepsilon:Z\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{F}_\varepsilon\xrightarrow{\Gamma(\tau)}\mathcal{F}_0\).

notation.meaning: Approximate energies indexed by a vanishing parameter.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential Gamma-limit in a fixed metrizable topology.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The approximation limit of \((\mathcal{F}_\varepsilon)\) in \(\tau\) is \(\mathcal{F}_0\) when, for every \(z\in Z\):
\[
z_\varepsilon\to_\tau z\Longrightarrow \mathcal{F}_0(z)\leq\liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathcal{F}_\varepsilon(z_\varepsilon),
\]
and there exists a recovery family \(\widehat z_\varepsilon\to_\tau z\) such that
\[
\mathcal{F}_0(z)\geq\limsup_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathcal{F}_\varepsilon(\widehat z_\varepsilon).
\]
These two conditions define \(\Gamma(\tau)\)-convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The approximation limit is the Gamma-limit characterized by a liminf inequality and a recovery family in the chosen topology.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximation Limit

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The liminf and recovery-family conditions express a standard Gamma-convergence definition and fit the Approximation Limit leaf. However, the cited locator is only Chapter 4, Set Convergence, page 108 of Rockafellar-Wets and does not specifically identify a Gamma-convergence definition or theorem supporting this epsilon-indexed formulation. A directly supporting source is required.

children.title: Relaxation Limit
children.top_down_role: Relaxation-driven limiting behavior prior to approximation.

assumptions_latex: \((Z,\tau)\) is metrizable and \(\mathcal{F}:Z\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is bounded below by a finite constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Relax}_\tau\mathcal{F}\) is the greatest sequentially \(\tau\)-lower-semicontinuous functional below \(\mathcal{F}\).

notation.meaning: Sequential relaxation of the functional in topology τ.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential lower-semicontinuous relaxation in a fixed metrizable topology.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The relaxation limit of \(\mathcal{F}\) with respect to \(\tau\) is
\[
(\operatorname{Relax}_\tau\mathcal{F})(z):=\inf\left\{\liminf_{j\to\infty}\mathcal{F}(z_j):z_j\to_\tau z\right\}.
\]
It satisfies \(\operatorname{Relax}_\tau\mathcal{F}\leq\mathcal{F}\), is sequentially \(\tau\)-lower semicontinuous, and dominates every sequentially \(\tau\)-lower-semicontinuous functional \(\mathcal{G}\) satisfying \(\mathcal{G}\leq\mathcal{F}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relaxation limit is the greatest lower-semicontinuous functional below the original energy, obtained by minimizing sequential liminf costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Limit

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential lower-semicontinuous-envelope formula is standard in a metrizable topology and matches the Relaxation Limit leaf. The supplied Chapter 4, page 108 locator does not specifically identify this relaxation formula or maximal-minorant property, so the citation is insufficient for candidate review.

children.title: Approximation-First Regime
children.top_down_role: Outcomes associated with taking the approximation limit before relaxation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{AF}}=\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\bigl(\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{n\to\infty}F_{n,\varepsilon}\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential \(\Gamma\)-convergence formulation with approximation index removed before the relaxation parameter.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), first form the approximation limit \(F^{\mathrm A}_{\varepsilon}:=\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{n\to\infty}F_{n,\varepsilon}\). The approximation-first effective energy is then defined by
\[
F_{\mathrm{AF}}:=\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}F^{\mathrm A}_{\varepsilon}=\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\left(\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{n\to\infty}F_{n,\varepsilon}\right).
\]
Thus discretization or approximation is eliminated while the relaxation scale remains fixed, and only afterward is the relaxation limit taken.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The approximation-first energy is obtained by taking the approximation Γ-limit at each fixed relaxation scale, then sending the relaxation parameter to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-First Regime

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but the cited general set-convergence page does not inspectably support this specific approximation-first construction or its interpretation.

children.title: Relaxation-First Regime
children.top_down_role: Outcomes associated with taking the relaxation limit before approximation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{RF}}=\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{n\to\infty}\bigl(\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}F_{n,\varepsilon}\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential \(\Gamma\)-convergence formulation with relaxation performed at every fixed approximation level.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each fixed \(n\in\mathbb N\), first form the relaxation limit \(F^{\mathrm R}_{n}:=\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}F_{n,\varepsilon}\). The relaxation-first effective energy is then defined by
\[
F_{\mathrm{RF}}:=\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{n\to\infty}F^{\mathrm R}_{n}=\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{n\to\infty}\left(\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}F_{n,\varepsilon}\right).
\]
Thus relaxation is completed at every approximation level before the approximation index is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relaxation-first energy is obtained by relaxing at each fixed approximation level and then taking the approximation Γ-limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-First Regime

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent and fits the leaf, but specific support for interpreting the inner epsilon limit as relaxation and taking it before approximation is not inspectable from the cited locator.

children.title: Limit Commutation Criteria
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions separating commuting limit regimes from order-sensitive regimes.

assumptions_latex: Painlevé--Kuratowski inner and outer limits are taken in \(X\times\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both iterated epigraph limits equal \(E\), so \(F_{\mathrm{AF}}=F_{\mathrm{RF}}\).

notation.meaning: Painlevé--Kuratowski inner and outer set limits

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient epigraphical criterion for commuting approximation and relaxation limits.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sufficient commutation criterion is the existence of a closed set \(E\subset X\times\mathbb R\) such that
\[
\operatorname{Li}_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\operatorname{Li}_{n\to\infty}E_{n,\varepsilon}=
\operatorname{Ls}_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\operatorname{Ls}_{n\to\infty}E_{n,\varepsilon}=
\operatorname{Li}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{Li}_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}E_{n,\varepsilon}=
\operatorname{Ls}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{Ls}_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}E_{n,\varepsilon}=E.
\]
If \(E=\operatorname{epi}F\), both iterated epigraphical limits exist and determine the same lower semicontinuous energy \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limits commute when the inner and outer epigraph limits coincide with one closed epigraph in both orders.
knowledge_statements.title: Limit Commutation Criteria

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed equalities do not transparently guarantee existence of the required intermediate epigraph limits. A source stating this precise sufficient criterion, including its hypotheses, is required.

children.title: Order-Sensitive Relaxed Energies
children.top_down_role: Variational consequences produced by distinct orders of approximation and relaxation.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is metrizable and all displayed sequential \(\Gamma\)-limits exist.
\(F_{\mathrm{AF}}\) and \(F_{\mathrm{RF}}\) are the two iterated effective energies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Order sensitivity occurs exactly when \(F_{\mathrm{AF}}\not\equiv F_{\mathrm{RF}}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary defined by noncommutation of two sequential variational limits.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The family \((F_{n,\varepsilon})\) has order-sensitive relaxed energies when
\[
F_{\mathrm{AF}}:=\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{n\to\infty}F_{n,\varepsilon}
\quad\text{and}\quad
F_{\mathrm{RF}}:=\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{n\to\infty}\Gamma\!\operatorname{-lim}_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}F_{n,\varepsilon}
\]
are not identical. Equivalently, there exists \(x\in X\) with \(F_{\mathrm{AF}}(x)\ne F_{\mathrm{RF}}(x)\). Equality of minimum values alone does not establish commutation; equality is required as extended-real functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxed energies are order-sensitive when reversing approximation and relaxation produces different extended-real functionals, even if their minimum values happen to agree.
knowledge_statements.title: Order-Sensitive Relaxed Energies

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary is internally correct and the content kind fits, but the cited general set-convergence locator does not inspectably support this specialized pair of iterated relaxation energies.

children.title: Compactness Loss
children.top_down_role: Failure regimes where admissible or minimizing sequences lack the required precompactness.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space with an orthonormal sequence \((e_n)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n(e_n)=1\), but \((e_n)\) has no strongly convergent subsequence.

notation.meaning: orthonormal sequence witnessing loss of strong compactness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-topology compactness can fail despite uniform boundedness of energy and norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be infinite-dimensional and let \((e_n)\) be orthonormal. For the constant family \(F_n(x):=\lVert x\rVert_H^2\), one has \(F_n(e_n)=1\) for every \(n\). Moreover, \(\lVert e_n-e_m\rVert_H=\sqrt{2}\) whenever \(n\ne m\). Hence the bounded-energy sequence \((e_n)\) contains no strongly convergent subsequence, demonstrating compactness loss in the strong topology even though \((e_n)\) is bounded and converges weakly to \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthonormal sequence has uniformly bounded quadratic energy but no strongly convergent subsequence, exhibiting loss of compactness in infinite dimension.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Loss

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hilbert-space counterexample is mathematically standard and fits Compactness Loss, but it has no citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Concentration Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms producing localization of energy, mass, or variation along limiting sequences.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_k\rightharpoonup0\) in \(L^p\), while \(|u_k|^p\,dx\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}\delta_0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mass concentration under norm-preserving dilation in \(L^p(\mathbb R^d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The dilation \(u_k(x):=k^{d/p}\varphi(kx)\) preserves mass: \(\lVert u_k\rVert_{L^p}=1\). Its support shrinks to the origin, and \(u_k\rightharpoonup0\) in \(L^p(\mathbb R^d)\). Nevertheless, for every \(\psi\in C_c(\mathbb R^d)\),
\[
\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(x)|u_k(x)|^p\,dx\longrightarrow\psi(0).
\]
Thus \(|u_k|^p\,dx\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}\delta_0\), while strong convergence to \(0\) is impossible because the norms remain one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Norm-preserving dilations converge weakly to zero while their energy densities collapse to a Dirac mass, producing concentration without strong compactness.
knowledge_statements.title: Concentration Mechanisms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The norm-preserving concentration example is correct for 1<p<infinity and fits the leaf, but no source is supplied.

children.title: Equicoercivity Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of uniform coercive control across a converging family of functionals.

knowledge_statements.title: Equicoercivity Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization of failure of equicoercivity in a metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The family \((F_n)\) is not equicoercive precisely when there exists \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) for which
\[
K_\alpha:=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}\{x\in X:F_n(x)\le\alpha\}
\]
is not relatively compact. Equivalently, there exist sequences \((m_j)\subset\mathbb N\) and \((x_j)\subset X\) such that \(F_{m_j}(x_j)\le\alpha\) for every \(j\), while \((x_j)\) has no convergent subsequence in \(X\). The indices \((m_j)\) need not be distinct or tend to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equicoercivity fails when some common level union contains a sequence with no convergent subsequence; the energy indices associated with that sequence need not increase.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(F_n:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) for \(n\in\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equicoercivity fails if and only if, for some \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), there are \(m_j\in\mathbb N\) and \(x_j\in X\) with \(F_{m_j}(x_j)\le\alpha\) such that \((x_j)\) has no convergent subsequence.

notation.meaning: energy indices associated with the selected level-set points

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sequential characterization of relative compactness in metric spaces

children.title: Concentration Defects
children.top_down_role: Residual limiting effects not captured by the ordinary weak limit.

assumptions_latex: \(1<p<\infty\), \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is open, and \(u_k\rightharpoonup u\) in \(L^p(\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu:=\mu-|u|^p\,dx\) is a nonnegative Radon measure.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weak lower semicontinuity against nonnegative compactly supported weights
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure representation of energy not carried by the weak \(L^p\) limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Weak lower semicontinuity gives \(\mu\ge |u|^p\,dx\) as Radon measures. Consequently the concentration defect is represented by
\[
\nu:=\mu-|u|^p\,dx\ge0,
\qquad
\mu=|u|^p\,dx+\nu.
\]
For every nonnegative \(\psi\in C_c(\Omega)\), this means \(\int_\Omega\psi\,d\nu=\lim_k\int_\Omega\psi|u_k|^p\,dx-\int_\Omega\psi|u|^p\,dx\ge0\). An atom \(\nu(\{x\})>0\) records energy concentrated at \(x\) but absent from the weak limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The excess of the limiting energy measure over the weak limit’s density is a nonnegative defect measure; its atoms quantify point concentration.
knowledge_statements.title: Concentration Defects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the stated weak and measure convergence assumptions, the nonnegative defect-measure representation is mathematically sound and fits the leaf, but no source is supplied.

children.title: Escape from Bounded Domains
children.top_down_role: Loss of compactness through mass or energy moving beyond controlled spatial regions.

assumptions_latex: \(u_k(x):=\varphi(x-ke_1)\), where \(e_1\) is the first coordinate vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local mass vanishes, total mass is fixed, and \((u_k)\) is not relatively compact in \(L^p(\mathbb R^d)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of tightness by translation to spatial infinity on an unbounded domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Translations preserve the norm, so \(\lVert u_k\rVert_{L^p}=\lVert\varphi\rVert_{L^p}>0\). For every bounded set \(B\subset\mathbb R^d\), one has \(u_k=0\) on \(B\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), and hence
\[
\int_B|u_k|^p\,dx\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus all mass escapes every bounded region while total mass remains fixed. The family \((|u_k|^p\,dx)\) is not tight, and \((u_k)\) has no strongly convergent subsequence in \(L^p(\mathbb R^d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translating a fixed compactly supported profile to infinity preserves total mass but removes it from every bounded region, destroying tightness and strong compactness.
knowledge_statements.title: Escape from Bounded Domains

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The translation example correctly demonstrates escape of mass and failure of strong compactness on an unbounded domain, but it lacks a cited source and locator.
